Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 26, verse 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾. When He finished mentioning their performance of acts of obedience, He began to explain their avoidance of acts of disobedience, so He said: "And those who do not invoke with Allah, glorified is He, any lord among the lords."

The meaning: they do not associate anything with Him, but rather they affirm His oneness and devote worship and supplication sincerely to Him. ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾, meaning: He has forbidden its killing except by right, that is, by that for which souls may rightly be killed: disbelief after belief, or fornication after being chaste (ihsan), or killing a soul without a soul (qisas). ﴿Nor do they commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾, meaning: they do not make lawful the forbidden private parts without marriage (nikah) or ownership of the right hand (milk al-yamin). ﴿And whoever does that﴾, meaning: any of what has been mentioned, ﴿will meet a penalty (athaman) in the Hereafter﴾. The athām in the speech of the Arabs means: punishment. Al-Farra' said: Allah "athamahu" (yu'thimuhu) athaman and athaman, meaning: He requited him with the recompense of sin. Ikrimah and Mujahid said: "Athaman" is a valley in Hell which Allah made a punishment for the disbelievers. As-Suddi said: it is a mountain within it. It was recited as (yulaqq) with a damma on the ya' and a shadda on the qaf. Abu Muslim said: athaman and ithm are one and the same, and what is meant here is the recompense of sins, so the name of the thing was applied to its recompense.

Al-Hasan recited (yalqa ayyaman), the plural of yawm, meaning hardships; the Arabs express that by "days," and I do not think this recitation is authentically transmitted from him. ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him﴾. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited yudda'af and yakhlud with the jazm; Ibn Kathir recited (yudda'af) with a shadda on the 'ain, dropping the alif, and with the jazm; Talhah ibn Sulayman recited (nudda'if) with a damma on the nun, a kasra on the shadded 'ain, and the jazm, and this is the recitation of Abu Ja'far and Shaybah.

'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, recited with the raf' in both verbs, by way of resumption (isti'naf).

Talhah ibn Sulayman recited (wa-takhlud) with the feminine second person, addressing the disbeliever.

It is narrated from Abu 'Amr that he recited (wa-yukhlad) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the lam.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: this is an error from the standpoint of transmission. The reason for the jazm in (yudda'af) is that it is a substitute (badal) for (yalqa), because the two are unified in meaning, and similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed upon me is Allah's (covenant) that you pledge allegiance, you will be seized unwillingly or you will come willingly."

The pronoun in His saying (yakhlud) fihi refers to the doubled punishment, meaning: he will abide in the doubled punishment, humiliated, abased, despised.

﴿Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds﴾. It was said this is an exceptive (istithna' muttasil), and it was said it is disjunctive (munqati').

Abu Hayyan said: connection does not appear, because the one excepted from is judged as being one for whom the punishment is doubled, so the sense becomes: except those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds, then the punishment is not doubled for them; and the negation of doubling does not necessitate the negation of the punishment that is not doubled.

He said: What is preferable in my view is that it is disjunctive, meaning: but whoever repents.

Al-Qurtubi said: There is no disagreement among the scholars that the exception is general, covering the disbeliever and the fornicator. They differed concerning the Muslim killer, and its explanation has already preceded in al-Nisa' and al-Ma'idah.

The indication in His saying: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ refers to those mentioned previously. The meaning of the replacement of evil deeds with good deeds is that He erases their sins and establishes in their place acts of obedience.

Al-Nahhas said: Among the best of what has been said about this is that where a disbeliever was written, a believer is written, and where a disobedient one was, an obedient one is written. Al-Hasan said: some people say: the replacement is in the Hereafter, and that is not so; rather the replacement is in this world: Allah replaces for them faith in place of polytheism, sincerity in place of doubt, and chastity in place of immorality.

Al-Zajjaj said: He does not make a good deed in place of an evil deed, but He makes repentance in place of an evil deed, and a good deed along with repentance.

It was said: evil deeds are replaced by good deeds, and this was the view of a group of the Companions and those after them.

It was said: replacement is an expression for forgiveness, meaning Allah forgives them those evil deeds, not that He replaces them with good deeds. It was said: what is meant by replacement is that He enables him to the opposites of what had previously occurred from him. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾. This sentence confirms what came before it concerning the replacement.

﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he returns to Allah with a (sincere) return﴾, meaning: whoever repents from what he committed and does a righteous deed after that, then he returns by that to Allah with a (sincere) return, meaning: he returns to Him with a sound, strong return.

Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that the first verse concerns those who repent from the polytheists, which is why He said: ﴿except those who repent and believe﴾; then He conjoined to it those who repent from the Muslims and follow their repentance with righteous deeds, so they too have the ruling of the repentant.

It was said: meaning (p-1050) whoever repents with his tongue but does not realize the repentance with his action, that repentance is not beneficial; rather whoever repents and does righteous deeds, realizing his repentance through righteous works, is the one who truly returns to Allah with a return, meaning: he repents with the true repentance, which is sincere (nasuh), and for this reason it is emphasized with the verbal noun. The meaning of the verse: whoever wishes to repent and resolves upon it, let him turn to Allah. So the statement is in the sense of a command. This was said so that the condition and the consequent would not be identical, for one does not say of one who repents: "then indeed he returns."

Then Allah, glorified is He, described these repentant ones who do righteous deeds, saying: ﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾, meaning they do not bear false testimony, or they do not attend falsehood. Falsehood (zur) is lying and vanity, and they do not witness it. Jumhur al-mufassirin went to the second meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: zur in the language means lying, and there is no lying worse than associating partners with Allah.

Al-Wahidi said: most of the exegetes hold that zur here means polytheism.

The summary is that (yashhadun), if it is from testimony (shahadah), then there is an elided genitive in the speech, meaning: they do not bear the testimony of falsehood; and if it is from attendance (shuhud), meaning presence, as the majority went, then they differed about its meaning. Qatadah said: they do not assist the people of falsehood in their falsehood. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: they do not attend idle talk and singing. Ibn Juraij said: lying.

It is also narrated from Mujahid. The preferable view is not to restrict it to one kind of falsehood, but rather the meaning is those who do not attend anything that truly bears the name of falsehood, whoever it may be. ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾, meaning: turning away from it, not inclining toward it. Lagh is every worthless utterance or deed.

Al-Hasan said: lagh is all sins. It was said: what is meant is they pass by people of idle talk; it is said: "So-and-so is honored above what disgraces him," meaning: he keeps himself pure and honors himself from entering into idle talk and mixing with its people.

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord﴾, meaning with the Qur'an, or with what in it is admonition and lesson, ﴿do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾, meaning: they do not fall upon them while being deaf and blind, but rather they attend to them, hearing and seeing, and benefit from them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is they do not neglect them, as if they were deaf who did not hear them, and blind who did not see them.

Ibn Jarir said: there is no falling here; rather it is like the saying "he sat weeping," though he is not sitting.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is as if the listener to the reminder is standing, so when he turns away from it, that is a falling, which is collapse without order.

It was said the meaning is: when the verses of Allah are recited to them, their hearts tremble, and they fall down prostrating and weeping, and do not fall upon them deaf and blind.

Al-Farra' said: meaning they do not remain in their former state as if they had not heard.

In al-Kashshaf he said: it is not a negation of the falling; rather it is an affirmation of it and a negation of deafness and blindness, and he meant that the negation is directed at the qualifier, not at the qualified.

﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort of the eyes"﴾. (Min) is either inceptive (ibtida'iyyah) or explanatory (bayaniyyah).

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan recited ﴿wa-dhurriyyatina﴾ in the plural; Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Talhah and 'Isa recited (wa-dhurriyyatina) in the singular. Dhurriyyah is used for the plural, as in His saying: ﴿dhurriyyatan di'afa'﴾ [al-Nisa' 9], and used for the singular, as in His saying: ﴿dhurriyyatan tayyibah﴾ [Al 'Imran 38]. Qurrata a'yun is in the accusative as an object; it is said: "qarrat 'aynuhu qurratan" (his eye became cool).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "Allah cool your eye," meaning: your heart encounters what it loves.

Al-Mufaddal said: regarding qurrat al-'ayn there are three views: the first is the coolness of its tears, because that is a sign of joy and laughter, just as their heat is a sign of sorrow and grief. The second is its sleep, because that occurs with the leisure of the mind and the departure of sorrow. The third is the attainment of contentment.

﴿And make us leaders for the righteous﴾, meaning: examples who are followed in goodness. He said "imaman" and did not say "a'immah" because it is intended as a genus, like His saying: ﴿then We bring you out as a child﴾ [al-Hajj 5]. Al-Farra' said: He said "imaman" and did not say "a'immah," just as He said for the two: ﴿indeed we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 16], meaning that it is a singular used with the sense of the plural.

Al-Akhfash said: imam is the plural of umm, from amma yaummu, a plural on the pattern fi'al, like sahib and sihab, and qa'im and qiyam.

It was said: imaman is a verbal noun; it is said "amma fulanun fulanan imaman," like siyam and qiyam.

It was said: they meant: make each one of us an imam. It was said: they meant: make us one imam, due to the unity of our word. It was said: it is from the inverted speech, and the meaning is: make the righteous an imam for us; this was the view of Mujahid.

It was said: this supplication issued from them individually, and that the expression of each one of them at the supplication was: "make me an imam for the righteous," but the expressions of all were related in the first-person plural form for the sake of brevity, like His saying: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Mu'minun 51]. In this, "imaman" remains in its state. Similar to what is in the verse is the saying of the poet:

"O my blamers, do not increase my reproach; indeed the blamers are not trustworthy to me,"

meaning: trustworthy ones (umana'). Al-Qaffal said: in my view, when imam is treated as a name, it is made singular, as if it were said: make us a proof (hujjah) for the righteous, and similarly bayyinah: one says "these are the bayyinah of so-and-so." Al-Naysaburi said: it was said that the verse indicates that religious leadership is among the things that should be sought and desired; the closer view is that they asked Allah to bring them in obedience to the degree by which they would be pointed to and followed.

The indication in His saying: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber for what they endured﴾ refers to those described with those attributes. It is the subject, and its predicate is what follows, and the sentences are independent (mustanfah).

It was said: "Those" and what follows is a predicate of His saying: ﴿and the servants of the Most Merciful﴾; so said al-Zajjaj. Al-ghurfah is the high rank, which is the highest and best of the dwellings of Paradise; in origin it applies to any elevated building, and its plural is ghuraf.

Al-Dahhak said: al-ghurfah is Paradise. The ba' in ﴿for what they endured﴾ is causal, and ma is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: they are rewarded the high chamber because of their patience in the hardships of obligation.

﴿And they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾. Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited (yalqawna) with a fatha on the ya' and sukun on the lam and lightened qaf; al-Farra' chose this recitation, saying: because the Arabs say: "so-and-so yulqi with greetings, peace and good," and they seldom say yulqi. The rest recited with a damma on the ya' and fatha on the lam and shadda on the qaf, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this recitation because of His saying: ﴿and He gave them radiance and joy﴾. The meaning is that they greet one another, and the Lord, glorified is He, sends to them greetings of peace. It was said: al-tahiyyah is lasting survival and great dominion; it was said: it is (p-1051) the same meaning as salam; it was said: the angels greet them and give them peace. The apparent view is that this greeting and peace are from Allah, glorified is He, to them, and of this is His saying: ﴿their greeting on the day they meet Him is peace﴾ [al-Ahzab 44]. It was said: the meaning of tahiyyah is the supplication for them of long life. The meaning of salam is the supplication for them of safety from calamities.

The accusative of *khalidina* (﻿خالِدِينَ) here is a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: abiding therein, remaining there without dying.

﴿Excellent is it as a place of settling and dwelling﴾, meaning the chamber was excellent as a place where they settle and a place where they dwell. This is in contrast to His earlier words: ﴿Evil is it as a place of settling and dwelling﴾ [al-Furqan: 66].

﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication."﴾ He, glorified is He, explains that He is free of need for the obedience of all, and that He imposed obligations only so that people might benefit from them. It is said: *mā ʿabaʾtu bi-fulān* (ما عَبَأْتُ بِفُلانٍ), meaning: I did not care for him, and he had no weight in my estimation. The root of *yaʿbaʾu* (يَعْبَأُ) is *al-ʿibʾ* (العِبْءُ), meaning burden or weight.

Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) said: *mā aʿbaʾu bi-fulān* means "I do nothing with him," as if he considers him insignificant and contemptible, and claims that his existence and non-existence are the same. Abu ʿUbayda also said likewise.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿What does my Lord care for you﴾ means: what weight do you have in His sight? *Al-ʿibʾ* is weight, and (*mā*) (ما) is either interrogative or negative. Al-Farra' stated explicitly that it is interrogative. Ibn al-Shajari said: The true position in my view is that the place of (*mā*) is accusative, and the meaning is: what weight does He give you, i.e., what concern does He have for you?

﴿Were it not for your supplication﴾ means: were it not for your calling upon Him to worship Him. On this reading, the verbal noun *al-duʿāʾ* (الدُّعاءُ) is in the genitive construction with its object, which is the view al-Farra' preferred, and its subject is omitted. The response of *lawlā* (لَوْلا) is omitted, and its estimated form is: "were it not for your supplication, He would not care for you." This is supported by His words: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they might worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. The address is to all people, and then He specified the disbelievers among them, saying: ﴿So you have denied﴾. Ibn al-Zubayr read: "So the disbelievers have denied" (فَقَدْ كَذَّبَ الكافِرُونَ). In this reading there is clear evidence that the address is to all people.

It is also said that the verbal noun is in the genitive construction with its subject, meaning: were it not for your appeal to Him in times of hardship.

It is also said that the meaning is: He does not weigh you (for the forgiveness of your sins) were it not for your calling upon the gods alongside Him.

Ibn Jinni reported that Ibn ʿAbbas read in the same way as Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Zahrawi and al-Nahhas reported that Ibn Masʿud read in the same way as they both did. Among those who held that *al-duʿāʾ* is in the genitive construction with its subject were al-Qutaybi and al-Farisi, who said: the original is "were it not for your calling upon the gods alongside Him."

Ibn Jinni reported that Ibn ʿAbbas read in the same way as Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Zahrawi and al-Nahhas reported that Ibn Masʿud read in the same way as they both did. Among those who held that *al-duʿāʾ* is omitted, its estimated form on this view is: "were it not for your supplication, He would not have punished you." The meaning of "So you have denied" on the first view is: you have denied what you were called to. On the second view: you have denied monotheism.

Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So it will be *lizāman*﴾, meaning: the consequence of your denial will inevitably be binding upon you. Most exegetes hold that what is meant by *al-lizām* (اللِّزامُ) here is what befell the polytheists on the Day of Badr. Another group said it is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *lizāman* (لِزامًا) means a decisive separation, i.e., it will be a decisive separation between you and the believers.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿So it will be your denial is *lizāman*﴾, meaning it will cling to you, so you will not be granted repentance. Most readers pronounce the *lām* of *lizāman* with a kasra. Abu ʿUbayda cited the verse of Sakhr:

"If they survive the collapse of the earth, / then they have met their deaths *lizāman*."

Ibn Jarir said: *lizāman* means a lasting punishment and a destroying ruin that joins some of you to others, like the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"So it overtook him with a *ʿādiyah lizām*, / as the crumbling pool pours forth."

By *al-lizām* he means that which follows one another, and by *al-lafīf* he means the stones that fall from what has collapsed.

Abu Hatim reported from Abu Zayd, who said: I heard Abu al-Sammak recite *lizāman* with a fatha on the *lām*. Abu Jaʿfar said: it would be the verbal noun of *lazima* (لَزِمَ), but the kasra is preferable.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others have also reported from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: 'Which sin is greatest?' He said: 'That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you kill your child for fear that he will share your food.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife.'" Then Allah revealed as confirmation of this: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except in truth, nor commit adultery﴾.

Al-Bukhari and others also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that some people from among the polytheists had killed much and committed much adultery, then they came to Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: "What you say and call to is good indeed, if you would tell us that there is expiation for what we have done." So ﴿And those who do not call upon﴾ was revealed, and the verse ﴿Say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves"﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] was revealed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr concerning His words ﴿he will meet *athāman*﴾ that he said: it is a valley in Hell.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When ﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with Allah﴾ was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims, and they said: "There is none among us who has not associated partners, killed, and committed adultery." Then Allah revealed ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, which speaks to those who did these things in polytheism. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Except for those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾. So Allah replaced for them disbelief with Islam, disobedience with obedience, denial with recognition, and ignorance with knowledge.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: We recited it during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for years: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except in truth, nor commit adultery; and whoever does that will meet *athāman*﴾. Then this was revealed: ﴿except for those who repent and believe﴾. I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoice at anything as he rejoiced at this, and at ﴿Indeed We have granted you a manifest victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1].

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His words ﴿Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾ that he said: they are the believers who used to commit evil deeds before their faith. Allah turned away from that in them and transformed them to good deeds, replacing their evil deeds with good deeds.

Ahmad, Hannad, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asmaʾ wa al-Sifat* reported from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'Present to him his minor sins,' and his minor sins will be presented to him, and his major sins will be kept away from him. It will be said: 'On such and such a day you did such and such,' and he will acknowledge it, not denying, while he is fearful of the major sins coming. It will be said: 'Give him for every evil deed he did a good deed.'" The narrations concerning the expiation of evil deeds and their replacement with good deeds are numerous.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words ﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾ (p-1052) that he said: *al-zūr* was an idol in Medina, around which they would dance every seven days, and when the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by it, they would pass with dignity, not looking at it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes"﴾ that he said: they mean whoever acts in obedience, so that our eyes are gladdened by him in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And make us a model for the righteous﴾ means: leaders of guidance, by whom people are guided, and do not make us leaders of misguidance, because He said of the people of felicity: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 73], and of the people of wretchedness: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas: 41].

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported from Sahl ibn Saʿd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His words ﴿Those will be rewarded with the chamber﴾, that he said: the chamber is of red ruby, or green emerald, or white pearl, with no crack or flaw in it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words ﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication"﴾ that he said: were it not for your faith. Allah informed that He has no need of them if He had not created them believers. Had He needed them, He would have made faith beloved to them as He made it beloved to the believers. ﴿So it will be *lizāman*﴾, he said: death.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Anbari reported from him that he used to read: "So the disbelievers have denied" and ﴿So it will be *lizāman*﴾. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn al-Zubayr that he recited it in the same way.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported ﴿So it will be *lizāman*﴾ and said: it is the killing on the Day of Badr. In the two *Sahihs* it is reported from him that he said: Five have passed: the smoke, the moon, the *luzūm*, the grasping assault, and the *lizām*.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 26, verse 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾. When He finished mentioning their performance of acts of obedience, He began to explain their avoidance of acts of disobedience, so He said: "And those who do not invoke with Allah, glorified is He, any lord among the lords."

The meaning: they do not associate anything with Him, but rather they affirm His oneness and devote worship and supplication sincerely to Him. ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾, meaning: He has forbidden its killing except by right, that is, by that for which souls may rightly be killed: disbelief after belief, or fornication after being chaste (ihsan), or killing a soul without a soul (qisas). ﴿Nor do they commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾, meaning: they do not make lawful the forbidden private parts without marriage (nikah) or ownership of the right hand (milk al-yamin). ﴿And whoever does that﴾, meaning: any of what has been mentioned, ﴿will meet a penalty (athaman) in the Hereafter﴾. The athām in the speech of the Arabs means: punishment. Al-Farra' said: Allah "athamahu" (yu'thimuhu) athaman and athaman, meaning: He requited him with the recompense of sin. Ikrimah and Mujahid said: "Athaman" is a valley in Hell which Allah made a punishment for the disbelievers. As-Suddi said: it is a mountain within it. It was recited as (yulaqq) with a damma on the ya' and a shadda on the qaf. Abu Muslim said: athaman and ithm are one and the same, and what is meant here is the recompense of sins, so the name of the thing was applied to its recompense.

Al-Hasan recited (yalqa ayyaman), the plural of yawm, meaning hardships; the Arabs express that by "days," and I do not think this recitation is authentically transmitted from him. ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him﴾. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited yudda'af and yakhlud with the jazm; Ibn Kathir recited (yudda'af) with a shadda on the 'ain, dropping the alif, and with the jazm; Talhah ibn Sulayman recited (nudda'if) with a damma on the nun, a kasra on the shadded 'ain, and the jazm, and this is the recitation of Abu Ja'far and Shaybah.

'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, recited with the raf' in both verbs, by way of resumption (isti'naf).

Talhah ibn Sulayman recited (wa-takhlud) with the feminine second person, addressing the disbeliever.

It is narrated from Abu 'Amr that he recited (wa-yukhlad) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the lam.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: this is an error from the standpoint of transmission. The reason for the jazm in (yudda'af) is that it is a substitute (badal) for (yalqa), because the two are unified in meaning, and similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed upon me is Allah's (covenant) that you pledge allegiance, you will be seized unwillingly or you will come willingly."

The pronoun in His saying (yakhlud) fihi refers to the doubled punishment, meaning: he will abide in the doubled punishment, humiliated, abased, despised.

﴿Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds﴾. It was said this is an exceptive (istithna' muttasil), and it was said it is disjunctive (munqati').

Abu Hayyan said: connection does not appear, because the one excepted from is judged as being one for whom the punishment is doubled, so the sense becomes: except those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds, then the punishment is not doubled for them; and the negation of doubling does not necessitate the negation of the punishment that is not doubled.

He said: What is preferable in my view is that it is disjunctive, meaning: but whoever repents.

Al-Qurtubi said: There is no disagreement among the scholars that the exception is general, covering the disbeliever and the fornicator. They differed concerning the Muslim killer, and its explanation has already preceded in al-Nisa' and al-Ma'idah.

The indication in His saying: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ refers to those mentioned previously. The meaning of the replacement of evil deeds with good deeds is that He erases their sins and establishes in their place acts of obedience.

Al-Nahhas said: Among the best of what has been said about this is that where a disbeliever was written, a believer is written, and where a disobedient one was, an obedient one is written. Al-Hasan said: some people say: the replacement is in the Hereafter, and that is not so; rather the replacement is in this world: Allah replaces for them faith in place of polytheism, sincerity in place of doubt, and chastity in place of immorality.

Al-Zajjaj said: He does not make a good deed in place of an evil deed, but He makes repentance in place of an evil deed, and a good deed along with repentance.

It was said: evil deeds are replaced by good deeds, and this was the view of a group of the Companions and those after them.

It was said: replacement is an expression for forgiveness, meaning Allah forgives them those evil deeds, not that He replaces them with good deeds. It was said: what is meant by replacement is that He enables him to the opposites of what had previously occurred from him. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾. This sentence confirms what came before it concerning the replacement.

﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he returns to Allah with a (sincere) return﴾, meaning: whoever repents from what he committed and does a righteous deed after that, then he returns by that to Allah with a (sincere) return, meaning: he returns to Him with a sound, strong return.

Al-Qaffal said: It is possible that the first verse concerns those who repent from the polytheists, which is why He said: ﴿except those who repent and believe﴾; then He conjoined to it those who repent from the Muslims and follow their repentance with righteous deeds, so they too have the ruling of the repentant.

It was said: meaning (p-1050) whoever repents with his tongue but does not realize the repentance with his action, that repentance is not beneficial; rather whoever repents and does righteous deeds, realizing his repentance through righteous works, is the one who truly returns to Allah with a return, meaning: he repents with the true repentance, which is sincere (nasuh), and for this reason it is emphasized with the verbal noun. The meaning of the verse: whoever wishes to repent and resolves upon it, let him turn to Allah. So the statement is in the sense of a command. This was said so that the condition and the consequent would not be identical, for one does not say of one who repents: "then indeed he returns."

Then Allah, glorified is He, described these repentant ones who do righteous deeds, saying: ﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾, meaning they do not bear false testimony, or they do not attend falsehood. Falsehood (zur) is lying and vanity, and they do not witness it. Jumhur al-mufassirin went to the second meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: zur in the language means lying, and there is no lying worse than associating partners with Allah.

Al-Wahidi said: most of the exegetes hold that zur here means polytheism.

The summary is that (yashhadun), if it is from testimony (shahadah), then there is an elided genitive in the speech, meaning: they do not bear the testimony of falsehood; and if it is from attendance (shuhud), meaning presence, as the majority went, then they differed about its meaning. Qatadah said: they do not assist the people of falsehood in their falsehood. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: they do not attend idle talk and singing. Ibn Juraij said: lying.

It is also narrated from Mujahid. The preferable view is not to restrict it to one kind of falsehood, but rather the meaning is those who do not attend anything that truly bears the name of falsehood, whoever it may be. ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾, meaning: turning away from it, not inclining toward it. Lagh is every worthless utterance or deed.

Al-Hasan said: lagh is all sins. It was said: what is meant is they pass by people of idle talk; it is said: "So-and-so is honored above what disgraces him," meaning: he keeps himself pure and honors himself from entering into idle talk and mixing with its people.

﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord﴾, meaning with the Qur'an, or with what in it is admonition and lesson, ﴿do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾, meaning: they do not fall upon them while being deaf and blind, but rather they attend to them, hearing and seeing, and benefit from them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is they do not neglect them, as if they were deaf who did not hear them, and blind who did not see them.

Ibn Jarir said: there is no falling here; rather it is like the saying "he sat weeping," though he is not sitting.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is as if the listener to the reminder is standing, so when he turns away from it, that is a falling, which is collapse without order.

It was said the meaning is: when the verses of Allah are recited to them, their hearts tremble, and they fall down prostrating and weeping, and do not fall upon them deaf and blind.

Al-Farra' said: meaning they do not remain in their former state as if they had not heard.

In al-Kashshaf he said: it is not a negation of the falling; rather it is an affirmation of it and a negation of deafness and blindness, and he meant that the negation is directed at the qualifier, not at the qualified.

﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort of the eyes"﴾. (Min) is either inceptive (ibtida'iyyah) or explanatory (bayaniyyah).

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan recited ﴿wa-dhurriyyatina﴾ in the plural; Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Talhah and 'Isa recited (wa-dhurriyyatina) in the singular. Dhurriyyah is used for the plural, as in His saying: ﴿dhurriyyatan di'afa'﴾ [al-Nisa' 9], and used for the singular, as in His saying: ﴿dhurriyyatan tayyibah﴾ [Al 'Imran 38]. Qurrata a'yun is in the accusative as an object; it is said: "qarrat 'aynuhu qurratan" (his eye became cool).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "Allah cool your eye," meaning: your heart encounters what it loves.

Al-Mufaddal said: regarding qurrat al-'ayn there are three views: the first is the coolness of its tears, because that is a sign of joy and laughter, just as their heat is a sign of sorrow and grief. The second is its sleep, because that occurs with the leisure of the mind and the departure of sorrow. The third is the attainment of contentment.

﴿And make us leaders for the righteous﴾, meaning: examples who are followed in goodness. He said "imaman" and did not say "a'immah" because it is intended as a genus, like His saying: ﴿then We bring you out as a child﴾ [al-Hajj 5]. Al-Farra' said: He said "imaman" and did not say "a'immah," just as He said for the two: ﴿indeed we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 16], meaning that it is a singular used with the sense of the plural.

Al-Akhfash said: imam is the plural of umm, from amma yaummu, a plural on the pattern fi'al, like sahib and sihab, and qa'im and qiyam.

It was said: imaman is a verbal noun; it is said "amma fulanun fulanan imaman," like siyam and qiyam.

It was said: they meant: make each one of us an imam. It was said: they meant: make us one imam, due to the unity of our word. It was said: it is from the inverted speech, and the meaning is: make the righteous an imam for us; this was the view of Mujahid.

It was said: this supplication issued from them individually, and that the expression of each one of them at the supplication was: "make me an imam for the righteous," but the expressions of all were related in the first-person plural form for the sake of brevity, like His saying: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Mu'minun 51]. In this, "imaman" remains in its state. Similar to what is in the verse is the saying of the poet:

"O my blamers, do not increase my reproach; indeed the blamers are not trustworthy to me,"

meaning: trustworthy ones (umana'). Al-Qaffal said: in my view, when imam is treated as a name, it is made singular, as if it were said: make us a proof (hujjah) for the righteous, and similarly bayyinah: one says "these are the bayyinah of so-and-so." Al-Naysaburi said: it was said that the verse indicates that religious leadership is among the things that should be sought and desired; the closer view is that they asked Allah to bring them in obedience to the degree by which they would be pointed to and followed.

The indication in His saying: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber for what they endured﴾ refers to those described with those attributes. It is the subject, and its predicate is what follows, and the sentences are independent (mustanfah).

It was said: "Those" and what follows is a predicate of His saying: ﴿and the servants of the Most Merciful﴾; so said al-Zajjaj. Al-ghurfah is the high rank, which is the highest and best of the dwellings of Paradise; in origin it applies to any elevated building, and its plural is ghuraf.

Al-Dahhak said: al-ghurfah is Paradise. The ba' in ﴿for what they endured﴾ is causal, and ma is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: they are rewarded the high chamber because of their patience in the hardships of obligation.

﴿And they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾. Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited (yalqawna) with a fatha on the ya' and sukun on the lam and lightened qaf; al-Farra' chose this recitation, saying: because the Arabs say: "so-and-so yulqi with greetings, peace and good," and they seldom say yulqi. The rest recited with a damma on the ya' and fatha on the lam and shadda on the qaf, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this recitation because of His saying: ﴿and He gave them radiance and joy﴾. The meaning is that they greet one another, and the Lord, glorified is He, sends to them greetings of peace. It was said: al-tahiyyah is lasting survival and great dominion; it was said: it is (p-1051) the same meaning as salam; it was said: the angels greet them and give them peace. The apparent view is that this greeting and peace are from Allah, glorified is He, to them, and of this is His saying: ﴿their greeting on the day they meet Him is peace﴾ [al-Ahzab 44]. It was said: the meaning of tahiyyah is the supplication for them of long life. The meaning of salam is the supplication for them of safety from calamities.

The accusative of *khalidina* (﻿خالِدِينَ) here is a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: abiding therein, remaining there without dying.

﴿Excellent is it as a place of settling and dwelling﴾, meaning the chamber was excellent as a place where they settle and a place where they dwell. This is in contrast to His earlier words: ﴿Evil is it as a place of settling and dwelling﴾ [al-Furqan: 66].

﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication."﴾ He, glorified is He, explains that He is free of need for the obedience of all, and that He imposed obligations only so that people might benefit from them. It is said: *mā ʿabaʾtu bi-fulān* (ما عَبَأْتُ بِفُلانٍ), meaning: I did not care for him, and he had no weight in my estimation. The root of *yaʿbaʾu* (يَعْبَأُ) is *al-ʿibʾ* (العِبْءُ), meaning burden or weight.

Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) said: *mā aʿbaʾu bi-fulān* means "I do nothing with him," as if he considers him insignificant and contemptible, and claims that his existence and non-existence are the same. Abu ʿUbayda also said likewise.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿What does my Lord care for you﴾ means: what weight do you have in His sight? *Al-ʿibʾ* is weight, and (*mā*) (ما) is either interrogative or negative. Al-Farra' stated explicitly that it is interrogative. Ibn al-Shajari said: The true position in my view is that the place of (*mā*) is accusative, and the meaning is: what weight does He give you, i.e., what concern does He have for you?

﴿Were it not for your supplication﴾ means: were it not for your calling upon Him to worship Him. On this reading, the verbal noun *al-duʿāʾ* (الدُّعاءُ) is in the genitive construction with its object, which is the view al-Farra' preferred, and its subject is omitted. The response of *lawlā* (لَوْلا) is omitted, and its estimated form is: "were it not for your supplication, He would not care for you." This is supported by His words: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they might worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. The address is to all people, and then He specified the disbelievers among them, saying: ﴿So you have denied﴾. Ibn al-Zubayr read: "So the disbelievers have denied" (فَقَدْ كَذَّبَ الكافِرُونَ). In this reading there is clear evidence that the address is to all people.

It is also said that the verbal noun is in the genitive construction with its subject, meaning: were it not for your appeal to Him in times of hardship.

It is also said that the meaning is: He does not weigh you (for the forgiveness of your sins) were it not for your calling upon the gods alongside Him.

Ibn Jinni reported that Ibn ʿAbbas read in the same way as Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Zahrawi and al-Nahhas reported that Ibn Masʿud read in the same way as they both did. Among those who held that *al-duʿāʾ* is in the genitive construction with its subject were al-Qutaybi and al-Farisi, who said: the original is "were it not for your calling upon the gods alongside Him."

Ibn Jinni reported that Ibn ʿAbbas read in the same way as Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Zahrawi and al-Nahhas reported that Ibn Masʿud read in the same way as they both did. Among those who held that *al-duʿāʾ* is omitted, its estimated form on this view is: "were it not for your supplication, He would not have punished you." The meaning of "So you have denied" on the first view is: you have denied what you were called to. On the second view: you have denied monotheism.

Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So it will be *lizāman*﴾, meaning: the consequence of your denial will inevitably be binding upon you. Most exegetes hold that what is meant by *al-lizām* (اللِّزامُ) here is what befell the polytheists on the Day of Badr. Another group said it is the punishment of the Hereafter.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *lizāman* (لِزامًا) means a decisive separation, i.e., it will be a decisive separation between you and the believers.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿So it will be your denial is *lizāman*﴾, meaning it will cling to you, so you will not be granted repentance. Most readers pronounce the *lām* of *lizāman* with a kasra. Abu ʿUbayda cited the verse of Sakhr:

"If they survive the collapse of the earth, / then they have met their deaths *lizāman*."

Ibn Jarir said: *lizāman* means a lasting punishment and a destroying ruin that joins some of you to others, like the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"So it overtook him with a *ʿādiyah lizām*, / as the crumbling pool pours forth."

By *al-lizām* he means that which follows one another, and by *al-lafīf* he means the stones that fall from what has collapsed.

Abu Hatim reported from Abu Zayd, who said: I heard Abu al-Sammak recite *lizāman* with a fatha on the *lām*. Abu Jaʿfar said: it would be the verbal noun of *lazima* (لَزِمَ), but the kasra is preferable.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others have also reported from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: 'Which sin is greatest?' He said: 'That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you kill your child for fear that he will share your food.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife.'" Then Allah revealed as confirmation of this: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except in truth, nor commit adultery﴾.

Al-Bukhari and others also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that some people from among the polytheists had killed much and committed much adultery, then they came to Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: "What you say and call to is good indeed, if you would tell us that there is expiation for what we have done." So ﴿And those who do not call upon﴾ was revealed, and the verse ﴿Say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves"﴾ [al-Zumar: 53] was revealed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr concerning His words ﴿he will meet *athāman*﴾ that he said: it is a valley in Hell.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When ﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with Allah﴾ was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims, and they said: "There is none among us who has not associated partners, killed, and committed adultery." Then Allah revealed ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, which speaks to those who did these things in polytheism. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Except for those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾. So Allah replaced for them disbelief with Islam, disobedience with obedience, denial with recognition, and ignorance with knowledge.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: We recited it during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for years: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god along with Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except in truth, nor commit adultery; and whoever does that will meet *athāman*﴾. Then this was revealed: ﴿except for those who repent and believe﴾. I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoice at anything as he rejoiced at this, and at ﴿Indeed We have granted you a manifest victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1].

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His words ﴿Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾ that he said: they are the believers who used to commit evil deeds before their faith. Allah turned away from that in them and transformed them to good deeds, replacing their evil deeds with good deeds.

Ahmad, Hannad, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asmaʾ wa al-Sifat* reported from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'Present to him his minor sins,' and his minor sins will be presented to him, and his major sins will be kept away from him. It will be said: 'On such and such a day you did such and such,' and he will acknowledge it, not denying, while he is fearful of the major sins coming. It will be said: 'Give him for every evil deed he did a good deed.'" The narrations concerning the expiation of evil deeds and their replacement with good deeds are numerous.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words ﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾ (p-1052) that he said: *al-zūr* was an idol in Medina, around which they would dance every seven days, and when the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by it, they would pass with dignity, not looking at it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And those who say: "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes"﴾ that he said: they mean whoever acts in obedience, so that our eyes are gladdened by him in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And make us a model for the righteous﴾ means: leaders of guidance, by whom people are guided, and do not make us leaders of misguidance, because He said of the people of felicity: ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 73], and of the people of wretchedness: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas: 41].

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported from Sahl ibn Saʿd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His words ﴿Those will be rewarded with the chamber﴾, that he said: the chamber is of red ruby, or green emerald, or white pearl, with no crack or flaw in it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words ﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication"﴾ that he said: were it not for your faith. Allah informed that He has no need of them if He had not created them believers. Had He needed them, He would have made faith beloved to them as He made it beloved to the believers. ﴿So it will be *lizāman*﴾, he said: death.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Anbari reported from him that he used to read: "So the disbelievers have denied" and ﴿So it will be *lizāman*﴾. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn al-Zubayr that he recited it in the same way.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported ﴿So it will be *lizāman*﴾ and said: it is the killing on the Day of Badr. In the two *Sahihs* it is reported from him that he said: Five have passed: the smoke, the moon, the *luzūm*, the grasping assault, and the *lizām*.

It is Meccan according to the majority. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated this from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Shuʿara was revealed at Mecca, except for five verses at its end, which were revealed at Medina, namely ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them﴾ to the end."

Al-Tabarani narrated in his tafsir from al-Bara', that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah gave me the seven long surahs (al-sab' al-tiwal) in place of the Torah, He gave me the mi'in (surahs of about a hundred verses) in place of the Gospel, He gave me the tawasin (surahs beginning with ṭā-sīn) in place of the Psalms, and He favoured me with the hawamim (surahs beginning with ḥā-mīm) and the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an), which no prophet before me recited."

He also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which the Cow is mentioned from the first Reminder (al-dhikr al-awwal), I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the final verses of Surat al-Baqara from beneath the Throne, and I was given the mufassal as a supererogatory gift (nafila)."

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "It occurs in the tafsir of Malik, narrated from him, that it is named Surat al-Jumuʿa."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm﴾. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the ṭāʾ with imala (a fronting of the vowel, pronounced between a and i). Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Zuhri read it between the two sounds (bayna al-lafzayn). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. The rest read it with a fully lengthened fatha.

The people of Medina, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i assimilated the nūn of "ṭa-sin-n" (ط س ن) into the mīm. Al-A'mash and Hamza made it clear (izhar) without assimilation. Al-Tha'labi said: "Assimilation is the choice of Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim."

Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Zajjaj reported in his book Fima yajri wa-ma la yajri (On what is declined and what is not) that it is permissible to say ṭā sīna mīmu (طا سِينَ مِيمُ) with a fatha on the nūn and a ḍamma on the mīm, as one says 'hadha Ma'di Karib' (this is Ma'di Karib)."

ʿĪsa, and what is transmitted from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasra, as an indeclinable (ʿalā al-binaʾ).

In the Mushaf of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is written as (ط س م), letters separated, so one pauses on each letter with a distinct pause that marks it off from the others. Abu Ja'far also read it this way.

Its place in the grammar is raf' (nominative) if it is a name of the surah, as most scholars hold, or it is the predicate of a omitted subject. It may be in a nasb (accusative) position, with the implied verb "udhkur" (mention) or "iqra'" (recite). If it is recited as a sequence of letters in the manner of enumeration, as has been noted at more than one place in this tafsir, then it has no place in grammatical analysis (la mahalla lahu min al-iʿrab).

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, and it has been said that it is one of the names of the Qur'an. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ refers to the surah. Its place is raf', as it and what follows it are the predicate if we take (ط س م) as the subject. If we take it as the predicate of an omitted subject, its place is raf' as the subject whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition (badal) to (ط س م). The Book here means the Qur'an. Al-Mubin means "the one who makes clear" (al-mudhhir), or "the clear, evident one" if it is from abana in the sense of bana (to be clear).

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself (laʿallaka bakhiʿun nafsaka) that they do not believe﴾: that is, you will kill and destroy yourself. Al-bakh' originally means slaughtering to the point of reaching the nukhaʿ (نُخاع), spelled with a nūn. Al-Qamus says it is a vein at the back of the neck. Its full treatment has passed in Surat al-Kahf. Qatada read bakhiʿu nafsika (باخِعُ نَفْسِكَ) with an idafa (genitive construction), while the rest read it with tanwin (indefinite, separated). Al-Farra' said: "(an) in ﴿that they do not believe﴾ is in the accusative position, because it is a conditional." Al-Nahhas said: "It is said that 'in' (إن) with a kasra is because it is a particle (juz'), and this is the common usage." The view on this is what al-Zajjaj said in his book on the Qur'an: that it is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and the meaning is: "Perhaps you will kill yourself because of their refusal to believe." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he was eager for the faith of his people and deeply grieved at their turning away.

The clause ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven﴾ is a new, independent sentence, intended to give the reason for the preceding consolation. The meaning: If We willed, We would send down upon them from the heaven a sign that would compel them to faith, but the decree has already preceded that We do not send such a thing. The meaning of ﴿their necks remained bowed before it﴾ is that they would become submissive to it, that is, ﴿then their necks would remain bowed...﴾ etc. It has been said that the original form was "fa-zallū lahā khāḍiʿīn" (so they would remain bowed to it), and the word "necks" (aʿnāq) was inserted to add emphasis and vividness, since the necks are the place of humility. It has also been said that when the necks were placed where humility is, they were described with the attributes of rational beings, and so were treated as such and described with what they are described with.

ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar said: "Khāḍiʿīn (masculine plural) and khāḍiʿa (feminine) are the same here," and al-Mubarrad chose this. The meaning is that when their necks are humbled, they themselves are humbled, so reporting about the necks is reporting about their owners. It is permissible in the speech of the Arabs to leave the predicate about the first and report about the second. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"Long nights hastened to wear me down; they folded my length and folded my breadth."

So he reported about the nights and left out "the length" (al-tul). From this is the saying of Jarir:

"I see the passing years have taken from me as the dark period (al-sirar) takes from the crescent."

Abu ʿUbayd and al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is "khāḍiʿīhā hum" (they themselves are its humbled ones). Al-Nahhas considered this weak. Mujahid said: "aʿnāquhum" means their leaders (kubarāʾuhum).

Al-Nahhas said: "This is well known in the language. One says: 'A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me,' meaning leaders among them."

Abu Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "Aʿnāquhum" means their groups (jamaʿātuhum). One says: "A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me," meaning a company.

﴿And there never comes to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful but they turn away from it.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, made clear that, although He is able to make them compelled to faith, He brings them the Qur'an, state after state, and does not renew for them any admonition or reminder except that they renew what is the opposite of the purpose: turning away, denial and mockery. The min in ﴿min dhikrin﴾ is extra, for emphasis of generality. The min in ﴿min rabbihim﴾ denotes the starting point. The exception is a "mufarragh" (exception from a general context) drawn from the most general category; its place is the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the object of ﴿yatīhim﴾ (comes to them). The tafsir of a similar verse has passed in Surat al-Anbiya'.

﴿So they have denied﴾: that is, they denied the reminder that came to them with an explicit denial, and did not suffice with mere turning away. It has been said that turning away means denial, because whoever turns away from something and does not accept it has denied it. On this view, the mention of denial shows that it came from them explicitly. But the first view is better. Turning away from something is not paying attention to it. Then they moved from that to something worse, which is explicit denial. Then they moved from denial to something even worse, which is mockery, as His saying indicates: ﴿So the news (anbaʾ) of what they used to mock will come to them.﴾ Al-anbaʾ (the news) refers to the punishment they deserve, both in the near term and later. It is called "news" because it is among the things the Qur'an reported about, and He said ﴿what they used to mock﴾ and did not say "what they used to turn away from" or "what they used to deny," because mockery is worse than both and implies them. In this there is a severe warning. The tafsir of a similar expression has passed in Surat al-Anʿam.

Then He mentioned, the Exalted, what shows His complete power, from sensory matters through which whoever reflects on them, looks at them, and reasons from them obtains the greatest proof and the clearest evidence. He said:

﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how much of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ The hamza (ء) is for rebuke (tawbikh), and the waw is for coordination with an implied preceding clause, as in its parallels. Allah, the Exalted, drew attention to His greatness and power, and that these deniers and mockers, if they looked properly, would know that He is the One who deserves to be worshipped. The meaning of zawj (kind) here is "type" (ṣinf).

Al-Farra' said: "It is the colour (lawn)." Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of zawj is 'kind' (nawʿ), and karim means praised." The meaning is: of every beneficial kind, which none can cause to grow except the Lord of the worlds. Karim originally means good and noble. One says "a noble palm" (nakhla karima), meaning one with abundant fruit. "A noble man" (rajul karim) means noble and virtuous. "A noble book" (kitab karim) means one whose meanings are pleasing. A "noble plant" (nabat karim) is one that is pleasing in its benefits.

Al-Shaʿbi said: "People are like the plants of the earth: whoever among them goes to Paradise is noble (karim), and whoever among them goes to the Fire is base (laʾim)."

The reference of ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is to what was mentioned before it. That is: indeed, in what was mentioned of growth in the earth there is a clear proof and a plain sign of the complete power of Allah, the Exalted, and the wondrous artistry of His creation.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed that most of these people persist in their error, insisting on their rejection, denial and mockery. He said: ﴿And most of them were not believers.﴾ That is: there was a prior knowledge (sabq ʿilmi) in Him that they would be like this.

Sibawayh said: "Kāna (was) here is a filler (ṣila)."

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾ That is: the Dominant, the Subduer of these people, by taking vengeance on them, while being abundant in mercy. For this reason He gave them respite and did not hasten to punish them. Or the meaning is: He takes vengeance on His enemies and is merciful to His friends.

The clause ﴿And when your Lord called Moses...﴾ and so on is a new sentence, intended to confirm what preceded it of turning away, denial and mockery. The factor governing the adverbial time expression is omitted, and its estimated form is: "Recite, when He called," or "Mention." Al-nida' means calling (al-duʿa'). The ʾan in His saying ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾ may be explanatory (mufassira) or verbal-source (maṣdariyya). Their description as wrongdoers is because they combined disbelief, by which they wronged themselves, with the sins by which they wronged others, such as enslaving the children of Israel and slaughtering their sons.

﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾ is in the accusative position, either as an apposition (badal) or as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "the wrongdoing people." The meaning of ﴿Will they not be wary?﴾ is: will they not fear the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, so that they avert Allah's punishment from themselves by obeying Him?

It has been said that the meaning is: "Say to them: Will you not be wary?" It came with the yāʾ (third person) because they were absent at the time of address. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Abu Hazim read ﴿Will you not be wary?﴾ with the second person (tāʾ fawqiyya), that is, "Say to them that." A similar example is ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome﴾ [Al ʿImran 12], read with both the third and second person.

﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear they will deny me."﴾ That is: Moses said this statement, and the meaning is: I fear they will deny me regarding the message. ﴿And my chest tightens and my tongue does not speak freely﴾: these two are coordinated with "I fear." That is: my chest tightens because of their denial of me, and my tongue does not speak freely in delivering the message.

The majority read ﴿tightens﴾ and ﴿does not speak freely﴾ with ḍamma (nominative), coordinated with "I fear," as we mentioned, or as a new sentence (istiʾnaf). Yaʿqub, ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar and Abu Haywa read both with a fatha (accusative), coordinated with "they will deny me." Al-Farra' said: "Both readings have a basis." Al-Nahhas said: "The better is the nominative, because the accusative is coordinated with 'they will deny me,' and this is distant."

﴿So send to Harun﴾: that is, send to him Gabriel with the revelation, so that he may be with me as a messenger, a helper, a supporter, an assistant. He did not mention the helping here because it is known from other places, such as His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿and appoint for me a helper﴾ [Ta-Ha 29], and in al-Qasas: ﴿so send him with me as a supporter to confirm me﴾ [al-Qasas 34]. This request from Moses, peace be upon him, is a request for help by sending his brother, not a request to be excused from the message, nor a hesitation in swiftly obeying.

﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me.﴾ The charge (dhanb) is his killing of the Copt. He called it a dhanb according to their claim. Moses feared they would kill him for it. In this is evidence that fear may occur even among prophets, let alone among the virtuous. Then Allah, the Exalted, answered him with what contains a kind of deterrence and a measure of rebuke.

(p-1053)

He said, "No! So go, both of you, with Our signs." Within this reply is Musa's acceptance of his request that his brother be joined with him, as the address directed at both of them indicates. It is as if He had said: "Desist from that, O Musa, and go, you and whoever you asked for, and do not fear the Copts (al-Qibt)." ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening.﴾ In this is a reason for the prohibition of fear. It is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]. By this, glorified is He, intended to strengthen their hearts, and that He is the one who takes charge of their protection and safeguarding. He treated the two of them as a plural, so He said "with you" (maʿakum). But two is the least plural according to some of the scholars (al-aʾimma), or because He intended Musa, Harun, and those to whom they were sent. It is also possible that the intended meaning is "both of them with the Children of Israel." "With you" and "listening" may be two predicates of inna, or the predicate is "listening" and "with you" is related to it. The figurative usage (al-majaz) in "with" (al-maʿiyya) is not hidden, since companionship (al-muṣāḥaba) is one of the attributes of physical bodies. So the intended meaning is the being-with of support and help.

﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ The particle الفاء (al-fāʾ, "so") indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. Here the word رَسُول (rasūl, "messenger") is in the singular and not dual, unlike His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. This is because it is used as a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "a message" (risāla), and a verbal noun remains singular. But when it means "one who is sent" (al-mursal), it takes the dual with the dual and the plural with the plural. Abu ʿUbayda said: rasūl here means "a message," and the implied sense is: "Indeed, we are two bearers of the message of the Lord of the worlds." From this is the poet's saying:

*Ah, convey to Abu ʿAmr a message,*
*For I am free of your fataḥa (i.e., your dealings).*

That is, a message.

Al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas said:

*Ah, is there anyone to convey from me to Khufaf a message,*
*Whose house is the end of your family's journey?*

That is, a message.

Abu ʿUbayda also said: rasūl may mean the dual and the plural. The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent (wakīl)," "These two are my messenger and my agent," and "These are my messenger and my agent." From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 77]. It was also said: its meaning is that each one of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. And it was said: since the two of them were mutually supportive and reinforcing in the message, they were in the position of a single messenger.

The أنْ (an, "that") in His saying ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾ is explanatory (mufassira), because the sending implied by "messenger" includes the meaning of saying.

﴿He said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child?"﴾ That is, Pharaoh said to Musa after they came to him and said to him what Allah had commanded them. The phrase فِينا (fīnā, "among us") means "in our care and our homes." By this he intended to remind him of favor and to belittle him: that is, "We raised you with us as a little child, and we did not kill you among those children we killed." ﴿And you stayed among us for years of your life.﴾ Then when was this that you claim? It was said: he stayed among them eighteen years; it was said thirty years; and it was said forty years. Then he rebuked him for killing the Copt, saying: ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾. The word الفَعْلَة (al-faʿla, "deed") with a fatḥa on the fāʾ means a single occurrence of the action. Al-Shaʿbi read فِعْلَتَكَ (fiʿlataka) with a kasra on the fāʾ, but the fatḥa is preferable because it denotes a single occurrence, not a type. The meaning is that when he enumerated the blessings upon him, he mentioned his sins to him, and by "the deed" he meant the killing of the Copt. Then he said: ﴿And you are of the disbelievers﴾, that is, among those who are ungrateful for the blessing, since you killed a man from my people. It was also said that the meaning is: among the disbelievers in the claim that Pharaoh is a god. It was also said: among the disbelievers in Allah according to his own belief, since he was with them on their religion. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was of the astray."﴾ That is, Musa replied to Pharaoh: "I did this deed you mentioned, which is killing the Copt, and at that time I was among the astray," that is, the ignorant. Peace be upon him negated disbelief from himself and informed that he did that out of ignorance before the knowledge Allah taught him came to him. It was also said: the meaning is "among those ignorant that that blow would reach killing." Abu ʿUbayda said: "among the forgetful."

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾, that is, I went out from among you to Madyan, as in the surah of al-Qasas. ﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom (ḥukm)﴾, that is, prophethood, or knowledge and understanding. Al-Zajjaj said: by ḥukm is meant His teaching him the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah.

﴿And made me among the messengers. And is this a favor you count upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾ It was said: this speech from Musa is by way of acknowledging the blessing, as if he said: "Yes, that upbringing is a blessing you count upon me, but that does not negate my messengership." This is what al-Farraʾ and Ibn Jarir said.

It was also said: it is from Musa by way of denial, meaning: "Do you count upon me that you raised me as a child, while you had enslaved the Children of Israel and killed them, and they are my people?"

Al-Zajjaj said: the commentators took this as a denial, namely that what Pharaoh mentioned was a favor upon Musa, while the wording is that of a statement, and in it is a rebuke of the addressee, meaning: "If you had not been killing the sons of the Children of Israel, my mother would not have needed to cast me into the river. So you count as a favor upon me what your affliction was the cause of." Al-Azhari mentioned something similar, in more detail.

Al-Mubarrad said: he means that the upbringing happened because of the cause you mentioned, namely the enslavement; that is, your raising me was for the sake of dominating and subjugating my people.

It was also said that there is an implied interrogative in the speech, meaning: "Is that a favor?" This was said by al-Akhfash, and al-Nahhas rejected it.

Al-Farraʾ said: whoever says the speech is a denial means: "Is that a favor?" The meaning of ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ is that you took them as slaves. It is said: ʿabbadtuhu and aʿbadtuhu have the same meaning. This is what al-Farraʾ said. Its grammatical position is nominative, as a substitute (badal) for a favor, with an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ) as its predicate; the genitive is by implied preposition (the bāʾ), and the accusative is by its omission.

(p-1055) Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿then their necks remained humbled before it﴾: he said, "humiliated."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada regarding ﴿and they have a charge against me﴾: he said, "the killing of a soul."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you are of the disbelievers﴾: he said, "ungrateful for the blessing. Pharaoh did not know what disbelief was." And regarding His saying ﴿I did it then, while I was of the astray﴾: he said, "of the ignorant."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾: he said, "You subdued them and used them."

It is Meccan according to the majority. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated this from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Shuʿara was revealed at Mecca, except for five verses at its end, which were revealed at Medina, namely ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them﴾ to the end."

Al-Tabarani narrated in his tafsir from al-Bara', that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah gave me the seven long surahs (al-sab' al-tiwal) in place of the Torah, He gave me the mi'in (surahs of about a hundred verses) in place of the Gospel, He gave me the tawasin (surahs beginning with ṭā-sīn) in place of the Psalms, and He favoured me with the hawamim (surahs beginning with ḥā-mīm) and the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an), which no prophet before me recited."

He also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which the Cow is mentioned from the first Reminder (al-dhikr al-awwal), I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the final verses of Surat al-Baqara from beneath the Throne, and I was given the mufassal as a supererogatory gift (nafila)."

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "It occurs in the tafsir of Malik, narrated from him, that it is named Surat al-Jumuʿa."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm﴾. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the ṭāʾ with imala (a fronting of the vowel, pronounced between a and i). Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Zuhri read it between the two sounds (bayna al-lafzayn). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. The rest read it with a fully lengthened fatha.

The people of Medina, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i assimilated the nūn of "ṭa-sin-n" (ط س ن) into the mīm. Al-A'mash and Hamza made it clear (izhar) without assimilation. Al-Tha'labi said: "Assimilation is the choice of Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim."

Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Zajjaj reported in his book Fima yajri wa-ma la yajri (On what is declined and what is not) that it is permissible to say ṭā sīna mīmu (طا سِينَ مِيمُ) with a fatha on the nūn and a ḍamma on the mīm, as one says 'hadha Ma'di Karib' (this is Ma'di Karib)."

ʿĪsa, and what is transmitted from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasra, as an indeclinable (ʿalā al-binaʾ).

In the Mushaf of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is written as (ط س م), letters separated, so one pauses on each letter with a distinct pause that marks it off from the others. Abu Ja'far also read it this way.

Its place in the grammar is raf' (nominative) if it is a name of the surah, as most scholars hold, or it is the predicate of a omitted subject. It may be in a nasb (accusative) position, with the implied verb "udhkur" (mention) or "iqra'" (recite). If it is recited as a sequence of letters in the manner of enumeration, as has been noted at more than one place in this tafsir, then it has no place in grammatical analysis (la mahalla lahu min al-iʿrab).

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, and it has been said that it is one of the names of the Qur'an. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ refers to the surah. Its place is raf', as it and what follows it are the predicate if we take (ط س م) as the subject. If we take it as the predicate of an omitted subject, its place is raf' as the subject whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition (badal) to (ط س م). The Book here means the Qur'an. Al-Mubin means "the one who makes clear" (al-mudhhir), or "the clear, evident one" if it is from abana in the sense of bana (to be clear).

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself (laʿallaka bakhiʿun nafsaka) that they do not believe﴾: that is, you will kill and destroy yourself. Al-bakh' originally means slaughtering to the point of reaching the nukhaʿ (نُخاع), spelled with a nūn. Al-Qamus says it is a vein at the back of the neck. Its full treatment has passed in Surat al-Kahf. Qatada read bakhiʿu nafsika (باخِعُ نَفْسِكَ) with an idafa (genitive construction), while the rest read it with tanwin (indefinite, separated). Al-Farra' said: "(an) in ﴿that they do not believe﴾ is in the accusative position, because it is a conditional." Al-Nahhas said: "It is said that 'in' (إن) with a kasra is because it is a particle (juz'), and this is the common usage." The view on this is what al-Zajjaj said in his book on the Qur'an: that it is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and the meaning is: "Perhaps you will kill yourself because of their refusal to believe." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he was eager for the faith of his people and deeply grieved at their turning away.

The clause ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven﴾ is a new, independent sentence, intended to give the reason for the preceding consolation. The meaning: If We willed, We would send down upon them from the heaven a sign that would compel them to faith, but the decree has already preceded that We do not send such a thing. The meaning of ﴿their necks remained bowed before it﴾ is that they would become submissive to it, that is, ﴿then their necks would remain bowed...﴾ etc. It has been said that the original form was "fa-zallū lahā khāḍiʿīn" (so they would remain bowed to it), and the word "necks" (aʿnāq) was inserted to add emphasis and vividness, since the necks are the place of humility. It has also been said that when the necks were placed where humility is, they were described with the attributes of rational beings, and so were treated as such and described with what they are described with.

ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar said: "Khāḍiʿīn (masculine plural) and khāḍiʿa (feminine) are the same here," and al-Mubarrad chose this. The meaning is that when their necks are humbled, they themselves are humbled, so reporting about the necks is reporting about their owners. It is permissible in the speech of the Arabs to leave the predicate about the first and report about the second. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"Long nights hastened to wear me down; they folded my length and folded my breadth."

So he reported about the nights and left out "the length" (al-tul). From this is the saying of Jarir:

"I see the passing years have taken from me as the dark period (al-sirar) takes from the crescent."

Abu ʿUbayd and al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is "khāḍiʿīhā hum" (they themselves are its humbled ones). Al-Nahhas considered this weak. Mujahid said: "aʿnāquhum" means their leaders (kubarāʾuhum).

Al-Nahhas said: "This is well known in the language. One says: 'A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me,' meaning leaders among them."

Abu Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "Aʿnāquhum" means their groups (jamaʿātuhum). One says: "A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me," meaning a company.

﴿And there never comes to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful but they turn away from it.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, made clear that, although He is able to make them compelled to faith, He brings them the Qur'an, state after state, and does not renew for them any admonition or reminder except that they renew what is the opposite of the purpose: turning away, denial and mockery. The min in ﴿min dhikrin﴾ is extra, for emphasis of generality. The min in ﴿min rabbihim﴾ denotes the starting point. The exception is a "mufarragh" (exception from a general context) drawn from the most general category; its place is the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the object of ﴿yatīhim﴾ (comes to them). The tafsir of a similar verse has passed in Surat al-Anbiya'.
