It is as if He had said: "Desist from that, O Musa, and go, you and whoever you asked for, and do not fear the Copts (al-Qibt)." ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening.﴾ In this is a reason for the prohibition of fear. It is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]. By this, glorified is He, intended to strengthen their hearts, and that He is the one who takes charge of their protection and safeguarding. He treated the two of them as a plural, so He said "with you" (maʿakum). But two is the least plural according to some of the scholars (al-aʾimma), or because He intended Musa, Harun, and those to whom they were sent. It is also possible that the intended meaning is "both of them with the Children of Israel." "With you" and "listening" may be two predicates of inna, or the predicate is "listening" and "with you" is related to it. The figurative usage (al-majaz) in "with" (al-maʿiyya) is not hidden, since companionship (al-muṣāḥaba) is one of the attributes of physical bodies. So the intended meaning is the being-with of support and help.

﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ The particle الفاء (al-fāʾ, "so") indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. Here the word رَسُول (rasūl, "messenger") is in the singular and not dual, unlike His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. This is because it is used as a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "a message" (risāla), and a verbal noun remains singular. But when it means "one who is sent" (al-mursal), it takes the dual with the dual and the plural with the plural. Abu ʿUbayda said: rasūl here means "a message," and the implied sense is: "Indeed, we are two bearers of the message of the Lord of the worlds." From this is the poet's saying:

*Ah, convey to Abu ʿAmr a message,*
*For I am free of your fataḥa (i.e., your dealings).*

That is, a message.

Al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas said:

*Ah, is there anyone to convey from me to Khufaf a message,*
*Whose house is the end of your family's journey?*

That is, a message.

Abu ʿUbayda also said: rasūl may mean the dual and the plural. The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent (wakīl)," "These two are my messenger and my agent," and "These are my messenger and my agent." From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 77]. It was also said: its meaning is that each one of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. And it was said: since the two of them were mutually supportive and reinforcing in the message, they were in the position of a single messenger.

The أنْ (an, "that") in His saying ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾ is explanatory (mufassira), because the sending implied by "messenger" includes the meaning of saying.

﴿He said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child?"﴾ That is, Pharaoh said to Musa after they came to him and said to him what Allah had commanded them. The phrase فِينا (fīnā, "among us") means "in our care and our homes." By this he intended to remind him of favor and to belittle him: that is, "We raised you with us as a little child, and we did not kill you among those children we killed." ﴿And you stayed among us for years of your life.﴾ Then when was this that you claim? It was said: he stayed among them eighteen years; it was said thirty years; and it was said forty years. Then he rebuked him for killing the Copt, saying: ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾. The word الفَعْلَة (al-faʿla, "deed") with a fatḥa on the fāʾ means a single occurrence of the action. Al-Shaʿbi read فِعْلَتَكَ (fiʿlataka) with a kasra on the fāʾ, but the fatḥa is preferable because it denotes a single occurrence, not a type. The meaning is that when he enumerated the blessings upon him, he mentioned his sins to him, and by "the deed" he meant the killing of the Copt. Then he said: ﴿And you are of the disbelievers﴾, that is, among those who are ungrateful for the blessing, since you killed a man from my people. It was also said that the meaning is: among the disbelievers in the claim that Pharaoh is a god. It was also said: among the disbelievers in Allah according to his own belief, since he was with them on their religion. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was of the astray."﴾ That is, Musa replied to Pharaoh: "I did this deed you mentioned, which is killing the Copt, and at that time I was among the astray," that is, the ignorant. Peace be upon him negated disbelief from himself and informed that he did that out of ignorance before the knowledge Allah taught him came to him. It was also said: the meaning is "among those ignorant that that blow would reach killing." Abu ʿUbayda said: "among the forgetful."

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾, that is, I went out from among you to Madyan, as in the surah of al-Qasas. ﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom (ḥukm)﴾, that is, prophethood, or knowledge and understanding. Al-Zajjaj said: by ḥukm is meant His teaching him the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah.

﴿And made me among the messengers. And is this a favor you count upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾ It was said: this speech from Musa is by way of acknowledging the blessing, as if he said: "Yes, that upbringing is a blessing you count upon me, but that does not negate my messengership." This is what al-Farraʾ and Ibn Jarir said.

It was also said: it is from Musa by way of denial, meaning: "Do you count upon me that you raised me as a child, while you had enslaved the Children of Israel and killed them, and they are my people?"

Al-Zajjaj said: the commentators took this as a denial, namely that what Pharaoh mentioned was a favor upon Musa, while the wording is that of a statement, and in it is a rebuke of the addressee, meaning: "If you had not been killing the sons of the Children of Israel, my mother would not have needed to cast me into the river. So you count as a favor upon me what your affliction was the cause of." Al-Azhari mentioned something similar, in more detail.

Al-Mubarrad said: he means that the upbringing happened because of the cause you mentioned, namely the enslavement; that is, your raising me was for the sake of dominating and subjugating my people.

It was also said that there is an implied interrogative in the speech, meaning: "Is that a favor?" This was said by al-Akhfash, and al-Nahhas rejected it.

Al-Farraʾ said: whoever says the speech is a denial means: "Is that a favor?" The meaning of ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ is that you took them as slaves. It is said: ʿabbadtuhu and aʿbadtuhu have the same meaning. This is what al-Farraʾ said. Its grammatical position is nominative, as a substitute (badal) for a favor, with an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ) as its predicate; the genitive is by implied preposition (the bāʾ), and the accusative is by its omission.

(p-1055) Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿then their necks remained humbled before it﴾: he said, "humiliated."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada regarding ﴿and they have a charge against me﴾: he said, "the killing of a soul."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you are of the disbelievers﴾: he said, "ungrateful for the blessing. Pharaoh did not know what disbelief was." And regarding His saying ﴿I did it then, while I was of the astray﴾: he said, "of the ignorant."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾: he said, "You subdued them and used them."

It is Meccan according to the majority. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated this from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Shuʿara was revealed at Mecca, except for five verses at its end, which were revealed at Medina, namely ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them﴾ to the end."

Al-Tabarani narrated in his tafsir from al-Bara', that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah gave me the seven long surahs (al-sab' al-tiwal) in place of the Torah, He gave me the mi'in (surahs of about a hundred verses) in place of the Gospel, He gave me the tawasin (surahs beginning with ṭā-sīn) in place of the Psalms, and He favoured me with the hawamim (surahs beginning with ḥā-mīm) and the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an), which no prophet before me recited."

He also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which the Cow is mentioned from the first Reminder (al-dhikr al-awwal), I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the final verses of Surat al-Baqara from beneath the Throne, and I was given the mufassal as a supererogatory gift (nafila)."

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "It occurs in the tafsir of Malik, narrated from him, that it is named Surat al-Jumuʿa."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm﴾. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the ṭāʾ with imala (a fronting of the vowel, pronounced between a and i). Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Zuhri read it between the two sounds (bayna al-lafzayn). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. The rest read it with a fully lengthened fatha.

The people of Medina, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i assimilated the nūn of "ṭa-sin-n" (ط س ن) into the mīm. Al-A'mash and Hamza made it clear (izhar) without assimilation. Al-Tha'labi said: "Assimilation is the choice of Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim."

Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Zajjaj reported in his book Fima yajri wa-ma la yajri (On what is declined and what is not) that it is permissible to say ṭā sīna mīmu (طا سِينَ مِيمُ) with a fatha on the nūn and a ḍamma on the mīm, as one says 'hadha Ma'di Karib' (this is Ma'di Karib)."

ʿĪsa, and what is transmitted from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasra, as an indeclinable (ʿalā al-binaʾ).

In the Mushaf of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is written as (ط س م), letters separated, so one pauses on each letter with a distinct pause that marks it off from the others. Abu Ja'far also read it this way.

Its place in the grammar is raf' (nominative) if it is a name of the surah, as most scholars hold, or it is the predicate of a omitted subject. It may be in a nasb (accusative) position, with the implied verb "udhkur" (mention) or "iqra'" (recite). If it is recited as a sequence of letters in the manner of enumeration, as has been noted at more than one place in this tafsir, then it has no place in grammatical analysis (la mahalla lahu min al-iʿrab).

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, and it has been said that it is one of the names of the Qur'an. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ refers to the surah. Its place is raf', as it and what follows it are the predicate if we take (ط س م) as the subject. If we take it as the predicate of an omitted subject, its place is raf' as the subject whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition (badal) to (ط س م). The Book here means the Qur'an. Al-Mubin means "the one who makes clear" (al-mudhhir), or "the clear, evident one" if it is from abana in the sense of bana (to be clear).

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself (laʿallaka bakhiʿun nafsaka) that they do not believe﴾: that is, you will kill and destroy yourself. Al-bakh' originally means slaughtering to the point of reaching the nukhaʿ (نُخاع), spelled with a nūn. Al-Qamus says it is a vein at the back of the neck. Its full treatment has passed in Surat al-Kahf. Qatada read bakhiʿu nafsika (باخِعُ نَفْسِكَ) with an idafa (genitive construction), while the rest read it with tanwin (indefinite, separated). Al-Farra' said: "(an) in ﴿that they do not believe﴾ is in the accusative position, because it is a conditional." Al-Nahhas said: "It is said that 'in' (إن) with a kasra is because it is a particle (juz'), and this is the common usage." The view on this is what al-Zajjaj said in his book on the Qur'an: that it is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and the meaning is: "Perhaps you will kill yourself because of their refusal to believe." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he was eager for the faith of his people and deeply grieved at their turning away.

The clause ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven﴾ is a new, independent sentence, intended to give the reason for the preceding consolation. The meaning: If We willed, We would send down upon them from the heaven a sign that would compel them to faith, but the decree has already preceded that We do not send such a thing. The meaning of ﴿their necks remained bowed before it﴾ is that they would become submissive to it, that is, ﴿then their necks would remain bowed...﴾ etc. It has been said that the original form was "fa-zallū lahā khāḍiʿīn" (so they would remain bowed to it), and the word "necks" (aʿnāq) was inserted to add emphasis and vividness, since the necks are the place of humility. It has also been said that when the necks were placed where humility is, they were described with the attributes of rational beings, and so were treated as such and described with what they are described with.

ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar said: "Khāḍiʿīn (masculine plural) and khāḍiʿa (feminine) are the same here," and al-Mubarrad chose this. The meaning is that when their necks are humbled, they themselves are humbled, so reporting about the necks is reporting about their owners. It is permissible in the speech of the Arabs to leave the predicate about the first and report about the second. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"Long nights hastened to wear me down; they folded my length and folded my breadth."

So he reported about the nights and left out "the length" (al-tul). From this is the saying of Jarir:

"I see the passing years have taken from me as the dark period (al-sirar) takes from the crescent."

Abu ʿUbayd and al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is "khāḍiʿīhā hum" (they themselves are its humbled ones). Al-Nahhas considered this weak. Mujahid said: "aʿnāquhum" means their leaders (kubarāʾuhum).

Al-Nahhas said: "This is well known in the language. One says: 'A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me,' meaning leaders among them."

Abu Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "Aʿnāquhum" means their groups (jamaʿātuhum). One says: "A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me," meaning a company.

﴿And there never comes to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful but they turn away from it.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, made clear that, although He is able to make them compelled to faith, He brings them the Qur'an, state after state, and does not renew for them any admonition or reminder except that they renew what is the opposite of the purpose: turning away, denial and mockery. The min in ﴿min dhikrin﴾ is extra, for emphasis of generality. The min in ﴿min rabbihim﴾ denotes the starting point. The exception is a "mufarragh" (exception from a general context) drawn from the most general category; its place is the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the object of ﴿yatīhim﴾ (comes to them). The tafsir of a similar verse has passed in Surat al-Anbiya'.

﴿So they have denied﴾: that is, they denied the reminder that came to them with an explicit denial, and did not suffice with mere turning away. It has been said that turning away means denial, because whoever turns away from something and does not accept it has denied it. On this view, the mention of denial shows that it came from them explicitly. But the first view is better. Turning away from something is not paying attention to it. Then they moved from that to something worse, which is explicit denial. Then they moved from denial to something even worse, which is mockery, as His saying indicates: ﴿So the news (anbaʾ) of what they used to mock will come to them.﴾ Al-anbaʾ (the news) refers to the punishment they deserve, both in the near term and later. It is called "news" because it is among the things the Qur'an reported about, and He said ﴿what they used to mock﴾ and did not say "what they used to turn away from" or "what they used to deny," because mockery is worse than both and implies them. In this there is a severe warning. The tafsir of a similar expression has passed in Surat al-Anʿam.

Then He mentioned, the Exalted, what shows His complete power, from sensory matters through which whoever reflects on them, looks at them, and reasons from them obtains the greatest proof and the clearest evidence. He said:

﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how much of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ The hamza (ء) is for rebuke (tawbikh), and the waw is for coordination with an implied preceding clause, as in its parallels. Allah, the Exalted, drew attention to His greatness and power, and that these deniers and mockers, if they looked properly, would know that He is the One who deserves to be worshipped. The meaning of zawj (kind) here is "type" (ṣinf).

Al-Farra' said: "It is the colour (lawn)." Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of zawj is 'kind' (nawʿ), and karim means praised." The meaning is: of every beneficial kind, which none can cause to grow except the Lord of the worlds. Karim originally means good and noble. One says "a noble palm" (nakhla karima), meaning one with abundant fruit. "A noble man" (rajul karim) means noble and virtuous. "A noble book" (kitab karim) means one whose meanings are pleasing. A "noble plant" (nabat karim) is one that is pleasing in its benefits.

Al-Shaʿbi said: "People are like the plants of the earth: whoever among them goes to Paradise is noble (karim), and whoever among them goes to the Fire is base (laʾim)."

The reference of ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is to what was mentioned before it. That is: indeed, in what was mentioned of growth in the earth there is a clear proof and a plain sign of the complete power of Allah, the Exalted, and the wondrous artistry of His creation.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed that most of these people persist in their error, insisting on their rejection, denial and mockery. He said: ﴿And most of them were not believers.﴾ That is: there was a prior knowledge (sabq ʿilmi) in Him that they would be like this.

Sibawayh said: "Kāna (was) here is a filler (ṣila)."

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾ That is: the Dominant, the Subduer of these people, by taking vengeance on them, while being abundant in mercy. For this reason He gave them respite and did not hasten to punish them. Or the meaning is: He takes vengeance on His enemies and is merciful to His friends.

The clause ﴿And when your Lord called Moses...﴾ and so on is a new sentence, intended to confirm what preceded it of turning away, denial and mockery. The factor governing the adverbial time expression is omitted, and its estimated form is: "Recite, when He called," or "Mention." Al-nida' means calling (al-duʿa'). The ʾan in His saying ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾ may be explanatory (mufassira) or verbal-source (maṣdariyya). Their description as wrongdoers is because they combined disbelief, by which they wronged themselves, with the sins by which they wronged others, such as enslaving the children of Israel and slaughtering their sons.

﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾ is in the accusative position, either as an apposition (badal) or as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "the wrongdoing people." The meaning of ﴿Will they not be wary?﴾ is: will they not fear the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, so that they avert Allah's punishment from themselves by obeying Him?

It has been said that the meaning is: "Say to them: Will you not be wary?" It came with the yāʾ (third person) because they were absent at the time of address. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Abu Hazim read ﴿Will you not be wary?﴾ with the second person (tāʾ fawqiyya), that is, "Say to them that." A similar example is ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome﴾ [Al ʿImran 12], read with both the third and second person.

﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear they will deny me."﴾ That is: Moses said this statement, and the meaning is: I fear they will deny me regarding the message. ﴿And my chest tightens and my tongue does not speak freely﴾: these two are coordinated with "I fear." That is: my chest tightens because of their denial of me, and my tongue does not speak freely in delivering the message.

The majority read ﴿tightens﴾ and ﴿does not speak freely﴾ with ḍamma (nominative), coordinated with "I fear," as we mentioned, or as a new sentence (istiʾnaf). Yaʿqub, ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar and Abu Haywa read both with a fatha (accusative), coordinated with "they will deny me." Al-Farra' said: "Both readings have a basis." Al-Nahhas said: "The better is the nominative, because the accusative is coordinated with 'they will deny me,' and this is distant."

﴿So send to Harun﴾: that is, send to him Gabriel with the revelation, so that he may be with me as a messenger, a helper, a supporter, an assistant. He did not mention the helping here because it is known from other places, such as His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿and appoint for me a helper﴾ [Ta-Ha 29], and in al-Qasas: ﴿so send him with me as a supporter to confirm me﴾ [al-Qasas 34]. This request from Moses, peace be upon him, is a request for help by sending his brother, not a request to be excused from the message, nor a hesitation in swiftly obeying.

﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me.﴾ The charge (dhanb) is his killing of the Copt. He called it a dhanb according to their claim. Moses feared they would kill him for it. In this is evidence that fear may occur even among prophets, let alone among the virtuous. Then Allah, the Exalted, answered him with what contains a kind of deterrence and a measure of rebuke.

(p-1053)

He said, "No! So go, both of you, with Our signs." Within this reply is Musa's acceptance of his request that his brother be joined with him, as the address directed at both of them indicates. It is as if He had said: "Desist from that, O Musa, and go, you and whoever you asked for, and do not fear the Copts (al-Qibt)." ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening.﴾ In this is a reason for the prohibition of fear. It is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]. By this, glorified is He, intended to strengthen their hearts, and that He is the one who takes charge of their protection and safeguarding. He treated the two of them as a plural, so He said "with you" (maʿakum). But two is the least plural according to some of the scholars (al-aʾimma), or because He intended Musa, Harun, and those to whom they were sent. It is also possible that the intended meaning is "both of them with the Children of Israel." "With you" and "listening" may be two predicates of inna, or the predicate is "listening" and "with you" is related to it. The figurative usage (al-majaz) in "with" (al-maʿiyya) is not hidden, since companionship (al-muṣāḥaba) is one of the attributes of physical bodies. So the intended meaning is the being-with of support and help.

﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ The particle الفاء (al-fāʾ, "so") indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. Here the word رَسُول (rasūl, "messenger") is in the singular and not dual, unlike His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. This is because it is used as a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "a message" (risāla), and a verbal noun remains singular. But when it means "one who is sent" (al-mursal), it takes the dual with the dual and the plural with the plural. Abu ʿUbayda said: rasūl here means "a message," and the implied sense is: "Indeed, we are two bearers of the message of the Lord of the worlds." From this is the poet's saying:

*Ah, convey to Abu ʿAmr a message,*
*For I am free of your fataḥa (i.e., your dealings).*

That is, a message.

Al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas said:

*Ah, is there anyone to convey from me to Khufaf a message,*
*Whose house is the end of your family's journey?*

That is, a message.

Abu ʿUbayda also said: rasūl may mean the dual and the plural. The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent (wakīl)," "These two are my messenger and my agent," and "These are my messenger and my agent." From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 77]. It was also said: its meaning is that each one of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. And it was said: since the two of them were mutually supportive and reinforcing in the message, they were in the position of a single messenger.

The أنْ (an, "that") in His saying ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾ is explanatory (mufassira), because the sending implied by "messenger" includes the meaning of saying.

﴿He said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child?"﴾ That is, Pharaoh said to Musa after they came to him and said to him what Allah had commanded them. The phrase فِينا (fīnā, "among us") means "in our care and our homes." By this he intended to remind him of favor and to belittle him: that is, "We raised you with us as a little child, and we did not kill you among those children we killed." ﴿And you stayed among us for years of your life.﴾ Then when was this that you claim? It was said: he stayed among them eighteen years; it was said thirty years; and it was said forty years. Then he rebuked him for killing the Copt, saying: ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾. The word الفَعْلَة (al-faʿla, "deed") with a fatḥa on the fāʾ means a single occurrence of the action. Al-Shaʿbi read فِعْلَتَكَ (fiʿlataka) with a kasra on the fāʾ, but the fatḥa is preferable because it denotes a single occurrence, not a type. The meaning is that when he enumerated the blessings upon him, he mentioned his sins to him, and by "the deed" he meant the killing of the Copt. Then he said: ﴿And you are of the disbelievers﴾, that is, among those who are ungrateful for the blessing, since you killed a man from my people. It was also said that the meaning is: among the disbelievers in the claim that Pharaoh is a god. It was also said: among the disbelievers in Allah according to his own belief, since he was with them on their religion. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was of the astray."﴾ That is, Musa replied to Pharaoh: "I did this deed you mentioned, which is killing the Copt, and at that time I was among the astray," that is, the ignorant. Peace be upon him negated disbelief from himself and informed that he did that out of ignorance before the knowledge Allah taught him came to him. It was also said: the meaning is "among those ignorant that that blow would reach killing." Abu ʿUbayda said: "among the forgetful."

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾, that is, I went out from among you to Madyan, as in the surah of al-Qasas. ﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom (ḥukm)﴾, that is, prophethood, or knowledge and understanding. Al-Zajjaj said: by ḥukm is meant His teaching him the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah.

﴿And made me among the messengers. And is this a favor you count upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾ It was said: this speech from Musa is by way of acknowledging the blessing, as if he said: "Yes, that upbringing is a blessing you count upon me, but that does not negate my messengership." This is what al-Farraʾ and Ibn Jarir said.

It was also said: it is from Musa by way of denial, meaning: "Do you count upon me that you raised me as a child, while you had enslaved the Children of Israel and killed them, and they are my people?"

Al-Zajjaj said: the commentators took this as a denial, namely that what Pharaoh mentioned was a favor upon Musa, while the wording is that of a statement, and in it is a rebuke of the addressee, meaning: "If you had not been killing the sons of the Children of Israel, my mother would not have needed to cast me into the river. So you count as a favor upon me what your affliction was the cause of." Al-Azhari mentioned something similar, in more detail.

Al-Mubarrad said: he means that the upbringing happened because of the cause you mentioned, namely the enslavement; that is, your raising me was for the sake of dominating and subjugating my people.

It was also said that there is an implied interrogative in the speech, meaning: "Is that a favor?" This was said by al-Akhfash, and al-Nahhas rejected it.

Al-Farraʾ said: whoever says the speech is a denial means: "Is that a favor?" The meaning of ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ is that you took them as slaves. It is said: ʿabbadtuhu and aʿbadtuhu have the same meaning. This is what al-Farraʾ said. Its grammatical position is nominative, as a substitute (badal) for a favor, with an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ) as its predicate; the genitive is by implied preposition (the bāʾ), and the accusative is by its omission.

(p-1055) Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿then their necks remained humbled before it﴾: he said, "humiliated."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada regarding ﴿and they have a charge against me﴾: he said, "the killing of a soul."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you are of the disbelievers﴾: he said, "ungrateful for the blessing. Pharaoh did not know what disbelief was." And regarding His saying ﴿I did it then, while I was of the astray﴾: he said, "of the ignorant."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾: he said, "You subdued them and used them."

It is Meccan according to the majority. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated this from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Shuʿara was revealed at Mecca, except for five verses at its end, which were revealed at Medina, namely ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them﴾ to the end."

Al-Tabarani narrated in his tafsir from al-Bara', that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah gave me the seven long surahs (al-sab' al-tiwal) in place of the Torah, He gave me the mi'in (surahs of about a hundred verses) in place of the Gospel, He gave me the tawasin (surahs beginning with ṭā-sīn) in place of the Psalms, and He favoured me with the hawamim (surahs beginning with ḥā-mīm) and the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an), which no prophet before me recited."

He also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which the Cow is mentioned from the first Reminder (al-dhikr al-awwal), I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the final verses of Surat al-Baqara from beneath the Throne, and I was given the mufassal as a supererogatory gift (nafila)."

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "It occurs in the tafsir of Malik, narrated from him, that it is named Surat al-Jumuʿa."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm﴾. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the ṭāʾ with imala (a fronting of the vowel, pronounced between a and i). Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Zuhri read it between the two sounds (bayna al-lafzayn). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. The rest read it with a fully lengthened fatha.

The people of Medina, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i assimilated the nūn of "ṭa-sin-n" (ط س ن) into the mīm. Al-A'mash and Hamza made it clear (izhar) without assimilation. Al-Tha'labi said: "Assimilation is the choice of Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim."

Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Zajjaj reported in his book Fima yajri wa-ma la yajri (On what is declined and what is not) that it is permissible to say ṭā sīna mīmu (طا سِينَ مِيمُ) with a fatha on the nūn and a ḍamma on the mīm, as one says 'hadha Ma'di Karib' (this is Ma'di Karib)."

ʿĪsa, and what is transmitted from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasra, as an indeclinable (ʿalā al-binaʾ).

In the Mushaf of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is written as (ط س م), letters separated, so one pauses on each letter with a distinct pause that marks it off from the others. Abu Ja'far also read it this way.

Its place in the grammar is raf' (nominative) if it is a name of the surah, as most scholars hold, or it is the predicate of a omitted subject. It may be in a nasb (accusative) position, with the implied verb "udhkur" (mention) or "iqra'" (recite). If it is recited as a sequence of letters in the manner of enumeration, as has been noted at more than one place in this tafsir, then it has no place in grammatical analysis (la mahalla lahu min al-iʿrab).

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, and it has been said that it is one of the names of the Qur'an. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ refers to the surah. Its place is raf', as it and what follows it are the predicate if we take (ط س م) as the subject. If we take it as the predicate of an omitted subject, its place is raf' as the subject whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition (badal) to (ط س م). The Book here means the Qur'an. Al-Mubin means "the one who makes clear" (al-mudhhir), or "the clear, evident one" if it is from abana in the sense of bana (to be clear).

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself (laʿallaka bakhiʿun nafsaka) that they do not believe﴾: that is, you will kill and destroy yourself. Al-bakh' originally means slaughtering to the point of reaching the nukhaʿ (نُخاع), spelled with a nūn. Al-Qamus says it is a vein at the back of the neck. Its full treatment has passed in Surat al-Kahf. Qatada read bakhiʿu nafsika (باخِعُ نَفْسِكَ) with an idafa (genitive construction), while the rest read it with tanwin (indefinite, separated). Al-Farra' said: "(an) in ﴿that they do not believe﴾ is in the accusative position, because it is a conditional." Al-Nahhas said: "It is said that 'in' (إن) with a kasra is because it is a particle (juz'), and this is the common usage." The view on this is what al-Zajjaj said in his book on the Qur'an: that it is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and the meaning is: "Perhaps you will kill yourself because of their refusal to believe." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he was eager for the faith of his people and deeply grieved at their turning away.

The clause ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven﴾ is a new, independent sentence, intended to give the reason for the preceding consolation. The meaning: If We willed, We would send down upon them from the heaven a sign that would compel them to faith, but the decree has already preceded that We do not send such a thing. The meaning of ﴿their necks remained bowed before it﴾ is that they would become submissive to it, that is, ﴿then their necks would remain bowed...﴾ etc. It has been said that the original form was "fa-zallū lahā khāḍiʿīn" (so they would remain bowed to it), and the word "necks" (aʿnāq) was inserted to add emphasis and vividness, since the necks are the place of humility. It has also been said that when the necks were placed where humility is, they were described with the attributes of rational beings, and so were treated as such and described with what they are described with.

ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar said: "Khāḍiʿīn (masculine plural) and khāḍiʿa (feminine) are the same here," and al-Mubarrad chose this. The meaning is that when their necks are humbled, they themselves are humbled, so reporting about the necks is reporting about their owners. It is permissible in the speech of the Arabs to leave the predicate about the first and report about the second. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"Long nights hastened to wear me down; they folded my length and folded my breadth."

So he reported about the nights and left out "the length" (al-tul). From this is the saying of Jarir:

"I see the passing years have taken from me as the dark period (al-sirar) takes from the crescent."

Abu ʿUbayd and al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is "khāḍiʿīhā hum" (they themselves are its humbled ones). Al-Nahhas considered this weak. Mujahid said: "aʿnāquhum" means their leaders (kubarāʾuhum).

Al-Nahhas said: "This is well known in the language. One says: 'A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me,' meaning leaders among them."

Abu Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "Aʿnāquhum" means their groups (jamaʿātuhum). One says: "A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me," meaning a company.

﴿And there never comes to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful but they turn away from it.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, made clear that, although He is able to make them compelled to faith, He brings them the Qur'an, state after state, and does not renew for them any admonition or reminder except that they renew what is the opposite of the purpose: turning away, denial and mockery. The min in ﴿min dhikrin﴾ is extra, for emphasis of generality. The min in ﴿min rabbihim﴾ denotes the starting point. The exception is a "mufarragh" (exception from a general context) drawn from the most general category; its place is the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the object of ﴿yatīhim﴾ (comes to them). The tafsir of a similar verse has passed in Surat al-Anbiya'.

﴿So they have denied﴾: that is, they denied the reminder that came to them with an explicit denial, and did not suffice with mere turning away. It has been said that turning away means denial, because whoever turns away from something and does not accept it has denied it. On this view, the mention of denial shows that it came from them explicitly. But the first view is better. Turning away from something is not paying attention to it. Then they moved from that to something worse, which is explicit denial. Then they moved from denial to something even worse, which is mockery, as His saying indicates: ﴿So the news (anbaʾ) of what they used to mock will come to them.﴾ Al-anbaʾ (the news) refers to the punishment they deserve, both in the near term and later. It is called "news" because it is among the things the Qur'an reported about, and He said ﴿what they used to mock﴾ and did not say "what they used to turn away from" or "what they used to deny," because mockery is worse than both and implies them. In this there is a severe warning. The tafsir of a similar expression has passed in Surat al-Anʿam.

Then He mentioned, the Exalted, what shows His complete power, from sensory matters through which whoever reflects on them, looks at them, and reasons from them obtains the greatest proof and the clearest evidence. He said:

﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how much of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ The hamza (ء) is for rebuke (tawbikh), and the waw is for coordination with an implied preceding clause, as in its parallels. Allah, the Exalted, drew attention to His greatness and power, and that these deniers and mockers, if they looked properly, would know that He is the One who deserves to be worshipped. The meaning of zawj (kind) here is "type" (ṣinf).

Al-Farra' said: "It is the colour (lawn)." Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of zawj is 'kind' (nawʿ), and karim means praised." The meaning is: of every beneficial kind, which none can cause to grow except the Lord of the worlds. Karim originally means good and noble. One says "a noble palm" (nakhla karima), meaning one with abundant fruit. "A noble man" (rajul karim) means noble and virtuous. "A noble book" (kitab karim) means one whose meanings are pleasing. A "noble plant" (nabat karim) is one that is pleasing in its benefits.

Al-Shaʿbi said: "People are like the plants of the earth: whoever among them goes to Paradise is noble (karim), and whoever among them goes to the Fire is base (laʾim)."

The reference of ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is to what was mentioned before it. That is: indeed, in what was mentioned of growth in the earth there is a clear proof and a plain sign of the complete power of Allah, the Exalted, and the wondrous artistry of His creation.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed that most of these people persist in their error, insisting on their rejection, denial and mockery. He said: ﴿And most of them were not believers.﴾ That is: there was a prior knowledge (sabq ʿilmi) in Him that they would be like this.

Sibawayh said: "Kāna (was) here is a filler (ṣila)."

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾ That is: the Dominant, the Subduer of these people, by taking vengeance on them, while being abundant in mercy. For this reason He gave them respite and did not hasten to punish them. Or the meaning is: He takes vengeance on His enemies and is merciful to His friends.

The clause ﴿And when your Lord called Moses...﴾ and so on is a new sentence, intended to confirm what preceded it of turning away, denial and mockery. The factor governing the adverbial time expression is omitted, and its estimated form is: "Recite, when He called," or "Mention." Al-nida' means calling (al-duʿa'). The ʾan in His saying ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾ may be explanatory (mufassira) or verbal-source (maṣdariyya). Their description as wrongdoers is because they combined disbelief, by which they wronged themselves, with the sins by which they wronged others, such as enslaving the children of Israel and slaughtering their sons.

﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾ is in the accusative position, either as an apposition (badal) or as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "the wrongdoing people." The meaning of ﴿Will they not be wary?﴾ is: will they not fear the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, so that they avert Allah's punishment from themselves by obeying Him?

It has been said that the meaning is: "Say to them: Will you not be wary?" It came with the yāʾ (third person) because they were absent at the time of address. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Abu Hazim read ﴿Will you not be wary?﴾ with the second person (tāʾ fawqiyya), that is, "Say to them that." A similar example is ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome﴾ [Al ʿImran 12], read with both the third and second person.

﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear they will deny me."﴾ That is: Moses said this statement, and the meaning is: I fear they will deny me regarding the message. ﴿And my chest tightens and my tongue does not speak freely﴾: these two are coordinated with "I fear." That is: my chest tightens because of their denial of me, and my tongue does not speak freely in delivering the message.

The majority read ﴿tightens﴾ and ﴿does not speak freely﴾ with ḍamma (nominative), coordinated with "I fear," as we mentioned, or as a new sentence (istiʾnaf). Yaʿqub, ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar and Abu Haywa read both with a fatha (accusative), coordinated with "they will deny me." Al-Farra' said: "Both readings have a basis." Al-Nahhas said: "The better is the nominative, because the accusative is coordinated with 'they will deny me,' and this is distant."

﴿So send to Harun﴾: that is, send to him Gabriel with the revelation, so that he may be with me as a messenger, a helper, a supporter, an assistant. He did not mention the helping here because it is known from other places, such as His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿and appoint for me a helper﴾ [Ta-Ha 29], and in al-Qasas: ﴿so send him with me as a supporter to confirm me﴾ [al-Qasas 34]. This request from Moses, peace be upon him, is a request for help by sending his brother, not a request to be excused from the message, nor a hesitation in swiftly obeying.

﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me.﴾ The charge (dhanb) is his killing of the Copt. He called it a dhanb according to their claim. Moses feared they would kill him for it. In this is evidence that fear may occur even among prophets, let alone among the virtuous. Then Allah, the Exalted, answered him with what contains a kind of deterrence and a measure of rebuke.

(p-1053)

He said, "No! So go, both of you, with Our signs." Within this reply is Musa's acceptance of his request that his brother be joined with him, as the address directed at both of them indicates. It is as if He had said: "Desist from that, O Musa, and go, you and whoever you asked for, and do not fear the Copts (al-Qibt)." ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening.﴾ In this is a reason for the prohibition of fear. It is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]. By this, glorified is He, intended to strengthen their hearts, and that He is the one who takes charge of their protection and safeguarding. He treated the two of them as a plural, so He said "with you" (maʿakum). But two is the least plural according to some of the scholars (al-aʾimma), or because He intended Musa, Harun, and those to whom they were sent. It is also possible that the intended meaning is "both of them with the Children of Israel." "With you" and "listening" may be two predicates of inna, or the predicate is "listening" and "with you" is related to it. The figurative usage (al-majaz) in "with" (al-maʿiyya) is not hidden, since companionship (al-muṣāḥaba) is one of the attributes of physical bodies. So the intended meaning is the being-with of support and help.

﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ The particle الفاء (al-fāʾ, "so") indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. Here the word رَسُول (rasūl, "messenger") is in the singular and not dual, unlike His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. This is because it is used as a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "a message" (risāla), and a verbal noun remains singular. But when it means "one who is sent" (al-mursal), it takes the dual with the dual and the plural with the plural. Abu ʿUbayda said: rasūl here means "a message," and the implied sense is: "Indeed, we are two bearers of the message of the Lord of the worlds." From this is the poet's saying:

*Ah, convey to Abu ʿAmr a message,*
*For I am free of your fataḥa (i.e., your dealings).*

That is, a message.

Al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas said:

*Ah, is there anyone to convey from me to Khufaf a message,*
*Whose house is the end of your family's journey?*

That is, a message.

Abu ʿUbayda also said: rasūl may mean the dual and the plural. The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent (wakīl)," "These two are my messenger and my agent," and "These are my messenger and my agent." From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 77]. It was also said: its meaning is that each one of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. And it was said: since the two of them were mutually supportive and reinforcing in the message, they were in the position of a single messenger.

The أنْ (an, "that") in His saying ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾ is explanatory (mufassira), because the sending implied by "messenger" includes the meaning of saying.

﴿He said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child?"﴾ That is, Pharaoh said to Musa after they came to him and said to him what Allah had commanded them. The phrase فِينا (fīnā, "among us") means "in our care and our homes." By this he intended to remind him of favor and to belittle him: that is, "We raised you with us as a little child, and we did not kill you among those children we killed." ﴿And you stayed among us for years of your life.﴾ Then when was this that you claim? It was said: he stayed among them eighteen years; it was said thirty years; and it was said forty years. Then he rebuked him for killing the Copt, saying: ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾. The word الفَعْلَة (al-faʿla, "deed") with a fatḥa on the fāʾ means a single occurrence of the action. Al-Shaʿbi read فِعْلَتَكَ (fiʿlataka) with a kasra on the fāʾ, but the fatḥa is preferable because it denotes a single occurrence, not a type. The meaning is that when he enumerated the blessings upon him, he mentioned his sins to him, and by "the deed" he meant the killing of the Copt. Then he said: ﴿And you are of the disbelievers﴾, that is, among those who are ungrateful for the blessing, since you killed a man from my people. It was also said that the meaning is: among the disbelievers in the claim that Pharaoh is a god. It was also said: among the disbelievers in Allah according to his own belief, since he was with them on their religion. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was of the astray."﴾ That is, Musa replied to Pharaoh: "I did this deed you mentioned, which is killing the Copt, and at that time I was among the astray," that is, the ignorant. Peace be upon him negated disbelief from himself and informed that he did that out of ignorance before the knowledge Allah taught him came to him. It was also said: the meaning is "among those ignorant that that blow would reach killing." Abu ʿUbayda said: "among the forgetful."

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾, that is, I went out from among you to Madyan, as in the surah of al-Qasas. ﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom (ḥukm)﴾, that is, prophethood, or knowledge and understanding. Al-Zajjaj said: by ḥukm is meant His teaching him the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah.

﴿And made me among the messengers. And is this a favor you count upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾ It was said: this speech from Musa is by way of acknowledging the blessing, as if he said: "Yes, that upbringing is a blessing you count upon me, but that does not negate my messengership." This is what al-Farraʾ and Ibn Jarir said.

It was also said: it is from Musa by way of denial, meaning: "Do you count upon me that you raised me as a child, while you had enslaved the Children of Israel and killed them, and they are my people?"

Al-Zajjaj said: the commentators took this as a denial, namely that what Pharaoh mentioned was a favor upon Musa, while the wording is that of a statement, and in it is a rebuke of the addressee, meaning: "If you had not been killing the sons of the Children of Israel, my mother would not have needed to cast me into the river. So you count as a favor upon me what your affliction was the cause of." Al-Azhari mentioned something similar, in more detail.

Al-Mubarrad said: he means that the upbringing happened because of the cause you mentioned, namely the enslavement; that is, your raising me was for the sake of dominating and subjugating my people.

It was also said that there is an implied interrogative in the speech, meaning: "Is that a favor?" This was said by al-Akhfash, and al-Nahhas rejected it.

Al-Farraʾ said: whoever says the speech is a denial means: "Is that a favor?" The meaning of ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ is that you took them as slaves. It is said: ʿabbadtuhu and aʿbadtuhu have the same meaning. This is what al-Farraʾ said. Its grammatical position is nominative, as a substitute (badal) for a favor, with an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ) as its predicate; the genitive is by implied preposition (the bāʾ), and the accusative is by its omission.

(p-1055) Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿then their necks remained humbled before it﴾: he said, "humiliated."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada regarding ﴿and they have a charge against me﴾: he said, "the killing of a soul."

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you are of the disbelievers﴾: he said, "ungrateful for the blessing. Pharaoh did not know what disbelief was." And regarding His saying ﴿I did it then, while I was of the astray﴾: he said, "of the ignorant."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾: he said, "You subdued them and used them."

It is Meccan according to the majority. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated this from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Shuʿara was revealed at Mecca, except for five verses at its end, which were revealed at Medina, namely ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them﴾ to the end."

Al-Tabarani narrated in his tafsir from al-Bara', that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah gave me the seven long surahs (al-sab' al-tiwal) in place of the Torah, He gave me the mi'in (surahs of about a hundred verses) in place of the Gospel, He gave me the tawasin (surahs beginning with ṭā-sīn) in place of the Psalms, and He favoured me with the hawamim (surahs beginning with ḥā-mīm) and the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an), which no prophet before me recited."

He also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was given the surah in which the Cow is mentioned from the first Reminder (al-dhikr al-awwal), I was given the openings of the Qur'an and the final verses of Surat al-Baqara from beneath the Throne, and I was given the mufassal as a supererogatory gift (nafila)."

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: "It occurs in the tafsir of Malik, narrated from him, that it is named Surat al-Jumuʿa."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm﴾. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read the ṭāʾ with imala (a fronting of the vowel, pronounced between a and i). Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Zuhri read it between the two sounds (bayna al-lafzayn). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. The rest read it with a fully lengthened fatha.

The people of Medina, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim and al-Kisa'i assimilated the nūn of "ṭa-sin-n" (ط س ن) into the mīm. Al-A'mash and Hamza made it clear (izhar) without assimilation. Al-Tha'labi said: "Assimilation is the choice of Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim."

Al-Nahhas said: "Al-Zajjaj reported in his book Fima yajri wa-ma la yajri (On what is declined and what is not) that it is permissible to say ṭā sīna mīmu (طا سِينَ مِيمُ) with a fatha on the nūn and a ḍamma on the mīm, as one says 'hadha Ma'di Karib' (this is Ma'di Karib)."

ʿĪsa, and what is transmitted from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasra, as an indeclinable (ʿalā al-binaʾ).

In the Mushaf of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is written as (ط س م), letters separated, so one pauses on each letter with a distinct pause that marks it off from the others. Abu Ja'far also read it this way.

Its place in the grammar is raf' (nominative) if it is a name of the surah, as most scholars hold, or it is the predicate of a omitted subject. It may be in a nasb (accusative) position, with the implied verb "udhkur" (mention) or "iqra'" (recite). If it is recited as a sequence of letters in the manner of enumeration, as has been noted at more than one place in this tafsir, then it has no place in grammatical analysis (la mahalla lahu min al-iʿrab).

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, and it has been said that it is one of the names of the Qur'an. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ refers to the surah. Its place is raf', as it and what follows it are the predicate if we take (ط س م) as the subject. If we take it as the predicate of an omitted subject, its place is raf' as the subject whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition (badal) to (ط س م). The Book here means the Qur'an. Al-Mubin means "the one who makes clear" (al-mudhhir), or "the clear, evident one" if it is from abana in the sense of bana (to be clear).

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself (laʿallaka bakhiʿun nafsaka) that they do not believe﴾: that is, you will kill and destroy yourself. Al-bakh' originally means slaughtering to the point of reaching the nukhaʿ (نُخاع), spelled with a nūn. Al-Qamus says it is a vein at the back of the neck. Its full treatment has passed in Surat al-Kahf. Qatada read bakhiʿu nafsika (باخِعُ نَفْسِكَ) with an idafa (genitive construction), while the rest read it with tanwin (indefinite, separated). Al-Farra' said: "(an) in ﴿that they do not believe﴾ is in the accusative position, because it is a conditional." Al-Nahhas said: "It is said that 'in' (إن) with a kasra is because it is a particle (juz'), and this is the common usage." The view on this is what al-Zajjaj said in his book on the Qur'an: that it is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and the meaning is: "Perhaps you will kill yourself because of their refusal to believe." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he was eager for the faith of his people and deeply grieved at their turning away.

The clause ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven﴾ is a new, independent sentence, intended to give the reason for the preceding consolation. The meaning: If We willed, We would send down upon them from the heaven a sign that would compel them to faith, but the decree has already preceded that We do not send such a thing. The meaning of ﴿their necks remained bowed before it﴾ is that they would become submissive to it, that is, ﴿then their necks would remain bowed...﴾ etc. It has been said that the original form was "fa-zallū lahā khāḍiʿīn" (so they would remain bowed to it), and the word "necks" (aʿnāq) was inserted to add emphasis and vividness, since the necks are the place of humility. It has also been said that when the necks were placed where humility is, they were described with the attributes of rational beings, and so were treated as such and described with what they are described with.

ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar said: "Khāḍiʿīn (masculine plural) and khāḍiʿa (feminine) are the same here," and al-Mubarrad chose this. The meaning is that when their necks are humbled, they themselves are humbled, so reporting about the necks is reporting about their owners. It is permissible in the speech of the Arabs to leave the predicate about the first and report about the second. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"Long nights hastened to wear me down; they folded my length and folded my breadth."

So he reported about the nights and left out "the length" (al-tul). From this is the saying of Jarir:

"I see the passing years have taken from me as the dark period (al-sirar) takes from the crescent."

Abu ʿUbayd and al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is "khāḍiʿīhā hum" (they themselves are its humbled ones). Al-Nahhas considered this weak. Mujahid said: "aʿnāquhum" means their leaders (kubarāʾuhum).

Al-Nahhas said: "This is well known in the language. One says: 'A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me,' meaning leaders among them."

Abu Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "Aʿnāquhum" means their groups (jamaʿātuhum). One says: "A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me," meaning a company.

﴿And there never comes to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful but they turn away from it.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, made clear that, although He is able to make them compelled to faith, He brings them the Qur'an, state after state, and does not renew for them any admonition or reminder except that they renew what is the opposite of the purpose: turning away, denial and mockery. The min in ﴿min dhikrin﴾ is extra, for emphasis of generality. The min in ﴿min rabbihim﴾ denotes the starting point. The exception is a "mufarragh" (exception from a general context) drawn from the most general category; its place is the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the object of ﴿yatīhim﴾ (comes to them). The tafsir of a similar verse has passed in Surat al-Anbiya'.

﴿So they have denied﴾: that is, they denied the reminder that came to them with an explicit denial, and did not suffice with mere turning away. It has been said that turning away means denial, because whoever turns away from something and does not accept it has denied it. On this view, the mention of denial shows that it came from them explicitly. But the first view is better. Turning away from something is not paying attention to it. Then they moved from that to something worse, which is explicit denial. Then they moved from denial to something even worse, which is mockery, as His saying indicates: ﴿So the news (anbaʾ) of what they used to mock will come to them.﴾ Al-anbaʾ (the news) refers to the punishment they deserve, both in the near term and later. It is called "news" because it is among the things the Qur'an reported about, and He said ﴿what they used to mock﴾ and did not say "what they used to turn away from" or "what they used to deny," because mockery is worse than both and implies them. In this there is a severe warning. The tafsir of a similar expression has passed in Surat al-Anʿam.

Then He mentioned, the Exalted, what shows His complete power, from sensory matters through which whoever reflects on them, looks at them, and reasons from them obtains the greatest proof and the clearest evidence. He said:

﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how much of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ The hamza (ء) is for rebuke (tawbikh), and the waw is for coordination with an implied preceding clause, as in its parallels. Allah, the Exalted, drew attention to His greatness and power, and that these deniers and mockers, if they looked properly, would know that He is the One who deserves to be worshipped. The meaning of zawj (kind) here is "type" (ṣinf).

Al-Farra' said: "It is the colour (lawn)." Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning of zawj is 'kind' (nawʿ), and karim means praised." The meaning is: of every beneficial kind, which none can cause to grow except the Lord of the worlds. Karim originally means good and noble. One says "a noble palm" (nakhla karima), meaning one with abundant fruit. "A noble man" (rajul karim) means noble and virtuous. "A noble book" (kitab karim) means one whose meanings are pleasing. A "noble plant" (nabat karim) is one that is pleasing in its benefits.

Al-Shaʿbi said: "People are like the plants of the earth: whoever among them goes to Paradise is noble (karim), and whoever among them goes to the Fire is base (laʾim)."

The reference of ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is to what was mentioned before it. That is: indeed, in what was mentioned of growth in the earth there is a clear proof and a plain sign of the complete power of Allah, the Exalted, and the wondrous artistry of His creation.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed that most of these people persist in their error, insisting on their rejection, denial and mockery. He said: ﴿And most of them were not believers.﴾ That is: there was a prior knowledge (sabq ʿilmi) in Him that they would be like this.

Sibawayh said: "Kāna (was) here is a filler (ṣila)."

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty, the Most Merciful.﴾ That is: the Dominant, the Subduer of these people, by taking vengeance on them, while being abundant in mercy. For this reason He gave them respite and did not hasten to punish them. Or the meaning is: He takes vengeance on His enemies and is merciful to His friends.

The clause ﴿And when your Lord called Moses...﴾ and so on is a new sentence, intended to confirm what preceded it of turning away, denial and mockery. The factor governing the adverbial time expression is omitted, and its estimated form is: "Recite, when He called," or "Mention." Al-nida' means calling (al-duʿa'). The ʾan in His saying ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾ may be explanatory (mufassira) or verbal-source (maṣdariyya). Their description as wrongdoers is because they combined disbelief, by which they wronged themselves, with the sins by which they wronged others, such as enslaving the children of Israel and slaughtering their sons.

﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾ is in the accusative position, either as an apposition (badal) or as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "the wrongdoing people." The meaning of ﴿Will they not be wary?﴾ is: will they not fear the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, so that they avert Allah's punishment from themselves by obeying Him?

It has been said that the meaning is: "Say to them: Will you not be wary?" It came with the yāʾ (third person) because they were absent at the time of address. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Abu Hazim read ﴿Will you not be wary?﴾ with the second person (tāʾ fawqiyya), that is, "Say to them that." A similar example is ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome﴾ [Al ʿImran 12], read with both the third and second person.

﴿He said: "My Lord, I fear they will deny me."﴾ That is: Moses said this statement, and the meaning is: I fear they will deny me regarding the message. ﴿And my chest tightens and my tongue does not speak freely﴾: these two are coordinated with "I fear." That is: my chest tightens because of their denial of me, and my tongue does not speak freely in delivering the message.

The majority read ﴿tightens﴾ and ﴿does not speak freely﴾ with ḍamma (nominative), coordinated with "I fear," as we mentioned, or as a new sentence (istiʾnaf). Yaʿqub, ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar and Abu Haywa read both with a fatha (accusative), coordinated with "they will deny me." Al-Farra' said: "Both readings have a basis." Al-Nahhas said: "The better is the nominative, because the accusative is coordinated with 'they will deny me,' and this is distant."

﴿So send to Harun﴾: that is, send to him Gabriel with the revelation, so that he may be with me as a messenger, a helper, a supporter, an assistant. He did not mention the helping here because it is known from other places, such as His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿and appoint for me a helper﴾ [Ta-Ha 29], and in al-Qasas: ﴿so send him with me as a supporter to confirm me﴾ [al-Qasas 34]. This request from Moses, peace be upon him, is a request for help by sending his brother, not a request to be excused from the message, nor a hesitation in swiftly obeying.

﴿And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me.﴾ The charge (dhanb) is his killing of the Copt. He called it a dhanb according to their claim. Moses feared they would kill him for it. In this is evidence that fear may occur even among prophets, let alone among the virtuous. Then Allah, the Exalted, answered him with what contains a kind of deterrence and a measure of rebuke.

(p-1053)

He said, "No! So go, both of you, with Our signs." Within this reply is Musa's acceptance of his request that his brother be joined with him, as the address directed at both of them indicates. It is as if He had said: "Desist from that, O Musa, and go, you and whoever you asked for, and do not fear the Copts (al-Qibt)." ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening.﴾ In this is a reason for the prohibition of fear. It is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]. By this, glorified is He, intended to strengthen their hearts, and that He is the one who takes charge of their protection and safeguarding. He treated the two of them as a plural, so He said "with you" (maʿakum). But two is the least plural according to some of the scholars (al-aʾimma), or because He intended Musa, Harun, and those to whom they were sent. It is also possible that the intended meaning is "both of them with the Children of Israel." "With you" and "listening" may be two predicates of inna, or the predicate is "listening" and "with you" is related to it. The figurative usage (al-majaz) in "with" (al-maʿiyya) is not hidden, since companionship (al-muṣāḥaba) is one of the attributes of physical bodies. So the intended meaning is the being-with of support and help.

﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ The particle الفاء (al-fāʾ, "so") indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. Here the word رَسُول (rasūl, "messenger") is in the singular and not dual, unlike His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]. This is because it is used as a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "a message" (risāla), and a verbal noun remains singular. But when it means "one who is sent" (al-mursal), it takes the dual with the dual and the plural with the plural. Abu ʿUbayda said: rasūl here means "a message," and the implied sense is: "Indeed, we are two bearers of the message of the Lord of the worlds." From this is the poet's saying:

*Ah, convey to Abu ʿAmr a message,*
*For I am free of your fataḥa (i.e., your dealings).*

That is, a message.

Al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas said:

*Ah, is there anyone to convey from me to Khufaf a message,*
*Whose house is the end of your family's journey?*

That is, a message.

Abu ʿUbayda also said: rasūl may mean the dual and the plural. The Arabs say: "This is my messenger and my agent (wakīl)," "These two are my messenger and my agent," and "These are my messenger and my agent." From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 77]. It was also said: its meaning is that each one of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. And it was said: since the two of them were mutually supportive and reinforcing in the message, they were in the position of a single messenger.

The أنْ (an, "that") in His saying ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾ is explanatory (mufassira), because the sending implied by "messenger" includes the meaning of saying.

﴿He said, "Did we not raise you among us as a child?"﴾ That is, Pharaoh said to Musa after they came to him and said to him what Allah had commanded them. The phrase فِينا (fīnā, "among us") means "in our care and our homes." By this he intended to remind him of favor and to belittle him: that is, "We raised you with us as a little child, and we did not kill you among those children we killed." ﴿And you stayed among us for years of your life.﴾ Then when was this that you claim? It was said: he stayed among them eighteen years; it was said thirty years; and it was said forty years. Then he rebuked him for killing the Copt, saying: ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾. The word الفَعْلَة (al-faʿla, "deed") with a fatḥa on the fāʾ means a single occurrence of the action. Al-Shaʿbi read فِعْلَتَكَ (fiʿlataka) with a kasra on the fāʾ, but the fatḥa is preferable because it denotes a single occurrence, not a type. The meaning is that when he enumerated the blessings upon him, he mentioned his sins to him, and by "the deed" he meant the killing of the Copt. Then he said: ﴿And you are of the disbelievers﴾, that is, among those who are ungrateful for the blessing, since you killed a man from my people. It was also said that the meaning is: among the disbelievers in the claim that Pharaoh is a god. It was also said: among the disbelievers in Allah according to his own belief, since he was with them on their religion. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was of the astray."﴾ That is, Musa replied to Pharaoh: "I did this deed you mentioned, which is killing the Copt, and at that time I was among the astray," that is, the ignorant. Peace be upon him negated disbelief from himself and informed that he did that out of ignorance before the knowledge Allah taught him came to him. It was also said: the meaning is "among those ignorant that that blow would reach killing." Abu ʿUbayda said: "among the forgetful."

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾, that is, I went out from among you to Madyan, as in the surah of al-Qasas. ﴿Then my Lord granted me wisdom (ḥukm)﴾, that is, prophethood, or knowledge and understanding. Al-Zajjaj said: by ḥukm is meant His teaching him the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah.

﴿And made me among the messengers. And is this a favor you count upon me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾ It was said: this speech from Musa is by way of acknowledging the blessing, as if he said: "Yes, that upbringing is a blessing you count upon me, but that does not negate my messengership." This is what al-Farraʾ and Ibn Jarir said.

It was also said: it is from Musa by way of denial, meaning: "Do you count upon me that you raised me as a child, while you had enslaved the Children of Israel and killed them, and they are my people?"

Al-Zajjaj said: the commentators took this as a denial, namely that what Pharaoh mentioned was a favor upon Musa, while the wording is that of a statement, and in it is a rebuke of the addressee, meaning: "If you had not been killing the sons of the Children of Israel, my mother would not have needed to cast me into the river. So you count as a favor upon me what your affliction was the cause of." Al-Azhari mentioned something similar, in more detail.

Al-Mubarrad said: he means that the upbringing happened because of the cause you mentioned, namely the enslavement; that is, your raising me was for the sake of dominating and subjugating my people.

It was also said that there is an implied interrogative in the speech, meaning: "Is that a favor?" This was said by al-Akhfash, and al-Nahhas rejected it.

Al-Farraʾ said: whoever says the speech is a denial means: "Is that a favor?" The meaning of ﴿that you enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ is that you took them as slaves. It is said: ʿabbadtuhu and aʿbadtuhu have the same meaning. This is what al-Farraʾ said. Its grammatical position is nominative, as a substitute (badal) for a favor, with an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ) as its predicate; the genitive is by implied preposition (the bāʾ), and the accusative is by its omission.

In the Mushaf of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is written as (ط س م), letters separated, so one pauses on each letter with a distinct pause that marks it off from the others. Abu Ja'far also read it this way.

Its place in the grammar is raf' (nominative) if it is a name of the surah, as most scholars hold, or it is the predicate of a omitted subject. It may be in a nasb (accusative) position, with the implied verb "udhkur" (mention) or "iqra'" (recite). If it is recited as a sequence of letters in the manner of enumeration, as has been noted at more than one place in this tafsir, then it has no place in grammatical analysis (la mahalla lahu min al-iʿrab).

It has been said that it is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, and it has been said that it is one of the names of the Qur'an. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ refers to the surah. Its place is raf', as it and what follows it are the predicate if we take (ط س م) as the subject. If we take it as the predicate of an omitted subject, its place is raf' as the subject whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as an apposition (badal) to (ط س م). The Book here means the Qur'an. Al-Mubin means "the one who makes clear" (al-mudhhir), or "the clear, evident one" if it is from abana in the sense of bana (to be clear).

﴿Perhaps you will kill yourself (laʿallaka bakhiʿun nafsaka) that they do not believe﴾: that is, you will kill and destroy yourself. Al-bakh' originally means slaughtering to the point of reaching the nukhaʿ (نُخاع), spelled with a nūn. Al-Qamus says it is a vein at the back of the neck. Its full treatment has passed in Surat al-Kahf. Qatada read bakhiʿu nafsika (باخِعُ نَفْسِكَ) with an idafa (genitive construction), while the rest read it with tanwin (indefinite, separated). Al-Farra' said: "(an) in ﴿that they do not believe﴾ is in the accusative position, because it is a conditional." Al-Nahhas said: "It is said that 'in' (إن) with a kasra is because it is a particle (juz'), and this is the common usage." The view on this is what al-Zajjaj said in his book on the Qur'an: that it is in the accusative position as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and the meaning is: "Perhaps you will kill yourself because of their refusal to believe." In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he was eager for the faith of his people and deeply grieved at their turning away.

The clause ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them a sign from the heaven﴾ is a new, independent sentence, intended to give the reason for the preceding consolation. The meaning: If We willed, We would send down upon them from the heaven a sign that would compel them to faith, but the decree has already preceded that We do not send such a thing. The meaning of ﴿their necks remained bowed before it﴾ is that they would become submissive to it, that is, ﴿then their necks would remain bowed...﴾ etc. It has been said that the original form was "fa-zallū lahā khāḍiʿīn" (so they would remain bowed to it), and the word "necks" (aʿnāq) was inserted to add emphasis and vividness, since the necks are the place of humility. It has also been said that when the necks were placed where humility is, they were described with the attributes of rational beings, and so were treated as such and described with what they are described with.

ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar said: "Khāḍiʿīn (masculine plural) and khāḍiʿa (feminine) are the same here," and al-Mubarrad chose this. The meaning is that when their necks are humbled, they themselves are humbled, so reporting about the necks is reporting about their owners. It is permissible in the speech of the Arabs to leave the predicate about the first and report about the second. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"Long nights hastened to wear me down; they folded my length and folded my breadth."

So he reported about the nights and left out "the length" (al-tul). From this is the saying of Jarir:

"I see the passing years have taken from me as the dark period (al-sirar) takes from the crescent."

Abu ʿUbayd and al-Kisa'i said: the meaning is "khāḍiʿīhā hum" (they themselves are its humbled ones). Al-Nahhas considered this weak. Mujahid said: "aʿnāquhum" means their leaders (kubarāʾuhum).

Al-Nahhas said: "This is well known in the language. One says: 'A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me,' meaning leaders among them."

Abu Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "Aʿnāquhum" means their groups (jamaʿātuhum). One says: "A group (ʿunuq) of people came to me," meaning a company.

﴿And there never comes to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful but they turn away from it.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, made clear that, although He is able to make them compelled to faith, He brings them the Qur'an, state after state, and does not renew for them any admonition or reminder except that they renew what is the opposite of the purpose: turning away, denial and mockery. The min in ﴿min dhikrin﴾ is extra, for emphasis of generality. The min in ﴿min rabbihim﴾ denotes the starting point. The exception is a "mufarragh" (exception from a general context) drawn from the most general category; its place is the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the object of ﴿yatīhim﴾ (comes to them). The tafsir of a similar verse has passed in Surat al-Anbiya'.

﴿So they have denied﴾: that is, they denied the reminder that came to them with an explicit denial, and did not suffice with mere turning away. It has been said that turning away means denial, because whoever turns away from something and does not accept it has denied it. On this view, the mention of denial shows that it came from them explicitly. But the first view is better. Turning away from something is not paying attention to it. Then they moved from that to something worse, which is explicit denial.
