Otherwise, he was too arrogant and too proud to address them with such words, which indicate that he is one individual among them and one of them, while before this time he had been claiming that he was their god and they had submitted to him in that and affirmed his claim.

The meaning of ﴿Put him off, and his brother﴾ is: delay their matter. It derives from "arjatuhu," meaning I postponed him when I delayed him. It was also said that the meaning is: detain them both. ﴿And send into the cities gatherers﴾, who are the police who gather people, that is, they assemble them.

﴿They will bring you every skilled magician.﴾ This is what they advised him, and "al-sahhār al-'alīm" means the one who excels in knowledge of magic and its craft.

﴿So the magicians were gathered for the appointed time of a known day﴾. It was the Day of Adornment, as in His words: ﴿He said, "Your appointment is the Day of Adornment"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 59].

﴿And it was said to the people, "Will you gather?"﴾ This urged them to assemble so that they could witness what would happen between Musa and the magicians, and to whom victory would belong. This was Pharaoh's confidence in his prevailing and his desire to have a gathering of people so that none of them would believe in Musa. But it happened, from Musa's side, in the way he intended, because he knew that the proof of God is the one that prevails and the proof of the disbelievers is the one that is refuted. Demonstrating God's proof before a gathering of people adds to the reinforcement of the truthful and the humiliation of the falsifiers.

The meaning of ﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾ is: we will follow them in their religion, ﴿if they are the victors﴾. What is meant by following the magicians in their religion is remaining upon what they were upon, because that was the religion of the magicians at that time, and the intent was opposition to what Musa called them to. At that point the magicians requested from Musa a reward for what they would do. So they said to Pharaoh: ﴿Will we indeed have a reward?﴾, that is: a recompense that you will give us in wealth or rank. It was also said that they meant: indeed we will have a great reward. Then they restricted that to the manifestation of their victory over Musa, saying: ﴿If we are the victors﴾. So Pharaoh agreed with them on that and said: ﴿Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near.﴾ That is: yes, you will have that from me, with an addition to it, which is that you will be among those brought near to me.

﴿Musa said to them, "Throw what you are going to throw."﴾ In another verse: ﴿They said, "O Musa, either you throw or we will be the ones who throw"﴾ [al-A'raf: 115]. So what is here is interpreted to mean that he said to them, "Throw," after they had said this statement. This was not a command from Musa, peace be upon him, for them to perform magic. Rather, he wanted to overpower them with proof and to show them that what he brought was not of the kind they wanted to oppose it with.

﴿So they threw their ropes and their staffs and said﴾ at the time of throwing, ﴿"By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we will be the victors."﴾ Their saying ﴿by the might of Pharaoh﴾ may have two interpretations. The first is that it is an oath, and its answer is "Indeed we will be the victors." The second is that it is connected to an omitted element, and the "bā'" is for causation: that is, we will prevail because of his might. What is meant by "might" is greatness.

﴿So Musa threw his staff, and at once it swallowed what they were falsifying﴾. The explanation of this has already been given in full. The meaning is that it swallowed what they had produced of falsehood by removing the thing from its true form.

﴿So the magicians fell down in prostration﴾, that is: when they witnessed that and knew that it was the work of a wise creator, not the handiwork of humans, nor a deception of magicians, they believed in God, prostrated to Him, responded to Musa's call, and accepted his prophethood. The explanation of the meaning of "fell" (ulqiya) has already been given, and who is its doer is clear from its being explicitly stated. When they prostrated, ﴿they said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun."﴾ "The Lord of Musa" is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān, an explanatory appositive) for "the Lord of the worlds." They attributed Him, glorified is He, to these two because they were the ones carrying the call at that time.

In this there is a rebuke to Pharaoh, that he is not a lord, and that the true Lord is this One. When Pharaoh heard that from them and saw their prostration to God, ﴿he said, "Have you believed in Him before I give you permission?"﴾, that is: without any permission from me. Then he said, deceiving the magicians who had believed and giving the people the impression that Musa's act was magic of the same kind as that magic: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic.﴾ He only acknowledged that Musa was their chief while he does not like to acknowledge anything by which Musa's status would be elevated. This is because he knew that everyone present understood that what Musa brought was more dazzling than what the magicians brought. So he wanted to cast doubt on the people, saying that this which you have witnessed, though it surpassed what these magicians did, is the act of their chief, their master from whom they took up this craft. So do not think it is an act that no human can do, and that it is from the act of the Lord to whom Musa calls. Then he threatened those magicians who had believed in God, because the proof of God had overwhelmed them, and he said: ﴿Then you will soon know.﴾ He first stated the threat in general terms to inspire terror, then he detailed it, saying: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all.﴾

When they heard that from his statement, ﴿they said, "No harm. Indeed, we are to our Lord returning."﴾ That is: there is no harm upon us in what befalls us of punishment in this world, for that will end, and we will return after it to our Lord, and He will give us of everlasting bliss what is without limit and cannot be described.

Al-Harawi said: "lā ḍayr," "lā ḍarar," and "lā ḍurr" have one meaning. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

For indeed, after a year, it will not harm you, whether you were the offspring of a gazelle or a donkey.

Al-Jawhari said: "ḍārrahu yaḍūruhu wa-yuḍīruhu ḍayran wa-ḍūran," that is, he harmed him. Al-Kisa'i said: I heard some of them say: "That does not benefit me, nor does it harm me."

﴿Indeed, we hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾. Then they gave the reason for this by their saying: ﴿because we were the first of the believers.﴾ With the "an" pronounced with a fatha, that is: because we were the first of the believers. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i permitted its being read with a kasra, to make it a conditional clause (mujāzah, conditional construction). The meaning of ﴿the first of the believers﴾ is that they were the first of Pharaoh's people to believe after the sign appeared.

Al-Farra' said: "the first of the believers of their time." Al-Zajjaj rejected this. He said: It has been narrated that six hundred and seventy thousand believed with them. They were the small group whom Pharaoh meant by his saying: ﴿Indeed, these are a small band﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 54].

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿So he threw his staff, and at once it was a clearly visible serpent﴾, he said: "Clearly visible means that it was a clear creation of a serpent."

(p-1057) ﴿And he drew out his hand﴾, he said: Musa drew his hand out of his collar, ﴿and at once it was white﴾, shining for the onlookers, for whoever looks at it and sees it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿And it was said to the people, "Will you gather?"﴾ He said: They were in Alexandria. He said: It is said that the tail of the serpent reached beyond the lake that day. He said: They fled, and Pharaoh's people embraced Islam and he was determined about him, and he said: "Take it, O Musa." And among the things that afflicted people because of him was that he would not place anything on the ground, that is, he made them think that he did not defecate. But that day he defecated beneath himself.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd, regarding His saying ﴿No harm﴾, that he said: They (the magicians) say: "What you say will not harm us, even if you do to us what you do and crucify us." ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾: they say, "Indeed, to our Lord we are returning, and He will reward us for our patience under your punishment of us and our steadfastness upon His Oneness and our disavowal of disbelief."

And regarding His saying: ﴿That we were the first of the believers﴾, they said: They were like that on that day, the first to believe in His signs when they saw them.

When Pharaoh heard the words of Musa and Harun, ﴿Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16], he said, seeking clarification from them about this and intent on objecting to what they had said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ That is, what is He? He used the interrogative "mā," which is used to ask about the unknown and to seek the specification of the genus.

When Pharaoh said that, Musa said: ﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾. He specified for him what he meant by "the worlds," and he left aside answering what Pharaoh had asked, because Pharaoh had asked about the genus of the Lord of the worlds, and He has no genus. So Musa answered him with what indicates the great power of God, which is evident to every listener, that He, glorified is He, is the Lord and there is no lord besides Him. ﴿If you are certain﴾, that is: if you are certain of anything at all, then this is more deserving of certainty.

Pharaoh said to those around him, ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ That is, to the nobles around him: do you not listen to what he says, meaning Musa, as if he were astonishing them at the weakness of the statement, as if he were saying: Do you hear and marvel? This is sophistry from the accursed one, because he could find no answer to the argument that Musa had presented against him. When Musa heard what Pharaoh said, he presented another argument, which falls under the first argument but is closer to the understanding of his listeners. So he said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾. He made clear to them that Pharaoh is a created being, not a lord, as he claims. The meaning is: this Lord to whom I call you is the One who created your forefathers, the earliest ones, and created you. How then do you worship one who is one of you, created like you, and who has forefathers who have perished like your forefathers?

Pharaoh had no answer that deserved consideration at that point. Instead, he produced something to make his people doubt and to make them imagine that what Musa had said was something sane people would not say. So he said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad!﴾ He intended by this to deceive and to plunge them into confusion, showing that he treated what Musa said lightly and mocked it. Musa then answered him with something that completed his first answer. So he said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them﴾. Musa did not occupy himself with rebutting what Pharaoh attributed to him of madness. Rather, he showed Pharaoh the comprehensiveness of God's lordship, glorified is He, over the east and the west and what is between them, even though that was included within His lordship over the heavens and the earth and what is between them. However, there is an explicit attribution to God, glorified is He, of the movements of the heavens and what is in them, and of the changing of their states and conditions, sometimes by light and sometimes by darkness. The dual pronoun in "wa-mā baynahumā" the first time refers to the two kinds, the heavens and the earth, as in the verse of the poet:

I moved through the most noble of moves, between the spears of Nahshal and Malik.

﴿If you are rational﴾, that is: [if you understand] anything at all; or, if you are among the people of reason. That is: if you, O Pharaoh, and those with you among the rational, know, and they know, that there is no answer to your question except what I have mentioned to you.

Then the accursed one, when he ran out of argument, returned to domination and coercion. So he said: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾, that is: I will surely make you among the people of the prison. Pharaoh's prison was worse than killing, because if he imprisoned anyone, he would not release him until he died. When Musa, peace be upon him, heard that, he spoke to him gently, hoping for his acceptance and to loosen the reins of the debate with him, wishing to overpower him with the argument that is valid in the matter of prophethood, which is the manifestation of a miracle. So he presented it to him in a way that would compel him to request a miracle. So he said: ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾, that is: will you make me among the imprisoned even if I bring you something by which my truthfulness becomes evident and the validity of my claim appears? The hamza here is for interrogation, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element, as has been mentioned many times. When Pharaoh heard that, he asked for what Musa had offered him. So he said: ﴿Then bring it, if you are among the truthful﴾ in your claim. The conditional clause's answer is omitted, because what indicates it has already preceded. At that point Musa produced the miracle.

**Verse 52–70**

His saying: ﴿Travel by night with My servants﴾. God, glorified is He, commanded Moses to take the Children of Israel out at night. He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses and what he had brought. The explanation of this kind of phrase has already been given in Surat al-A'raf. The clause ﴿Indeed, you will be pursued﴾ is a ta'lil (causal clause giving the reason) for the preceding command: that is, Pharaoh and his people will pursue you to bring you back.

﴿So Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers﴾. This happened when news of their departure reached him. The meaning of "gatherers" (ḥāshirīn) is those who assemble the army from the places where Pharaoh's followers were. Then Pharaoh said to his people, after they had gathered before him: ﴿Indeed, these are a small band﴾, meaning the Children of Israel. The word shirdhimah (small band) is a contemptible, small group, and its plural is sharādhim. Al-Jawhari said: the shirdhimah is a group of people, and a piece of something; and a garment that is sharādhim means pieces (torn). From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Winter has come, and my shirt is worn into shreds, the tailor laughs at it."*

Al-Farra' said: it is said "a small company" (qalīlah) and "small ones" (qalīlūn), and "a large company" (kathīrah) and "large ones" (kathīrūn). Al-Mubarrad said: the shirdhimah is a piece of people, not many, and its plural is sharādhim.

Al-Wahidi said: the mufassirun said that the shirdhimah whom Pharaoh belittled were six hundred thousand, while the number of Pharaoh's companions cannot be counted.

﴿And indeed, they are enraging us﴾. It is said: "he enraged me (ghāẓanī) and angered me (aghāẓanī)." Al-ghayẓ means anger, and from it come tataghayyuz and ightiyāz. That is: they enrage us by their departure without my permission.

﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant host﴾. It was read ḥadhirūn, ḥādhirūn, and ḥadhurūn (with a damma on the dhal). Al-Akhfash related this.

Al-Farra' said: al-ḥādhir is one who is wary of you now, and al-ḥadhir is one created in such a state, you will not meet him except alert.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ḥādhir is one who is prepared, and al-ḥadhir is one who is watchful. Al-Kisa'i and Muhammad ibn Yazid said the same.

Al-Nahhas said: ḥadhirūn is the reading of the people of Madinah and Abu 'Amr, and ḥādhirūn is the reading of the people of Kufa. He said: Abu 'Ubaydah held that the meaning of ḥadhirūn and ḥādhirūn is one, and this is also the view of Sibawayh, and Sibawayh recited:

*"Ḥadhir (wary) of matters that do not harm him, and ḥādhir (aware) of what does not save him from fate."*

﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs, and treasures and a noble station﴾. That is: Pharaoh and his people, God expelled them from the land of Egypt, in which were gardens, springs, and treasures. These words are plurals of jannah (garden), 'ayn (spring), and kanz (treasure). By "treasures" is meant storehouses; it was said: buried wealth; and it was said: rivers. But this is open to question, because the "springs," according to the majority of the mufassirun, are springs of water, and so rivers fall under them.

As for the "noble station," it is disputed. It was said: fine dwellings; it was said: pulpits; it was said: assemblies of chiefs and rulers; it was said: places where horses are tethered. The first is the most apparent. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Among them are fine stations, their faces (fine), and assemblies which speech and deed frequent."*

﴿Thus, and We made it an inheritance for the Children of Israel﴾. It is possible that "thus" (kadhālika) is in the place of accusative (maḥall naṣb): that is, We expelled them in the manner of expulsion We have described. It is possible that it is in the place of genitive, as an adjectival description (wasfiyyah): that is, a noble station like that station which they had. It is possible that it is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, the matter is thus. The meaning of ﴿and We made it an inheritance for the Children of Israel﴾ is: We made it their possession. It is conjoined to "So We expelled them."

﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾. The reading of the majority is with a hamzat qaṭʿ (cutting hamza). Al-Hasan and al-Ḥārith al-Dīnārī read it with waṣl (connecting hamza) and with shaddah on the tā': that is, they overtook them while being at sunrise, that is, entering the time of sunrise. It is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat al-shams) sharūqan" when it rose, like "he entered the morning (aṣbaḥa) and the evening (amsā)": that is, he entered these two times. It was said: entering toward the east, like "he went to Najd (anjada)" and "he went to Tihamah (at</br>hama)." It was said: the meaning of mushriqīn is shining.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat)" when it rose, and "it shone (ashraqat)" when it gave light.

Al-Jawhari said: the shirdhimah is a group of people, and a piece of something; and a garment that is sharādhim means pieces (torn). From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Winter has come, and my shirt is worn into shreds, the tailor laughs at it."*

That is: Pharaoh and his people, God expelled them from the land of Egypt, in which were gardens, springs, and treasures. These words are plurals of jannah (garden), 'ayn (spring), and kanz (treasure). By "treasures" is meant storehouses; it was said: buried wealth; and it was said: rivers. ﴿Thus, and We made it an inheritance for the Children of Israel﴾. Al-Jawhari said: the shirdhimah is a group of people, and a piece of something; and a garment that is sharādhim means pieces (torn). From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Winter has come, and my shirt is worn into shreds, the tailor laughs at it."*

Al-Farra' said: it is said "a small company" (qalīlah) and "small ones" (qalīlūn), and "a large company" (kathīrah) and "large ones" (kathīrūn). Al-Mubarrad said: the shirdhimah is a piece of people, not many, and its plural is sharādhim.

Al-Wahidi said: the mufassirun said that the shirdhimah whom Pharaoh belittled were six hundred thousand, while the number of Pharaoh's companions cannot be counted.

﴿And indeed, they are enraging us﴾. It is said: "he enraged me (ghāẓanī) and angered me (aghāẓanī)." Al-ghayẓ means anger, and from it come tataghayyuz and ightiyāz. That is: they enrage us by their departure without my permission.

﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant host﴾. It was read ḥadhirūn, ḥādhirūn, and ḥadhurūn (with a damma on the dhal). Al-Akhfash related this.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ḥādhir is one who is prepared, and al-ḥadhir is one who is watchful. Al-Kisa'i and Muhammad ibn Yazid said the same.

Al-Nahhas said: ḥadhirūn is the reading of the people of Madinah and Abu 'Amr, and ḥādhirūn is the reading of the people of Kufa. He said: Abu 'Ubaydah held that the meaning of ḥadhirūn and ḥādhirūn is one, and this is also the view of Sibawayh, and Sibawayh recited:

*"Ḥadhir (wary) of matters that do not harm him, and ḥādhir (aware) of what does not save him from fate."*

That is: Pharaoh and his people, God expelled them from the land of Egypt, in which were gardens, springs, and treasures. These words are plurals of jannah (garden), 'ayn (spring), and kanz (treasure). By "treasures" is meant storehouses; it was said: buried wealth; and it was said: rivers. But this is open to question, because the "springs," according to the majority of the mufassirun, are springs of water, and so rivers fall under them.

As for the "noble station," it is disputed. It was said: fine dwellings; it was said: pulpits; it was said: assemblies of chiefs and rulers; it was said: places where horses are tethered. The first is the most apparent. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Among them are fine stations, their faces (fine), and assemblies which speech and deed frequent."*

﴿Thus, and We made it an inheritance for the Children of Israel﴾. It is possible that "thus" (kadhālika) is in the place of accusative (maḥall naṣb): that is, We expelled them in the manner of expulsion We have described. It is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat al-shams) sharūqan" when it rose, like "he entered the morning (aṣbaḥa) and the evening (amsā)": that is, he entered these two times. It was said: entering toward the east, like "he went to Najd (anjada)" and "he went to Tihamah (at</br>hama)." It was said: the meaning of mushriqīn is shining.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat)" when it rose, and "it shone (ashraqat)" when it gave light.

**Verse 52–70**

﴿So Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers﴾. This happened when news of their departure reached him. The meaning of "gatherers" (ḥāshirīn) is those who assemble the army from the places where Pharaoh's followers were. Then Pharaoh said to his people, after they had gathered before him: ﴿Indeed, these are a small band﴾, meaning the Children of Israel. The word shirdhimah (small band) is a contemptible, small group, and its plural is sharādhim. Al-Jawhari said: the shirdhimah is a group of people, and a piece of something; and a garment that is sharādhim means pieces (torn). From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Winter has come, and my shirt is worn into shreds, the tailor laughs at it."*

Al-Farra' said: it is said "a small company" (qalīlah) and "small ones" (qalīlūn), and "a large company" (kathīrah) and "large ones" (kathīrūn). Al-Mubarrad said: the shirdhimah is a piece of people, not many, and its plural is sharādhim.

Al-Wahidi said: the mufassirun said that the shirdhimah whom Pharaoh belittled were six hundred thousand, while the number of Pharaoh's companions cannot be counted.

﴿And indeed, they are enraging us﴾. It is said: "he enraged me (ghāẓanī) and angered me (aghāẓanī)." Al-ghayẓ means anger, and from it come tataghayyuz and ightiyāz. That is: they enrage us by their departure without my permission.

﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant host﴾. It was read ḥadhirūn, ḥādhirūn, and ḥadhurūn (with a damma on the dhal). Al-Akhfash related this.

*"Ḥadhir (wary) of matters that do not harm him, and ḥādhir (aware) of what does not save him from fate."*

﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs, and treasures and a noble station﴾. That is: Pharaoh and his people, God expelled them from the land of Egypt, in which were gardens, springs, and treasures. These words are plurals of jannah (garden), 'ayn (spring), and kanz (treasure). By "treasures" is meant storehouses; it was said: buried wealth; and it was said: rivers. But this is open to question, because the "springs," according to the majority of the mufassirun, are springs of water, and so rivers fall under them.

As for the "noble station," it is disputed. It was said: fine dwellings; it was said: pulpits; it was said: assemblies of chiefs and rulers; it was said: places where horses are tethered. The first is the most apparent. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Among them are fine stations, their faces (fine), and assemblies which speech and deed frequent."*

﴿Thus, and We made it an inheritance for the Children of Israel﴾. It is possible that "thus" (kadhālika) is in the place of accusative (maḥall naṣb): that is, We expelled them in the manner of expulsion We have described. It is possible that it is in the place of genitive, as an adjectival description (wasfiyyah): that is, a noble station like that station which they had. It is possible that it is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, the matter is thus. Al-Hasan and al-Ḥārith al-Dīnārī read it with waṣl (connecting hamza) and with shaddah on the tā': that is, they overtook them while being at sunrise, that is, entering the time of sunrise. It is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat al-shams) sharūqan" when it rose, like "he entered the morning (aṣbaḥa) and the evening (amsā)": that is, he entered these two times. It was said: entering toward the east, like "he went to Najd (anjada)" and "he went to Tihamah (at</br>hama)." It was said: the meaning of mushriqīn is shining.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat)" when it rose, and "it shone (ashraqat)" when it gave light.

﴿The companions of Moses said: Indeed, we are overtaken﴾. That is: the host of Pharaoh will overtake us, and we have no power against them.

Al-Farra' said: both have one meaning.

Al-Nahhas said: that is not so; the skilled grammarians say: mudrakūn with the light form means "joined" (mulḥaqūn), and with the shaddah form means "striving to catch up with them."

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of this reading is: indeed we are following one another to destruction at their hands, until none of us remains.

He reminded them of God's promise of guidance and victory. The meaning: indeed my Lord is with me, with victory and guidance; He will guide me: that is, He will show me the way to salvation.

When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw from the armies what they had no power to face, God, glorified is He, commanded Moses to strike the sea with his staff. This is His saying: ﴿So We revealed to Moses: Strike the sea with your staff﴾. When Moses said ﴿Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾, God, glorified is He, showed him the way of guidance and commanded him to strike the sea. By this, the Children of Israel were saved and their enemy perished.

The fa' in ﴿fa-infalaqa﴾ is faṣīḥah (an eloquent fa', indicating an omitted clause): that is, he struck, and it split, and it became twelve parts according to the number of the tribes. It was read as fil'q with a lam in place of the ra'. Al-ṭawd is a mountain. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"While a man was among the living, a mountain (ṭawd), the people threw him from close range, and he fell."*

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

*"They alighted at Anqarah, over them flows the water of the Euphrates, coming from mountains (aṭwād)."*

﴿And We brought near there the others﴾. That is: We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people.

The poet said:

*"Every day that has passed, or night that has elapsed, in which souls draw near to their appointed terms."*

Abu 'Ubaydah said: azlafnā means "we gathered," and from it the night of Muzdalifah is called "the night of gathering" (laylat jam'). Thamma (there) is an adverb of place for what is distant. It was also said: the meaning is: "We brought near" (qarrabnā) them to salvation. The "others" are Moses and his companions. The first is preferable.

Al-Hasan and Abu Ḥaywah read ﴿wa-zalafnā﴾ as a triliteral form. Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith read ﴿wa-azlaqnā﴾ with a qaf: that is, "We made slip and destroyed," from the saying: "the mare threw off (azlaqat) her foal" when she cast it.

Sibawayh and others said: "kāna" is extra (zā'idah), and the intended meaning is an informing about the polytheists after they had heard the admonition.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾: that is, the avenger against His enemies, the Merciful to His allies.

He called them "His servants" because they had believed in Moses and what he had brought. The explanation of this kind of phrase has already been given in Surat al-A'raf. The clause ﴿Indeed, you will be pursued﴾ is a ta'lil (causal clause giving the reason) for the preceding command: that is, Pharaoh and his people will pursue you to bring you back.

﴿So Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers﴾. This happened when news of their departure reached him. The meaning of "gatherers" (ḥāshirīn) is those who assemble the army from the places where Pharaoh's followers were. Then Pharaoh said to his people, after they had gathered before him: ﴿Indeed, these are a small band﴾, meaning the Children of Israel. The word shirdhimah (small band) is a contemptible, small group, and its plural is sharādhim. Al-Jawhari said: the shirdhimah is a group of people, and a piece of something; and a garment that is sharādhim means pieces (torn). From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Winter has come, and my shirt is worn into shreds, the tailor laughs at it."*

Al-Farra' said: it is said "a small company" (qalīlah) and "small ones" (qalīlūn), and "a large company" (kathīrah) and "large ones" (kathīrūn). Al-Mubarrad said: the shirdhimah is a piece of people, not many, and its plural is sharādhim.

Al-Wahidi said: the mufassirun said that the shirdhimah whom Pharaoh belittled were six hundred thousand, while the number of Pharaoh's companions cannot be counted.

﴿And indeed, they are enraging us﴾. It is said: "he enraged me (ghāẓanī) and angered me (aghāẓanī)." Al-ghayẓ means anger, and from it come tataghayyuz and ightiyāz. That is: they enrage us by their departure without my permission.

﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant host﴾. It was read ḥadhirūn, ḥādhirūn, and ḥadhurūn (with a damma on the dhal). Al-Akhfash related this.

Al-Farra' said: al-ḥādhir is one who is wary of you now, and al-ḥadhir is one created in such a state, you will not meet him except alert.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ḥādhir is one who is prepared, and al-ḥadhir is one who is watchful. Al-Kisa'i and Muhammad ibn Yazid said the same.

Al-Nahhas said: ḥadhirūn is the reading of the people of Madinah and Abu 'Amr, and ḥādhirūn is the reading of the people of Kufa. He said: Abu 'Ubaydah held that the meaning of ḥadhirūn and ḥādhirūn is one, and this is also the view of Sibawayh, and Sibawayh recited:

*"Ḥadhir (wary) of matters that do not harm him, and ḥādhir (aware) of what does not save him from fate."*

﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs, and treasures and a noble station﴾. That is: Pharaoh and his people, God expelled them from the land of Egypt, in which were gardens, springs, and treasures. These words are plurals of jannah (garden), 'ayn (spring), and kanz (treasure). By "treasures" is meant storehouses; it was said: buried wealth; and it was said: rivers. But this is open to question, because the "springs," according to the majority of the mufassirun, are springs of water, and so rivers fall under them.

As for the "noble station," it is disputed. It was said: fine dwellings; it was said: pulpits; it was said: assemblies of chiefs and rulers; it was said: places where horses are tethered. The first is the most apparent. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Among them are fine stations, their faces (fine), and assemblies which speech and deed frequent."*

﴿Thus, and We made it an inheritance for the Children of Israel﴾. It is possible that "thus" (kadhālika) is in the place of accusative (maḥall naṣb): that is, We expelled them in the manner of expulsion We have described. It is possible that it is in the place of genitive, as an adjectival description (wasfiyyah): that is, a noble station like that station which they had. It is possible that it is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, the matter is thus. The meaning of ﴿and We made it an inheritance for the Children of Israel﴾ is: We made it their possession. It is conjoined to "So We expelled them."

﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾. The reading of the majority is with a hamzat qaṭʿ (cutting hamza). Al-Hasan and al-Ḥārith al-Dīnārī read it with waṣl (connecting hamza) and with shaddah on the tā': that is, they overtook them while being at sunrise, that is, entering the time of sunrise. It is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat al-shams) sharūqan" when it rose, like "he entered the morning (aṣbaḥa) and the evening (amsā)": that is, he entered these two times. It was said: entering toward the east, like "he went to Najd (anjada)" and "he went to Tihamah (at</br>hama)." It was said: the meaning of mushriqīn is shining.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat)" when it rose, and "it shone (ashraqat)" when it gave light.

﴿So when the two hosts saw each other﴾. The majority read tarāʾā (with a light hamza). Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read it without hamza. The meaning: they faced each other, such that each group saw its companion. It is a tafā'ul form from ru'yah (seeing). It was read: ﴿the two companies saw each other﴾.

﴿The companions of Moses said: Indeed, we are overtaken﴾. That is: the host of Pharaoh will overtake us, and we have no power against them.

The majority read ﴿innā la-mudrakūn﴾ as an ism maf'ūl (passive participle) from adraka. From it is ﴿until when drowning overtook him﴾ [Yunus: 90]. Al-A'raj and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read it with a fatha on the dal, shaddah, and a kasra on the ra'.

Al-Farra' said: both have one meaning.

Al-Nahhas said: that is not so; the skilled grammarians say: mudrakūn with the light form means "joined" (mulḥaqūn), and with the shaddah form means "striving to catch up with them."

He said: this is the meaning of Sibawayh's words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of this reading is: indeed we are following one another to destruction at their hands, until none of us remains.

﴿He said: No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. Moses said this statement to restrain them and to deter them. The meaning: they will not overtake you. He reminded them of God's promise of guidance and victory. The meaning: indeed my Lord is with me, with victory and guidance; He will guide me: that is, He will show me the way to salvation.

When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw from the armies what they had no power to face, God, glorified is He, commanded Moses to strike the sea with his staff. This is His saying: ﴿So We revealed to Moses: Strike the sea with your staff﴾. When Moses said ﴿Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾, God, glorified is He, showed him the way of guidance and commanded him to strike the sea. By this, the Children of Israel were saved and their enemy perished.

The fa' in ﴿fa-infalaqa﴾ is faṣīḥah (an eloquent fa', indicating an omitted clause): that is, he struck, and it split, and it became twelve parts according to the number of the tribes. The water stood on the right and left of the path like a great mountain. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So each part was like a great mountain﴾. The firq (part) is a piece of the sea. It was read as fil'q with a lam in place of the ra'. Al-ṭawd is a mountain. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"While a man was among the living, a mountain (ṭawd), the people threw him from close range, and he fell."*

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

*"They alighted at Anqarah, over them flows the water of the Euphrates, coming from mountains (aṭwād)."*

﴿And We brought near there the others﴾. That is: We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people.

The poet said:

*"Every day that has passed, or night that has elapsed, in which souls draw near to their appointed terms."*

Abu 'Ubaydah said: azlafnā means "we gathered," and from it the night of Muzdalifah is called "the night of gathering" (laylat jam'). Thamma (there) is an adverb of place for what is distant. It was also said: the meaning is: "We brought near" (qarrabnā) them to salvation. The "others" are Moses and his companions. The first is preferable.

Al-Hasan and Abu Ḥaywah read ﴿wa-zalafnā﴾ as a triliteral form. Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith read ﴿wa-azlaqnā﴾ with a qaf: that is, "We made slip and destroyed," from the saying: "the mare threw off (azlaqat) her foal" when she cast it.

﴿And We saved Moses and those with him, all of them﴾, by their passing through the sea after God had made it into paths they walk upon.

﴿Then We drowned the others﴾. That is, Pharaoh and his people. God drowned them by closing the sea upon them after they had entered it, following Moses and his people.

The reference in His saying ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾ is to what has preceded of what took place between Moses and Pharaoh up to this end. In that is a great sign and a dazzling power, among the clearest indications of God's power, glorified is He, and His great sovereignty. ﴿And most of them were not believers﴾: that is, most of those who were with Pharaoh were not believers. For after this, only a few believed from among them, such as Ḥizqil and his daughter, Āsiyah the wife of Pharaoh, and the old woman who showed the grave of Joseph. The intended meaning is not "most of those who were with Pharaoh when he caught up with Moses," for they all perished in the sea. Rather, the intended meaning is "most of those who were with him from the origin, and those who followed him and were affiliated with him." This is the furthest that can be said.

Sibawayh and others said: "kāna" is extra (zā'idah), and the intended meaning is an informing about the polytheists after they had heard the admonition.

﴿And indeed, your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾: that is, the avenger against His enemies, the Merciful to His allies.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Ḥatim related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, these are a small band﴾ that he said: six hundred thousand and seventy thousand.

Ibn Abi Ḥatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: they were six hundred thousand.

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The companions of Moses who crossed the sea were twelve tribes, and in each path were twelve thousand, all of them sons of Ya'qub."

Ibn Mardawayh also related it from him, with a chain.

Al-Suyuti said: weak (wāh). He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Pharaoh, the enemy of God, when God drowned him and his companions, was with seventy commanders, and with each commander seventy thousand. And Moses was with seventy thousand when they crossed the sea."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim also related from him: "The vanguard of Pharaoh whom he sent in their pursuit were six hundred thousand, and not one of them was except upon a steed (bahīm)."

And I say: these disturbed reports have been related from many of the early generation with similar disturbance and disagreement, and nothing of them is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Ḥatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and a noble station﴾ that he said: the pulpits.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim related from him concerning His saying ﴿like the great mountain (ṭawd)﴾ that he said: like a mountain.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and We brought near﴾ that he said: "We brought near."

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, and al-Ḥakim, who declared it sound, related from Abu Musa, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "When Moses wanted to travel with the Children of Israel, he lost the way. He said to the Children of Israel: What is this? The scholars of the Children of Israel said to him: Joseph, when death came to him, took a covenant from us that we would not leave Egypt until we carried his coffin with us. Moses said to them: Which of you knows where his grave is? They said: No one knows the place of his grave except an old woman of the Children of Israel. Moses sent for her and said: Show us the grave of Joseph. She said: No, by God, not until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: That I be with you in Paradise. It seemed hard to him, so it was said to him: Give her her right. So he gave her her right. She went with them to a stagnant pool of water. She said to them: Drain the water from it. They did so. She said: Dig. They dug, and they extracted the grave of Joseph. When they lifted it, the road became like the light of day."

Al-Wahidi said: the mufassirun said that the shirdhimah whom Pharaoh belittled were six hundred thousand, while the number of Pharaoh's companions cannot be counted.

﴿And indeed, they are enraging us﴾. It is said: "he enraged me (ghāẓanī) and angered me (aghāẓanī)." Al-ghayẓ means anger, and from it come tataghayyuz and ightiyāz. That is: they enrage us by their departure without my permission.

﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant host﴾. It was read ḥadhirūn, ḥādhirūn, and ḥadhurūn (with a damma on the dhal). Al-Akhfash related this.

Al-Farra' said: al-ḥādhir is one who is wary of you now, and al-ḥadhir is one created in such a state, you will not meet him except alert.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ḥādhir is one who is prepared, and al-ḥadhir is one who is watchful. Al-Kisa'i and Muhammad ibn Yazid said the same.

Al-Nahhas said: ḥadhirūn is the reading of the people of Madinah and Abu 'Amr, and ḥādhirūn is the reading of the people of Kufa. He said: Abu 'Ubaydah held that the meaning of ḥadhirūn and ḥādhirūn is one, and this is also the view of Sibawayh, and Sibawayh recited:

*"Ḥadhir (wary) of matters that do not harm him, and ḥādhir (aware) of what does not save him from fate."*

That is: Pharaoh and his people, God expelled them from the land of Egypt, in which were gardens, springs, and treasures. These words are plurals of jannah (garden), 'ayn (spring), and kanz (treasure). By "treasures" is meant storehouses; it was said: buried wealth; and it was said: rivers. But this is open to question, because the "springs," according to the majority of the mufassirun, are springs of water, and so rivers fall under them.

As for the "noble station," it is disputed. It was said: fine dwellings; it was said: pulpits; it was said: assemblies of chiefs and rulers; it was said: places where horses are tethered. The first is the most apparent. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Among them are fine stations, their faces (fine), and assemblies which speech and deed frequent."*

﴿Thus, and We made it an inheritance for the Children of Israel﴾. It is possible that "thus" (kadhālika) is in the place of accusative (maḥall naṣb): that is, We expelled them in the manner of expulsion We have described. It is possible that it is in the place of genitive, as an adjectival description (wasfiyyah): that is, a noble station like that station which they had. It is possible that it is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, the matter is thus. Al-Hasan and al-Ḥārith al-Dīnārī read it with waṣl (connecting hamza) and with shaddah on the tā': that is, they overtook them while being at sunrise, that is, entering the time of sunrise. It is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat al-shams) sharūqan" when it rose, like "he entered the morning (aṣbaḥa) and the evening (amsā)": that is, he entered these two times. It was said: entering toward the east, like "he went to Najd (anjada)" and "he went to Tihamah (at</br>hama)." It was said: the meaning of mushriqīn is shining.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said: "the sun rose (sharaqat)" when it rose, and "it shone (ashraqat)" when it gave light.

﴿So when the two hosts saw each other﴾. The majority read tarāʾā (with a light hamza). Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read it without hamza. ﴿The companions of Moses said: Indeed, we are overtaken﴾. That is: the host of Pharaoh will overtake us, and we have no power against them.

﴿He said: No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. Moses said this statement to restrain them and to deter them. The meaning: they will not overtake you. He reminded them of God's promise of guidance and victory. The meaning: indeed my Lord is with me, with victory and guidance; He will guide me: that is, He will show me the way to salvation.

When the trial grew severe upon the Children of Israel, and they saw from the armies what they had no power to face, God, glorified is He, commanded Moses to strike the sea with his staff. This is His saying: ﴿So We revealed to Moses: Strike the sea with your staff﴾. When Moses said ﴿Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾, God, glorified is He, showed him the way of guidance and commanded him to strike the sea. By this, the Children of Israel were saved and their enemy perished.

The fa' in ﴿fa-infalaqa﴾ is faṣīḥah (an eloquent fa', indicating an omitted clause): that is, he struck, and it split, and it became twelve parts according to the number of the tribes. It was read as fil'q with a lam in place of the ra'. Al-ṭawd is a mountain. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"While a man was among the living, a mountain (ṭawd), the people threw him from close range, and he fell."*

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

*"They alighted at Anqarah, over them flows the water of the Euphrates, coming from mountains (aṭwād)."*

﴿And We brought near there the others﴾. That is: We brought them near to the sea, meaning Pharaoh and his people.

The poet said:

*"Every day that has passed, or night that has elapsed, in which souls draw near to their appointed terms."*

﴿And We saved Moses and those with him, all of them﴾, by their passing through the sea after God had made it into paths they walk upon.

﴿Then We drowned the others﴾. That is, Pharaoh and his people. God drowned them by closing the sea upon them after they had entered it, following Moses and his people.

The reference in His saying ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾ is to what has preceded of what took place between Moses and Pharaoh up to this end. Sibawayh and others said: "kāna" is extra (zā'idah), and the intended meaning is an informing about the polytheists after they had heard the admonition.

Ibn Abi Ḥatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: they were six hundred thousand.

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The companions of Moses who crossed the sea were twelve tribes, and in each path were twelve thousand, all of them sons of Ya'qub."

Ibn Mardawayh also related it from him, with a chain.

Al-Suyuti said: weak (wāh). He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Pharaoh, the enemy of God, when God drowned him and his companions, was with seventy commanders, and with each commander seventy thousand. And Moses was with seventy thousand when they crossed the sea."

Ibn Abi Ḥatim also related from him: "The vanguard of Pharaoh whom he sent in their pursuit were six hundred thousand, and not one of them was except upon a steed (bahīm)."

And I say: these disturbed reports have been related from many of the early generation with similar disturbance and disagreement, and nothing of them is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir related the same from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and We brought near﴾ that he said: "We brought near."

He said to the Children of Israel: What is this? The scholars of the Children of Israel said to him: Joseph, when death came to him, took a covenant from us that we would not leave Egypt until we carried his coffin with us. Moses said to them: Which of you knows where his grave is? They said: No one knows the place of his grave except an old woman of the Children of Israel. Moses sent for her and said: Show us the grave of Joseph. She said: No, by God, not until you give me my right. He said: And what is your right? She said: That I be with you in Paradise. It seemed hard to him, so it was said to him: Give her her right. So he gave her her right. She went with them to a stagnant pool of water. She said to them: Drain the water from it. They did so. She said: Dig. They dug, and they extracted the grave of Joseph. When they lifted it, the road became like the light of day."

(p. 1059) His words, ﴿And recite to them﴾, are conjoined to the governing element in His words, ﴿And when your Lord called Moses﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 10], which has already been discussed. By "the news of Abraham" is meant his account, i.e., "Recite to them, O Muhammad, the account and story of Abraham."

The clause ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "the news of Abraham," i.e., "at the time he said." It has also been said that "when" (idh) is a substitute (badal) for "news," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), so that the governing element would be "recite." The first view is the better one.

The meaning of "What do you worship?" is "What thing do you worship?" He knew that they worshipped idols, but he intended to impose the proof upon them.

﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ That is, we continue to maintain their worship constantly, not at a specific time. It is said: "zalla yaf'alu kadhā" means he does such-and-such during the day, and "bāta yaf'alu kadhā" means he does it during the night. The apparent meaning is that they persisted in worshipping them by day, not by night. By "devotion to them" is meant persistence in their worship. He said "to them" (lahā) to indicate that this devotion was for their sake. When they made this claim, Abraham said, drawing attention to the corruption of their position:

﴿"Do they hear you when you call?"﴾ Al-Akhfash said: there is an ellipsis here; the meaning is "Do they hear from you?" or "Do they hear your supplication?"

Qatadah read it as "hal yusmi'unakum" with a dammah on the yā', meaning "Do they make you hear their voices at the time you call upon them?"

﴿"Or do they benefit you"﴾ in any way of benefit, ﴿"or do they harm you?"﴾ That is, do they harm you if you abandon their worship? This interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir). For if they neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, there is no basis for worshipping them. When they say, "Yes, they are as such," they acknowledge that their worship of them is mere play and futility, and at that point the proof is established against them. When the Friend (al-Khalil) presented them with this decisive argument, they found no answer to it except to retreat to blind imitation (taqlid), namely that they found their fathers doing so: that is, they perform this worship of these idols while these idols possess this attribute of having no hearing, benefit, or harm. This answer is the staff upon which every helpless person leans, with which every lame person walks, by which every deceived person is deluded, and to which every person who is duped submits. For if you were to ask today those who blindly follow men, who have spread over the earth in length and breadth, and say to them, "What is the proof for your imitation of a single one of the scholars, and for taking up everything he says in religion and innovates from opinion contrary to the evidence?", they would find no answer other than this one, and would utter nothing else. They would begin enumerating for you those who preceded them in imitating this from their predecessors, and following their sayings and deeds. They have filled their hearts with awe, their minds have become too narrow to conceive the truth, and they think they are the best of the people of the earth, the most knowledgeable and the most noble. So they do not listen to a sincere advisor nor to one calling to the truth. Had they reflected, they would have found themselves in great delusion and shameful ignorance, and that they are like a blind beast, and those ancestors are like the blind who lead blind beasts, as the poet said:

"Like a blind beast whose rein is led by a blind man on the crooked, bewildering road."

So you, O one who acts by the Book and the Sunnah, free from partisanship and arbitrariness, must present to them the proofs of God and establish His demonstrations upon them. For perhaps some of them who have not had the disease of imitation firmly settled in their hearts will yield to you. As for one in whose heart this disease has become firmly rooted, even if you present to him every proof and establish every demonstration, he will lend you nothing but a deaf ear and a blind eye. But you have discharged the duty of clarification that the Qur'an made incumbent upon you, and guidance is in the hand of the Creator, the All-Knowing: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. When these imitators said this statement,

the Friend (al-Khalil) said: ﴿"Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your ancient fathers?"﴾ That is: have you looked at and reflected upon these idols you have been worshipping, which neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, so that you may know that you are in error and ignorance? Then he informed them of his disavowal of these idols that they worship.

He said: ﴿"Indeed, they are enemies to me"﴾. The meaning of their being an enemy to him, despite their being inanimate, is that if he worshipped them, they would be his enemies on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Farra' said: this is from the inverted (maqlub) construction; that is, "Indeed, I am an enemy to them, because whomever you oppose opposes you." "Enemy" (ʿaduww), like "friend" (sadiq), applies to the singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine. So said al-Farra'.

ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: whoever says "ʿaduwwat Allah" with the tā' marbutah treats it as meaning "one who opposes" (al-mu'adiyah). Whoever says "ʿaduww" for the feminine and plural treats it as meaning a relative noun (nisbah).

It has also been said that by his words ﴿"indeed, they are enemies to me"﴾ is meant their ancestors, the ancients, because of their worship of idols. This was rejected on the ground that the discourse concerns what they worshipped, not those who worship. The exception in His words ﴿"except the Lord of the worlds"﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), i.e., "but the Lord of the worlds is not like that; rather He is my protector in this world and the Hereafter."

Al-Zajjaj said: the grammarians said it is an exception not from the preceding; al-Zajjaj also permitted that it be from the preceding, on the basis that they used to worship God, Mighty and Majestic, and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disavowed what they worship except God.

Al-Jurjani said: its construction is: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your ancient fathers, except the Lord of the worlds? Indeed, they are enemies to me." He made this a case of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and made "illa" (except) mean "dun" (other than) and "siwa" (besides), like His words ﴿"They will not taste death therein except the first death"﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56], i.e., other than the first death.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the meaning is "except one who worships the Lord of the worlds."

Then he described the Lord of the worlds with His words: ﴿"Who created me, and it is He who guides me"﴾, i.e., He guides me to the interests of religion and the world.

It has been said that the relative clause is a subject (mubtada') and what follows it is its predicate, but the first view is better.

It is permissible that the relative clause be a substitute (badal) for "Lord," or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it, or that it be in the accusative by way of praise, with the implied "I mean" (aʿni) or "I praise" (amdaḥu). The Friend has described his Lord with what deserves worship on account of Him.

Creation, guidance, and provision are indicated by His words: ﴿"And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink"﴾. Repelling the harm of illness, bringing the benefit of healing, causing death and giving life, and forgiving sins are all blessings, for which the one blessed by some of them, let alone all of them, is obliged to thank the Benefactor with all kinds of thanks, the highest and most excellent of which is worship. The inclusion of these pronouns at the beginning of these clauses (p. 1060) serves to indicate that He alone is the doer of these things to the exclusion of others. He attributed illness to himself rather than to the Lord, out of courtesy toward the Lord, although illness and other things come from God, Glorified is He.

His words ﴿"Then He will give me life"﴾ mean resurrection. The omission of the yā' in these verbs is because they are the endings of verses (ru'us al-ayy).

Ibn Abi Ishaq read all these verbs with the yā' affirmed.

When Abraham, peace be upon him, said ﴿"And the One from whom I hope He will forgive my sin on the Day of Judgment"﴾, he was humbling himself. It has also been said that "hope" (tama') here means certainty with respect to himself, and means expectation with respect to others.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "khatayaya" (my sins, plural): they said his sin was not a single one.

Al-Nahhas said: khatiʾah in the sense of khataya is in the usage of the Arabs.

Mujahid said: by "his sin" he means his words ﴿"Rather, the biggest of them did it"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63], his words ﴿"Indeed, I am sick"﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his statement that Sarah was his sister. Al-Hasan added: and his words to the star, ﴿"This is my lord"﴾ [al-An'am: 77, 78]. Al-Wahidi related from the exegetes that they interpreted the sins (khataya) in the same way Mujahid did.

Al-Zajjaj said: the prophets are human, and sin may befall them, except that major sin does not come from them, because they are protected from it (ma'sum). By the Day of Religion is meant the Day of Recompense for the servants according to their deeds. It is not hidden that interpreting the sins as Mujahid and those with him mentioned is weak, for those were allusions (ma'arid), and they too came from him only after this exchange that took place between him and his people.

Then, when the Friend had finished praising his Lord and acknowledging His blessings, he followed it with supplication, so that others might follow him in that.

He said: ﴿"My Lord, grant me wisdom"﴾. By "wisdom" (hukm) is meant knowledge and understanding. It has been said: prophethood and messengership. It has also been said: knowledge of the limits of God and His rulings, and so on. ﴿"And join me with the righteous"﴾, meaning with the prophets before me. It has been said: with the people of Paradise.

﴿"And grant me a true tongue among later generations"﴾, i.e., grant me a good reputation among the later people who will come after me until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Qutaybi said: "tongue" was placed in the position of "speech" by metaphor, because speech is by means of it. The Arabs also use it as a metonym for word, and from this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"Indeed, a tongue has come to me, with which I do not keep secrets."

God, Glorified is He, has given Abraham this by His words ﴿"And We left for them among later generations"﴾ [al-Saffat: 108], since every nation adheres to him and venerates him.

Makki said: it has been said that the meaning of his request is that among his descendants at the end of time there would be someone who upholds the truth, and so his supplication was answered in Muhammad (ﷺ) and his family. But there is no basis for this specification.

Al-Qushayri said: he meant a good supplication until the Hour, and there is no basis for this either, for "a true tongue" is more general than that.

﴿"And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss"﴾. "Among the inheritors" may be a second object, or it may be an attribute of an omitted second object: i.e., an heir from among the heirs of the Garden of Bliss. When he, peace be upon him, asked in the first supplication for the happiness of this world, he asked in this supplication for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss, and he made it something inherited, to liken the spoils of the Hereafter to the spoils of this world. The meaning of inheritance has already been discussed in Surat Maryam.

﴿"And forgive my father, for he was among the misguided"﴾. His father had promised him that he would believe, so he asked forgiveness for him; but when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disavowed him. This has been explained fully in Surat al-Tawbah and Surat Maryam. The meaning of "among the misguided" is among the polytheists who strayed from the path of guidance. "Kana" here is redundant according to the view of Sibawayh, as has been mentioned in more than one place.

﴿"And do not disgrace me on the Day when they are resurrected"﴾, i.e., do not expose me before the assembled witnesses by rebuking me, or do not punish me on the Day of Resurrection, or do not disgrace me by punishing my father or by resurrecting him among the misguided. "Ikhza'" applies both to "khizy," which is humiliation, and to "khiza'," which is shame.

﴿"The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾: "the Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit" is a substitute for "the Day when they are resurrected," i.e., the Day on which neither wealth nor children will benefit any of the people, since the son is the closest kin and the most entitled to protection, aid, and benefit. If he does not benefit, then others among relatives and helpers are even less able to.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this and what follows it are from the words of God, but this is weak.

The exception in His words ﴿"except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾ has been said to be disjunctive, i.e., "but whoever comes to God with a sound heart." Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: it is "except" in the sense of the state (hal) of one who comes to God with a sound heart, supposing an omitted genitive construction (mudaf). Abu Hayyan said: there is no necessity for that.

It has also been said that this exception is a substitute for the omitted object, or an exception from it, since the implied meaning is "neither wealth nor children will benefit any of the people, except one who has this attribute." It may also be a substitute for the subject of "will benefit," in which case it is in the nominative. Abu al-Baqa' said: then the implied meaning is "except the wealth of one who, or the children of one who, for he will benefit."

There has been disagreement about the meaning of the sound heart. It has been said: it is sound from polytheism, for as for sins, no one is free from them; this was said by most of the exegetes. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: the sound heart is the healthy heart, which is the heart of the believer, for the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased. It has also been said: it is the heart free from innovation and at peace with the Sunnah. It has also been said: it is the one safe from the affliction of wealth and children.

Al-Dahhak said: "Salim" means sincere and pure.

Al-Junayd said: "Salim" in the language means "ladigh" (one who has been stung), so its meaning is that he was turned over like one stung by the fear of God, the Exalted. This is a distortion and an inversion of the meaning of the Qur'an.

Al-Razi said: The most correct of the opinions is that what is meant by it is the soundness of the soul from ignorance and vile character traits.

﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾, i.e., it will be brought close to them and made near for them, so that they may enter it.

Al-Zajjaj said: It means the nearness of their entering it and their looking at it.

﴿And Hellfire will be made manifest for the misguided﴾, i.e., it will be made visible to them. By "the misguided" is meant the disbelievers. The meaning is that it will be displayed before the believers enter it, so that the grief of the disbelievers will intensify and the joy of the believers will increase.

﴿And it will be said to them: "Where is what you used to worship besides God?"﴾ — of the idols and rivals — ﴿"Can they help you, or help themselves?"﴾ i.e., will they ward off the punishment from you, or will they defend themselves by repelling it from themselves?

All of this is rebuke and reproach directed at them. Malik ibn Dinar read "wa-barazat" (and it was made manifest) with a fatha on the ba' and the ra', making it active in form (mubayyan lil-fa'il).

﴿Then they will be thrown into it, they and the misguided,﴾ i.e., they will be cast into Hell: "they" refers to those who were worshipped, and "the misguided" refers to those who worshipped them.

It has been said: the meaning of "kubkibu" is that they were turned over onto their heads. It has also been said: some were thrown upon others. It has also been said: they were gathered together, derived from "kabkaba" (a group). This is related from al-Harawi.

Al-Nahhas said: it is derived from "kawkab al-shay'" (the bulk or main part of a thing), and a group of horses is called "kawkab" and "kabkaba". It has also been said: they were pushed down. These meanings are close to one another. Its original form is "kubbibu" with two bas', the first being doubled from two letters, and so the kaf was substituted for the middle ba'.

Al-Zajjaj preferred that the meaning is: some were cast upon others.

Ibn Qutaybah preferred that the meaning is: they were thrown on their faces.

It has been said: the pronoun in "kubkibu" refers to the Quraysh, and "the misguided" refers to the gods. By "the armies of Iblis" is meant his devils who lead the servants astray. It has been said: his offspring. It has been said: everyone who calls to the worship of idols.

"Ajma'un" (all of them) is an emphasis for the pronoun in "kubkibu" and what is conjoined to it.

The clause ﴿They will say, while they dispute therein﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What did they say when what was done to them was done?

The content of the saying is ﴿"By God, we were certainly in clear error"﴾. The clause ﴿while they dispute therein﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): i.e., they said this statement while being in Hell, disputing. The "in" in "in kunna" is the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and the lam is a distinguishing particle between it and the negating "in". That is: they said, "By God, indeed the matter is that we were in manifest, clear error." The meaning of "error" here is loss, perdition, and bewilderment from the truth. The governing element of the adverb of time, i.e., ﴿when we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds﴾, is their being in clear error.

It has been said: the governing element is the error itself. It has been said: it is what the speech indicates, as if it were said: "We were misguided at the time we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds."

The Kufans said: "in" in "in kunna" is negating, and the lam means "illa" (except), i.e., "we were only in clear error." The first is more preferable, and it is the view of the Basrans.

﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ who would intercede for us from the punishment as they do for the believers.

﴿Nor a close friend﴾ — i.e., a relative. "Hamim" is the one close to you whom you love and who loves you. The singular "sadiq" is used because it has been mentioned more than once before that it applies to the one, the two, the group, the masculine and the feminine. "Hamim" is derived from "hamimat al-rajul," i.e., his relatives. It is said: "hamma al-shay'" and "ahamma" when it drew near to him, and from this comes "al-humma" (fever), because it brings one close to the appointed term.

Ali ibn Isa said: the near relative is called "hamim" only because he protects (yahmi) out of the anger of his companion, so he derived it from "al-hamiyyah" (zeal, protectiveness).

﴿Then if only we had a return, so that we might be among the believers﴾. This is from them in the manner of wishing, which indicates the perfection of regret, as if they said: "Would that we had a return," i.e., a return to the world. The answer to the wish is ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾, i.e., that we might become part of them.

The reference in His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is to what was mentioned before of the account of Abraham. "Ayah" means lesson and sign, and the tanwin indicates magnification and grandeur. ﴿Yet most of them were not believers﴾ — i.e., most of those to whom the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, recites the account of Abraham, namely the Quraysh and whoever followed their religion. It has been said: "Most of the people of Abraham were not believers," but this is weak, because they were all non-believers.

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ — i.e., He is the Dominant over His enemies, the Merciful to His friends; or the Merciful to the enemies by delaying their punishment and not hastening it against them.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ that it means with the people of Paradise.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ that it means the agreement of the people of the religions upon Abraham.

He also related from him concerning ﴿And forgive my father﴾ that it means: bestow upon him a repentance by which he deserves Your forgiveness.

Al-Bukhari and others related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, who said: "Abraham will meet his father Azar on the Day of Resurrection, and on the face of Azar will be dust and dark gloom. Abraham will say to him: 'Did I not tell you not to disobey me?' His father will say: 'Today I will not disobey you.' Abraham will say: 'My Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected. What disgrace could be greater than my father, the most distant?' God will say: 'I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers.' Then He will say: 'O Abraham, what is under your feet?' Then he will look, and there will be a dhiykh (hyena) covered in filth; it will be seized by its legs and cast into the Fire." The dhiyk is the male of the hyenas, so it is as if Azar was transformed into the form of a dhiyk.

An-Nasa'i related it in a longer form than this.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ that it is the testimony that there is no god but God.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿So they will be thrown into it﴾ that it means they were gathered therein, ﴿they and the misguided﴾ — the polytheists of the Arabs and the gods.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him regarding ﴿Then if only we had a return﴾ that it means a return to the world, ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾ — so that intercession might become lawful for us as it became lawful for these (people).

(p. 1059) His words, ﴿And recite to them﴾, are conjoined to the governing element in His words, ﴿And when your Lord called Moses﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 10], which has already been discussed. By "the news of Abraham" is meant his account, i.e., "Recite to them, O Muhammad, the account and story of Abraham."

The clause ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "the news of Abraham," i.e., "at the time he said." It has also been said that "when" (idh) is a substitute (badal) for "news," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), so that the governing element would be "recite." The first view is the better one.

The meaning of "What do you worship?" is "What thing do you worship?" He knew that they worshipped idols, but he intended to impose the proof upon them.

﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ That is, we continue to maintain their worship constantly, not at a specific time. It is said: "zalla yaf'alu kadhā" means he does such-and-such during the day, and "bāta yaf'alu kadhā" means he does it during the night. The apparent meaning is that they persisted in worshipping them by day, not by night. By "devotion to them" is meant persistence in their worship. He said "to them" (lahā) to indicate that this devotion was for their sake. When they made this claim, Abraham said, drawing attention to the corruption of their position:

﴿"Do they hear you when you call?"﴾ Al-Akhfash said: there is an ellipsis here; the meaning is "Do they hear from you?" or "Do they hear your supplication?"

Qatadah read it as "hal yusmi'unakum" with a dammah on the yā', meaning "Do they make you hear their voices at the time you call upon them?"

﴿"Or do they benefit you"﴾ in any way of benefit, ﴿"or do they harm you?"﴾ That is, do they harm you if you abandon their worship? This interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir). For if they neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, there is no basis for worshipping them. When they say, "Yes, they are as such," they acknowledge that their worship of them is mere play and futility, and at that point the proof is established against them.
