(p. 1059) His words, ﴿And recite to them﴾, are conjoined to the governing element in His words, ﴿And when your Lord called Moses﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 10], which has already been discussed. By "the news of Abraham" is meant his account, i.e., "Recite to them, O Muhammad, the account and story of Abraham."

The clause ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "the news of Abraham," i.e., "at the time he said." It has also been said that "when" (idh) is a substitute (badal) for "news," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), so that the governing element would be "recite." The first view is the better one.

The meaning of "What do you worship?" is "What thing do you worship?" He knew that they worshipped idols, but he intended to impose the proof upon them.

﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ That is, we continue to maintain their worship constantly, not at a specific time. It is said: "zalla yaf'alu kadhā" means he does such-and-such during the day, and "bāta yaf'alu kadhā" means he does it during the night. The apparent meaning is that they persisted in worshipping them by day, not by night. By "devotion to them" is meant persistence in their worship. He said "to them" (lahā) to indicate that this devotion was for their sake. When they made this claim, Abraham said, drawing attention to the corruption of their position:

﴿"Do they hear you when you call?"﴾ Al-Akhfash said: there is an ellipsis here; the meaning is "Do they hear from you?" or "Do they hear your supplication?"

Qatadah read it as "hal yusmi'unakum" with a dammah on the yā', meaning "Do they make you hear their voices at the time you call upon them?"

﴿"Or do they benefit you"﴾ in any way of benefit, ﴿"or do they harm you?"﴾ That is, do they harm you if you abandon their worship? This interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir). For if they neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, there is no basis for worshipping them. When they say, "Yes, they are as such," they acknowledge that their worship of them is mere play and futility, and at that point the proof is established against them. When the Friend (al-Khalil) presented them with this decisive argument, they found no answer to it except to retreat to blind imitation (taqlid), namely that they found their fathers doing so: that is, they perform this worship of these idols while these idols possess this attribute of having no hearing, benefit, or harm. This answer is the staff upon which every helpless person leans, with which every lame person walks, by which every deceived person is deluded, and to which every person who is duped submits. For if you were to ask today those who blindly follow men, who have spread over the earth in length and breadth, and say to them, "What is the proof for your imitation of a single one of the scholars, and for taking up everything he says in religion and innovates from opinion contrary to the evidence?", they would find no answer other than this one, and would utter nothing else. They would begin enumerating for you those who preceded them in imitating this from their predecessors, and following their sayings and deeds. They have filled their hearts with awe, their minds have become too narrow to conceive the truth, and they think they are the best of the people of the earth, the most knowledgeable and the most noble. So they do not listen to a sincere advisor nor to one calling to the truth. Had they reflected, they would have found themselves in great delusion and shameful ignorance, and that they are like a blind beast, and those ancestors are like the blind who lead blind beasts, as the poet said:

"Like a blind beast whose rein is led by a blind man on the crooked, bewildering road."

So you, O one who acts by the Book and the Sunnah, free from partisanship and arbitrariness, must present to them the proofs of God and establish His demonstrations upon them. For perhaps some of them who have not had the disease of imitation firmly settled in their hearts will yield to you. As for one in whose heart this disease has become firmly rooted, even if you present to him every proof and establish every demonstration, he will lend you nothing but a deaf ear and a blind eye. But you have discharged the duty of clarification that the Qur'an made incumbent upon you, and guidance is in the hand of the Creator, the All-Knowing: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. When these imitators said this statement,

the Friend (al-Khalil) said: ﴿"Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your ancient fathers?"﴾ That is: have you looked at and reflected upon these idols you have been worshipping, which neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, so that you may know that you are in error and ignorance? Then he informed them of his disavowal of these idols that they worship.

He said: ﴿"Indeed, they are enemies to me"﴾. The meaning of their being an enemy to him, despite their being inanimate, is that if he worshipped them, they would be his enemies on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Farra' said: this is from the inverted (maqlub) construction; that is, "Indeed, I am an enemy to them, because whomever you oppose opposes you." "Enemy" (ʿaduww), like "friend" (sadiq), applies to the singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine. So said al-Farra'.

ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: whoever says "ʿaduwwat Allah" with the tā' marbutah treats it as meaning "one who opposes" (al-mu'adiyah). Whoever says "ʿaduww" for the feminine and plural treats it as meaning a relative noun (nisbah).

It has also been said that by his words ﴿"indeed, they are enemies to me"﴾ is meant their ancestors, the ancients, because of their worship of idols. This was rejected on the ground that the discourse concerns what they worshipped, not those who worship. The exception in His words ﴿"except the Lord of the worlds"﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), i.e., "but the Lord of the worlds is not like that; rather He is my protector in this world and the Hereafter."

Al-Zajjaj said: the grammarians said it is an exception not from the preceding; al-Zajjaj also permitted that it be from the preceding, on the basis that they used to worship God, Mighty and Majestic, and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disavowed what they worship except God.

Al-Jurjani said: its construction is: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your ancient fathers, except the Lord of the worlds? Indeed, they are enemies to me." He made this a case of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and made "illa" (except) mean "dun" (other than) and "siwa" (besides), like His words ﴿"They will not taste death therein except the first death"﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56], i.e., other than the first death.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the meaning is "except one who worships the Lord of the worlds."

Then he described the Lord of the worlds with His words: ﴿"Who created me, and it is He who guides me"﴾, i.e., He guides me to the interests of religion and the world.

It has been said that the relative clause is a subject (mubtada') and what follows it is its predicate, but the first view is better.

It is permissible that the relative clause be a substitute (badal) for "Lord," or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it, or that it be in the accusative by way of praise, with the implied "I mean" (aʿni) or "I praise" (amdaḥu). The Friend has described his Lord with what deserves worship on account of Him.

Creation, guidance, and provision are indicated by His words: ﴿"And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink"﴾. Repelling the harm of illness, bringing the benefit of healing, causing death and giving life, and forgiving sins are all blessings, for which the one blessed by some of them, let alone all of them, is obliged to thank the Benefactor with all kinds of thanks, the highest and most excellent of which is worship. The inclusion of these pronouns at the beginning of these clauses (p. 1060) serves to indicate that He alone is the doer of these things to the exclusion of others. He attributed illness to himself rather than to the Lord, out of courtesy toward the Lord, although illness and other things come from God, Glorified is He.

His words ﴿"Then He will give me life"﴾ mean resurrection. The omission of the yā' in these verbs is because they are the endings of verses (ru'us al-ayy).

Ibn Abi Ishaq read all these verbs with the yā' affirmed.

When Abraham, peace be upon him, said ﴿"And the One from whom I hope He will forgive my sin on the Day of Judgment"﴾, he was humbling himself. It has also been said that "hope" (tama') here means certainty with respect to himself, and means expectation with respect to others.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "khatayaya" (my sins, plural): they said his sin was not a single one.

Al-Nahhas said: khatiʾah in the sense of khataya is in the usage of the Arabs.

Mujahid said: by "his sin" he means his words ﴿"Rather, the biggest of them did it"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63], his words ﴿"Indeed, I am sick"﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his statement that Sarah was his sister. Al-Hasan added: and his words to the star, ﴿"This is my lord"﴾ [al-An'am: 77, 78]. Al-Wahidi related from the exegetes that they interpreted the sins (khataya) in the same way Mujahid did.

Al-Zajjaj said: the prophets are human, and sin may befall them, except that major sin does not come from them, because they are protected from it (ma'sum). By the Day of Religion is meant the Day of Recompense for the servants according to their deeds. It is not hidden that interpreting the sins as Mujahid and those with him mentioned is weak, for those were allusions (ma'arid), and they too came from him only after this exchange that took place between him and his people.

Then, when the Friend had finished praising his Lord and acknowledging His blessings, he followed it with supplication, so that others might follow him in that.

He said: ﴿"My Lord, grant me wisdom"﴾. By "wisdom" (hukm) is meant knowledge and understanding. It has been said: prophethood and messengership. It has also been said: knowledge of the limits of God and His rulings, and so on. ﴿"And join me with the righteous"﴾, meaning with the prophets before me. It has been said: with the people of Paradise.

﴿"And grant me a true tongue among later generations"﴾, i.e., grant me a good reputation among the later people who will come after me until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Qutaybi said: "tongue" was placed in the position of "speech" by metaphor, because speech is by means of it. The Arabs also use it as a metonym for word, and from this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"Indeed, a tongue has come to me, with which I do not keep secrets."

God, Glorified is He, has given Abraham this by His words ﴿"And We left for them among later generations"﴾ [al-Saffat: 108], since every nation adheres to him and venerates him.

Makki said: it has been said that the meaning of his request is that among his descendants at the end of time there would be someone who upholds the truth, and so his supplication was answered in Muhammad (ﷺ) and his family. But there is no basis for this specification.

Al-Qushayri said: he meant a good supplication until the Hour, and there is no basis for this either, for "a true tongue" is more general than that.

﴿"And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss"﴾. "Among the inheritors" may be a second object, or it may be an attribute of an omitted second object: i.e., an heir from among the heirs of the Garden of Bliss. When he, peace be upon him, asked in the first supplication for the happiness of this world, he asked in this supplication for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss, and he made it something inherited, to liken the spoils of the Hereafter to the spoils of this world. The meaning of inheritance has already been discussed in Surat Maryam.

﴿"And forgive my father, for he was among the misguided"﴾. His father had promised him that he would believe, so he asked forgiveness for him; but when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disavowed him. This has been explained fully in Surat al-Tawbah and Surat Maryam. The meaning of "among the misguided" is among the polytheists who strayed from the path of guidance. "Kana" here is redundant according to the view of Sibawayh, as has been mentioned in more than one place.

﴿"And do not disgrace me on the Day when they are resurrected"﴾, i.e., do not expose me before the assembled witnesses by rebuking me, or do not punish me on the Day of Resurrection, or do not disgrace me by punishing my father or by resurrecting him among the misguided. "Ikhza'" applies both to "khizy," which is humiliation, and to "khiza'," which is shame.

﴿"The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾: "the Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit" is a substitute for "the Day when they are resurrected," i.e., the Day on which neither wealth nor children will benefit any of the people, since the son is the closest kin and the most entitled to protection, aid, and benefit. If he does not benefit, then others among relatives and helpers are even less able to.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this and what follows it are from the words of God, but this is weak.

The exception in His words ﴿"except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾ has been said to be disjunctive, i.e., "but whoever comes to God with a sound heart." Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: it is "except" in the sense of the state (hal) of one who comes to God with a sound heart, supposing an omitted genitive construction (mudaf). Abu Hayyan said: there is no necessity for that.

It has also been said that this exception is a substitute for the omitted object, or an exception from it, since the implied meaning is "neither wealth nor children will benefit any of the people, except one who has this attribute." It may also be a substitute for the subject of "will benefit," in which case it is in the nominative. Abu al-Baqa' said: then the implied meaning is "except the wealth of one who, or the children of one who, for he will benefit."

There has been disagreement about the meaning of the sound heart. It has been said: it is sound from polytheism, for as for sins, no one is free from them; this was said by most of the exegetes. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: the sound heart is the healthy heart, which is the heart of the believer, for the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased. It has also been said: it is the heart free from innovation and at peace with the Sunnah. It has also been said: it is the one safe from the affliction of wealth and children.

Al-Dahhak said: "Salim" means sincere and pure.

Al-Junayd said: "Salim" in the language means "ladigh" (one who has been stung), so its meaning is that he was turned over like one stung by the fear of God, the Exalted. This is a distortion and an inversion of the meaning of the Qur'an.

Al-Razi said: The most correct of the opinions is that what is meant by it is the soundness of the soul from ignorance and vile character traits.

﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾, i.e., it will be brought close to them and made near for them, so that they may enter it.

Al-Zajjaj said: It means the nearness of their entering it and their looking at it.

﴿And Hellfire will be made manifest for the misguided﴾, i.e., it will be made visible to them. By "the misguided" is meant the disbelievers. The meaning is that it will be displayed before the believers enter it, so that the grief of the disbelievers will intensify and the joy of the believers will increase.

﴿And it will be said to them: "Where is what you used to worship besides God?"﴾ — of the idols and rivals — ﴿"Can they help you, or help themselves?"﴾ i.e., will they ward off the punishment from you, or will they defend themselves by repelling it from themselves?

All of this is rebuke and reproach directed at them. Malik ibn Dinar read "wa-barazat" (and it was made manifest) with a fatha on the ba' and the ra', making it active in form (mubayyan lil-fa'il).

﴿Then they will be thrown into it, they and the misguided,﴾ i.e., they will be cast into Hell: "they" refers to those who were worshipped, and "the misguided" refers to those who worshipped them.

It has been said: the meaning of "kubkibu" is that they were turned over onto their heads. It has also been said: some were thrown upon others. It has also been said: they were gathered together, derived from "kabkaba" (a group). This is related from al-Harawi.

Al-Nahhas said: it is derived from "kawkab al-shay'" (the bulk or main part of a thing), and a group of horses is called "kawkab" and "kabkaba". It has also been said: they were pushed down. These meanings are close to one another. Its original form is "kubbibu" with two bas', the first being doubled from two letters, and so the kaf was substituted for the middle ba'.

Al-Zajjaj preferred that the meaning is: some were cast upon others.

Ibn Qutaybah preferred that the meaning is: they were thrown on their faces.

It has been said: the pronoun in "kubkibu" refers to the Quraysh, and "the misguided" refers to the gods. By "the armies of Iblis" is meant his devils who lead the servants astray. It has been said: his offspring. It has been said: everyone who calls to the worship of idols.

"Ajma'un" (all of them) is an emphasis for the pronoun in "kubkibu" and what is conjoined to it.

The clause ﴿They will say, while they dispute therein﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What did they say when what was done to them was done?

The content of the saying is ﴿"By God, we were certainly in clear error"﴾. The clause ﴿while they dispute therein﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): i.e., they said this statement while being in Hell, disputing. The "in" in "in kunna" is the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and the lam is a distinguishing particle between it and the negating "in". That is: they said, "By God, indeed the matter is that we were in manifest, clear error." The meaning of "error" here is loss, perdition, and bewilderment from the truth. The governing element of the adverb of time, i.e., ﴿when we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds﴾, is their being in clear error.

It has been said: the governing element is the error itself. It has been said: it is what the speech indicates, as if it were said: "We were misguided at the time we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds."

The Kufans said: "in" in "in kunna" is negating, and the lam means "illa" (except), i.e., "we were only in clear error." The first is more preferable, and it is the view of the Basrans.

﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ who would intercede for us from the punishment as they do for the believers.

﴿Nor a close friend﴾ — i.e., a relative. "Hamim" is the one close to you whom you love and who loves you. The singular "sadiq" is used because it has been mentioned more than once before that it applies to the one, the two, the group, the masculine and the feminine. "Hamim" is derived from "hamimat al-rajul," i.e., his relatives. It is said: "hamma al-shay'" and "ahamma" when it drew near to him, and from this comes "al-humma" (fever), because it brings one close to the appointed term.

Ali ibn Isa said: the near relative is called "hamim" only because he protects (yahmi) out of the anger of his companion, so he derived it from "al-hamiyyah" (zeal, protectiveness).

﴿Then if only we had a return, so that we might be among the believers﴾. This is from them in the manner of wishing, which indicates the perfection of regret, as if they said: "Would that we had a return," i.e., a return to the world. The answer to the wish is ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾, i.e., that we might become part of them.

The reference in His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is to what was mentioned before of the account of Abraham. "Ayah" means lesson and sign, and the tanwin indicates magnification and grandeur. ﴿Yet most of them were not believers﴾ — i.e., most of those to whom the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, recites the account of Abraham, namely the Quraysh and whoever followed their religion. It has been said: "Most of the people of Abraham were not believers," but this is weak, because they were all non-believers.

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ — i.e., He is the Dominant over His enemies, the Merciful to His friends; or the Merciful to the enemies by delaying their punishment and not hastening it against them.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ that it means with the people of Paradise.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ that it means the agreement of the people of the religions upon Abraham.

He also related from him concerning ﴿And forgive my father﴾ that it means: bestow upon him a repentance by which he deserves Your forgiveness.

Al-Bukhari and others related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, who said: "Abraham will meet his father Azar on the Day of Resurrection, and on the face of Azar will be dust and dark gloom. Abraham will say to him: 'Did I not tell you not to disobey me?' His father will say: 'Today I will not disobey you.' Abraham will say: 'My Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected. What disgrace could be greater than my father, the most distant?' God will say: 'I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers.' Then He will say: 'O Abraham, what is under your feet?' Then he will look, and there will be a dhiykh (hyena) covered in filth; it will be seized by its legs and cast into the Fire." The dhiyk is the male of the hyenas, so it is as if Azar was transformed into the form of a dhiyk.

An-Nasa'i related it in a longer form than this.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ that it is the testimony that there is no god but God.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿So they will be thrown into it﴾ that it means they were gathered therein, ﴿they and the misguided﴾ — the polytheists of the Arabs and the gods.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him regarding ﴿Then if only we had a return﴾ that it means a return to the world, ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾ — so that intercession might become lawful for us as it became lawful for these (people).

(p. 1059) His words, ﴿And recite to them﴾, are conjoined to the governing element in His words, ﴿And when your Lord called Moses﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 10], which has already been discussed. By "the news of Abraham" is meant his account, i.e., "Recite to them, O Muhammad, the account and story of Abraham."

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the meaning is "except one who worships the Lord of the worlds."

Then he described the Lord of the worlds with His words: ﴿"Who created me, and it is He who guides me"﴾, i.e., He guides me to the interests of religion and the world.

It has been said that the relative clause is a subject (mubtada') and what follows it is its predicate, but the first view is better.

It is permissible that the relative clause be a substitute (badal) for "Lord," or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it, or that it be in the accusative by way of praise, with the implied "I mean" (aʿni) or "I praise" (amdaḥu). The Friend has described his Lord with what deserves worship on account of Him.

Creation, guidance, and provision are indicated by His words: ﴿"And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink"﴾. Repelling the harm of illness, bringing the benefit of healing, causing death and giving life, and forgiving sins are all blessings, for which the one blessed by some of them, let alone all of them, is obliged to thank the Benefactor with all kinds of thanks, the highest and most excellent of which is worship. The inclusion of these pronouns at the beginning of these clauses (p. 1060) serves to indicate that He alone is the doer of these things to the exclusion of others. He attributed illness to himself rather than to the Lord, out of courtesy toward the Lord, although illness and other things come from God, Glorified is He.

His words ﴿"Then He will give me life"﴾ mean resurrection. The omission of the yā' in these verbs is because they are the endings of verses (ru'us al-ayy).

Ibn Abi Ishaq read all these verbs with the yā' affirmed.

When Abraham, peace be upon him, said ﴿"And the One from whom I hope He will forgive my sin on the Day of Judgment"﴾, he was humbling himself. It has also been said that "hope" (tama') here means certainty with respect to himself, and means expectation with respect to others.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "khatayaya" (my sins, plural): they said his sin was not a single one.

Al-Nahhas said: khatiʾah in the sense of khataya is in the usage of the Arabs.

Mujahid said: by "his sin" he means his words ﴿"Rather, the biggest of them did it"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63], his words ﴿"Indeed, I am sick"﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his statement that Sarah was his sister. Al-Hasan added: and his words to the star, ﴿"This is my lord"﴾ [al-An'am: 77, 78]. Al-Wahidi related from the exegetes that they interpreted the sins (khataya) in the same way Mujahid did.

Al-Zajjaj said: the prophets are human, and sin may befall them, except that major sin does not come from them, because they are protected from it (ma'sum). By the Day of Religion is meant the Day of Recompense for the servants according to their deeds. It is not hidden that interpreting the sins as Mujahid and those with him mentioned is weak, for those were allusions (ma'arid), and they too came from him only after this exchange that took place between him and his people.

Then, when the Friend had finished praising his Lord and acknowledging His blessings, he followed it with supplication, so that others might follow him in that.

He said: ﴿"My Lord, grant me wisdom"﴾. By "wisdom" (hukm) is meant knowledge and understanding. It has been said: prophethood and messengership. It has also been said: knowledge of the limits of God and His rulings, and so on. ﴿"And join me with the righteous"﴾, meaning with the prophets before me. It has been said: with the people of Paradise.

﴿"And grant me a true tongue among later generations"﴾, i.e., grant me a good reputation among the later people who will come after me until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Qutaybi said: "tongue" was placed in the position of "speech" by metaphor, because speech is by means of it. The Arabs also use it as a metonym for word, and from this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"Indeed, a tongue has come to me, with which I do not keep secrets."

God, Glorified is He, has given Abraham this by His words ﴿"And We left for them among later generations"﴾ [al-Saffat: 108], since every nation adheres to him and venerates him.

Makki said: it has been said that the meaning of his request is that among his descendants at the end of time there would be someone who upholds the truth, and so his supplication was answered in Muhammad (ﷺ) and his family. But there is no basis for this specification.

Al-Qushayri said: he meant a good supplication until the Hour, and there is no basis for this either, for "a true tongue" is more general than that.

﴿"And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss"﴾. "Among the inheritors" may be a second object, or it may be an attribute of an omitted second object: i.e., an heir from among the heirs of the Garden of Bliss. When he, peace be upon him, asked in the first supplication for the happiness of this world, he asked in this supplication for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss, and he made it something inherited, to liken the spoils of the Hereafter to the spoils of this world. The meaning of inheritance has already been discussed in Surat Maryam.

﴿"And forgive my father, for he was among the misguided"﴾. His father had promised him that he would believe, so he asked forgiveness for him; but when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disavowed him. This has been explained fully in Surat al-Tawbah and Surat Maryam. The meaning of "among the misguided" is among the polytheists who strayed from the path of guidance. "Kana" here is redundant according to the view of Sibawayh, as has been mentioned in more than one place.

﴿"And do not disgrace me on the Day when they are resurrected"﴾, i.e., do not expose me before the assembled witnesses by rebuking me, or do not punish me on the Day of Resurrection, or do not disgrace me by punishing my father or by resurrecting him among the misguided. "Ikhza'" applies both to "khizy," which is humiliation, and to "khiza'," which is shame.

﴿"The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾: "the Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit" is a substitute for "the Day when they are resurrected," i.e., the Day on which neither wealth nor children will benefit any of the people, since the son is the closest kin and the most entitled to protection, aid, and benefit. If he does not benefit, then others among relatives and helpers are even less able to.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this and what follows it are from the words of God, but this is weak.

The exception in His words ﴿"except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾ has been said to be disjunctive, i.e., "but whoever comes to God with a sound heart." Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: it is "except" in the sense of the state (hal) of one who comes to God with a sound heart, supposing an omitted genitive construction (mudaf). Abu Hayyan said: there is no necessity for that.

It has also been said that this exception is a substitute for the omitted object, or an exception from it, since the implied meaning is "neither wealth nor children will benefit any of the people, except one who has this attribute." It may also be a substitute for the subject of "will benefit," in which case it is in the nominative. Abu al-Baqa' said: then the implied meaning is "except the wealth of one who, or the children of one who, for he will benefit."

There has been disagreement about the meaning of the sound heart. It has been said: it is sound from polytheism, for as for sins, no one is free from them; this was said by most of the exegetes. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: the sound heart is the healthy heart, which is the heart of the believer, for the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased. It has also been said: it is the heart free from innovation and at peace with the Sunnah. It has also been said: it is the one safe from the affliction of wealth and children.

Al-Dahhak said: "Salim" means sincere and pure.

Al-Junayd said: "Salim" in the language means "ladigh" (one who has been stung), so its meaning is that he was turned over like one stung by the fear of God, the Exalted. This is a distortion and an inversion of the meaning of the Qur'an.

Al-Razi said: The most correct of the opinions is that what is meant by it is the soundness of the soul from ignorance and vile character traits.

﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾, i.e., it will be brought close to them and made near for them, so that they may enter it.

Al-Zajjaj said: It means the nearness of their entering it and their looking at it.

﴿And Hellfire will be made manifest for the misguided﴾, i.e., it will be made visible to them. By "the misguided" is meant the disbelievers. The meaning is that it will be displayed before the believers enter it, so that the grief of the disbelievers will intensify and the joy of the believers will increase.

﴿And it will be said to them: "Where is what you used to worship besides God?"﴾ — of the idols and rivals — ﴿"Can they help you, or help themselves?"﴾ i.e., will they ward off the punishment from you, or will they defend themselves by repelling it from themselves?

All of this is rebuke and reproach directed at them. Malik ibn Dinar read "wa-barazat" (and it was made manifest) with a fatha on the ba' and the ra', making it active in form (mubayyan lil-fa'il).

﴿Then they will be thrown into it, they and the misguided,﴾ i.e., they will be cast into Hell: "they" refers to those who were worshipped, and "the misguided" refers to those who worshipped them.

It has been said: the meaning of "kubkibu" is that they were turned over onto their heads. It has also been said: some were thrown upon others. It has also been said: they were gathered together, derived from "kabkaba" (a group). This is related from al-Harawi.

Al-Nahhas said: it is derived from "kawkab al-shay'" (the bulk or main part of a thing), and a group of horses is called "kawkab" and "kabkaba". It has also been said: they were pushed down. These meanings are close to one another. Its original form is "kubbibu" with two bas', the first being doubled from two letters, and so the kaf was substituted for the middle ba'.

Al-Zajjaj preferred that the meaning is: some were cast upon others.

Ibn Qutaybah preferred that the meaning is: they were thrown on their faces.

It has been said: the pronoun in "kubkibu" refers to the Quraysh, and "the misguided" refers to the gods. By "the armies of Iblis" is meant his devils who lead the servants astray. It has been said: his offspring. It has been said: everyone who calls to the worship of idols.

"Ajma'un" (all of them) is an emphasis for the pronoun in "kubkibu" and what is conjoined to it.

The clause ﴿They will say, while they dispute therein﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What did they say when what was done to them was done?

The content of the saying is ﴿"By God, we were certainly in clear error"﴾. The clause ﴿while they dispute therein﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): i.e., they said this statement while being in Hell, disputing. The "in" in "in kunna" is the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and the lam is a distinguishing particle between it and the negating "in". That is: they said, "By God, indeed the matter is that we were in manifest, clear error." The meaning of "error" here is loss, perdition, and bewilderment from the truth. The governing element of the adverb of time, i.e., ﴿when we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds﴾, is their being in clear error.

It has been said: the governing element is the error itself. It has been said: it is what the speech indicates, as if it were said: "We were misguided at the time we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds."

The Kufans said: "in" in "in kunna" is negating, and the lam means "illa" (except), i.e., "we were only in clear error." The first is more preferable, and it is the view of the Basrans.

﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ who would intercede for us from the punishment as they do for the believers.

﴿Nor a close friend﴾ — i.e., a relative. "Hamim" is the one close to you whom you love and who loves you. The singular "sadiq" is used because it has been mentioned more than once before that it applies to the one, the two, the group, the masculine and the feminine. "Hamim" is derived from "hamimat al-rajul," i.e., his relatives. It is said: "hamma al-shay'" and "ahamma" when it drew near to him, and from this comes "al-humma" (fever), because it brings one close to the appointed term.

Ali ibn Isa said: the near relative is called "hamim" only because he protects (yahmi) out of the anger of his companion, so he derived it from "al-hamiyyah" (zeal, protectiveness).

﴿Then if only we had a return, so that we might be among the believers﴾. This is from them in the manner of wishing, which indicates the perfection of regret, as if they said: "Would that we had a return," i.e., a return to the world. The answer to the wish is ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾, i.e., that we might become part of them.

The reference in His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is to what was mentioned before of the account of Abraham. "Ayah" means lesson and sign, and the tanwin indicates magnification and grandeur. ﴿Yet most of them were not believers﴾ — i.e., most of those to whom the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, recites the account of Abraham, namely the Quraysh and whoever followed their religion. It has been said: "Most of the people of Abraham were not believers," but this is weak, because they were all non-believers.

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ — i.e., He is the Dominant over His enemies, the Merciful to His friends; or the Merciful to the enemies by delaying their punishment and not hastening it against them.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ that it means with the people of Paradise.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ that it means the agreement of the people of the religions upon Abraham.

He also related from him concerning ﴿And forgive my father﴾ that it means: bestow upon him a repentance by which he deserves Your forgiveness.

Al-Bukhari and others related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, who said: "Abraham will meet his father Azar on the Day of Resurrection, and on the face of Azar will be dust and dark gloom. Abraham will say to him: 'Did I not tell you not to disobey me?' His father will say: 'Today I will not disobey you.' Abraham will say: 'My Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected. What disgrace could be greater than my father, the most distant?' God will say: 'I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers.' Then He will say: 'O Abraham, what is under your feet?' Then he will look, and there will be a dhiykh (hyena) covered in filth; it will be seized by its legs and cast into the Fire." The dhiyk is the male of the hyenas, so it is as if Azar was transformed into the form of a dhiyk.

An-Nasa'i related it in a longer form than this.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ that it is the testimony that there is no god but God.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿So they will be thrown into it﴾ that it means they were gathered therein, ﴿they and the misguided﴾ — the polytheists of the Arabs and the gods.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him regarding ﴿Then if only we had a return﴾ that it means a return to the world, ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾ — so that intercession might become lawful for us as it became lawful for these (people).

(p. 1059) His words, ﴿And recite to them﴾, are conjoined to the governing element in His words, ﴿And when your Lord called Moses﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 10], which has already been discussed. By "the news of Abraham" is meant his account, i.e., "Recite to them, O Muhammad, the account and story of Abraham."

The clause ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "the news of Abraham," i.e., "at the time he said." It has also been said that "when" (idh) is a substitute (badal) for "news," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), so that the governing element would be "recite." The first view is the better one.

The meaning of "What do you worship?" is "What thing do you worship?" He knew that they worshipped idols, but he intended to impose the proof upon them.

﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ That is, we continue to maintain their worship constantly, not at a specific time. It is said: "zalla yaf'alu kadhā" means he does such-and-such during the day, and "bāta yaf'alu kadhā" means he does it during the night. The apparent meaning is that they persisted in worshipping them by day, not by night. By "devotion to them" is meant persistence in their worship. He said "to them" (lahā) to indicate that this devotion was for their sake. When they made this claim, Abraham said, drawing attention to the corruption of their position:

﴿"Do they hear you when you call?"﴾ Al-Akhfash said: there is an ellipsis here; the meaning is "Do they hear from you?" or "Do they hear your supplication?"

Qatadah read it as "hal yusmi'unakum" with a dammah on the yā', meaning "Do they make you hear their voices at the time you call upon them?"

﴿"Or do they benefit you"﴾ in any way of benefit, ﴿"or do they harm you?"﴾ That is, do they harm you if you abandon their worship? This interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir). For if they neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, there is no basis for worshipping them. When they say, "Yes, they are as such," they acknowledge that their worship of them is mere play and futility, and at that point the proof is established against them. When the Friend (al-Khalil) presented them with this decisive argument, they found no answer to it except to retreat to blind imitation (taqlid), namely that they found their fathers doing so: that is, they perform this worship of these idols while these idols possess this attribute of having no hearing, benefit, or harm. This answer is the staff upon which every helpless person leans, with which every lame person walks, by which every deceived person is deluded, and to which every person who is duped submits. For if you were to ask today those who blindly follow men, who have spread over the earth in length and breadth, and say to them, "What is the proof for your imitation of a single one of the scholars, and for taking up everything he says in religion and innovates from opinion contrary to the evidence?", they would find no answer other than this one, and would utter nothing else. They would begin enumerating for you those who preceded them in imitating this from their predecessors, and following their sayings and deeds. They have filled their hearts with awe, their minds have become too narrow to conceive the truth, and they think they are the best of the people of the earth, the most knowledgeable and the most noble. So they do not listen to a sincere advisor nor to one calling to the truth. Had they reflected, they would have found themselves in great delusion and shameful ignorance, and that they are like a blind beast, and those ancestors are like the blind who lead blind beasts, as the poet said:

"Like a blind beast whose rein is led by a blind man on the crooked, bewildering road."

So you, O one who acts by the Book and the Sunnah, free from partisanship and arbitrariness, must present to them the proofs of God and establish His demonstrations upon them. For perhaps some of them who have not had the disease of imitation firmly settled in their hearts will yield to you. As for one in whose heart this disease has become firmly rooted, even if you present to him every proof and establish every demonstration, he will lend you nothing but a deaf ear and a blind eye. But you have discharged the duty of clarification that the Qur'an made incumbent upon you, and guidance is in the hand of the Creator, the All-Knowing: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. When these imitators said this statement,

the Friend (al-Khalil) said: ﴿"Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your ancient fathers?"﴾ That is: have you looked at and reflected upon these idols you have been worshipping, which neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, so that you may know that you are in error and ignorance? Then he informed them of his disavowal of these idols that they worship.

He said: ﴿"Indeed, they are enemies to me"﴾. The meaning of their being an enemy to him, despite their being inanimate, is that if he worshipped them, they would be his enemies on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Farra' said: this is from the inverted (maqlub) construction; that is, "Indeed, I am an enemy to them, because whomever you oppose opposes you." "Enemy" (ʿaduww), like "friend" (sadiq), applies to the singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine. So said al-Farra'.

ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: whoever says "ʿaduwwat Allah" with the tā' marbutah treats it as meaning "one who opposes" (al-mu'adiyah). Whoever says "ʿaduww" for the feminine and plural treats it as meaning a relative noun (nisbah).

It has also been said that by his words ﴿"indeed, they are enemies to me"﴾ is meant their ancestors, the ancients, because of their worship of idols. This was rejected on the ground that the discourse concerns what they worshipped, not those who worship. The exception in His words ﴿"except the Lord of the worlds"﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), i.e., "but the Lord of the worlds is not like that; rather He is my protector in this world and the Hereafter."

Al-Zajjaj said: the grammarians said it is an exception not from the preceding; al-Zajjaj also permitted that it be from the preceding, on the basis that they used to worship God, Mighty and Majestic, and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disavowed what they worship except God.

Al-Jurjani said: its construction is: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your ancient fathers, except the Lord of the worlds? Indeed, they are enemies to me." He made this a case of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and made "illa" (except) mean "dun" (other than) and "siwa" (besides), like His words ﴿"They will not taste death therein except the first death"﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56], i.e., other than the first death.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the meaning is "except one who worships the Lord of the worlds."

Then he described the Lord of the worlds with His words: ﴿"Who created me, and it is He who guides me"﴾, i.e., He guides me to the interests of religion and the world.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this and what follows it are from the words of God, but this is weak.

The exception in His words ﴿"except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾ has been said to be disjunctive, i.e., "but whoever comes to God with a sound heart." Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: it is "except" in the sense of the state (hal) of one who comes to God with a sound heart, supposing an omitted genitive construction (mudaf). Abu Hayyan said: there is no necessity for that.

It has also been said that this exception is a substitute for the omitted object, or an exception from it, since the implied meaning is "neither wealth nor children will benefit any of the people, except one who has this attribute." It may also be a substitute for the subject of "will benefit," in which case it is in the nominative. Abu al-Baqa' said: then the implied meaning is "except the wealth of one who, or the children of one who, for he will benefit."

There has been disagreement about the meaning of the sound heart. It has been said: it is sound from polytheism, for as for sins, no one is free from them; this was said by most of the exegetes. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: the sound heart is the healthy heart, which is the heart of the believer, for the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased. It has also been said: it is the heart free from innovation and at peace with the Sunnah. It has also been said: it is the one safe from the affliction of wealth and children.

Al-Dahhak said: "Salim" means sincere and pure.

Al-Junayd said: "Salim" in the language means "ladigh" (one who has been stung), so its meaning is that he was turned over like one stung by the fear of God, the Exalted. This is a distortion and an inversion of the meaning of the Qur'an.

Al-Razi said: The most correct of the opinions is that what is meant by it is the soundness of the soul from ignorance and vile character traits.

﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾, i.e., it will be brought close to them and made near for them, so that they may enter it.

Al-Zajjaj said: It means the nearness of their entering it and their looking at it.

﴿And Hellfire will be made manifest for the misguided﴾, i.e., it will be made visible to them. By "the misguided" is meant the disbelievers. The meaning is that it will be displayed before the believers enter it, so that the grief of the disbelievers will intensify and the joy of the believers will increase.

﴿And it will be said to them: "Where is what you used to worship besides God?"﴾ — of the idols and rivals — ﴿"Can they help you, or help themselves?"﴾ i.e., will they ward off the punishment from you, or will they defend themselves by repelling it from themselves?

All of this is rebuke and reproach directed at them. Malik ibn Dinar read "wa-barazat" (and it was made manifest) with a fatha on the ba' and the ra', making it active in form (mubayyan lil-fa'il).

﴿Then they will be thrown into it, they and the misguided,﴾ i.e., they will be cast into Hell: "they" refers to those who were worshipped, and "the misguided" refers to those who worshipped them.

It has been said: the meaning of "kubkibu" is that they were turned over onto their heads. It has also been said: some were thrown upon others. It has also been said: they were gathered together, derived from "kabkaba" (a group). This is related from al-Harawi.

Al-Nahhas said: it is derived from "kawkab al-shay'" (the bulk or main part of a thing), and a group of horses is called "kawkab" and "kabkaba". It has also been said: they were pushed down. These meanings are close to one another. Its original form is "kubbibu" with two bas', the first being doubled from two letters, and so the kaf was substituted for the middle ba'.

Al-Zajjaj preferred that the meaning is: some were cast upon others.

Ibn Qutaybah preferred that the meaning is: they were thrown on their faces.

It has been said: the pronoun in "kubkibu" refers to the Quraysh, and "the misguided" refers to the gods. By "the armies of Iblis" is meant his devils who lead the servants astray. It has been said: his offspring. It has been said: everyone who calls to the worship of idols.

"Ajma'un" (all of them) is an emphasis for the pronoun in "kubkibu" and what is conjoined to it.

The clause ﴿They will say, while they dispute therein﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What did they say when what was done to them was done?

The content of the saying is ﴿"By God, we were certainly in clear error"﴾. The clause ﴿while they dispute therein﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): i.e., they said this statement while being in Hell, disputing. The "in" in "in kunna" is the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and the lam is a distinguishing particle between it and the negating "in". That is: they said, "By God, indeed the matter is that we were in manifest, clear error." The meaning of "error" here is loss, perdition, and bewilderment from the truth. The governing element of the adverb of time, i.e., ﴿when we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds﴾, is their being in clear error.

It has been said: the governing element is the error itself. It has been said: it is what the speech indicates, as if it were said: "We were misguided at the time we made you equal with the Lord of the worlds."

The Kufans said: "in" in "in kunna" is negating, and the lam means "illa" (except), i.e., "we were only in clear error." The first is more preferable, and it is the view of the Basrans.

﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ who would intercede for us from the punishment as they do for the believers.

﴿Nor a close friend﴾ — i.e., a relative. "Hamim" is the one close to you whom you love and who loves you. The singular "sadiq" is used because it has been mentioned more than once before that it applies to the one, the two, the group, the masculine and the feminine. "Hamim" is derived from "hamimat al-rajul," i.e., his relatives. It is said: "hamma al-shay'" and "ahamma" when it drew near to him, and from this comes "al-humma" (fever), because it brings one close to the appointed term.

Ali ibn Isa said: the near relative is called "hamim" only because he protects (yahmi) out of the anger of his companion, so he derived it from "al-hamiyyah" (zeal, protectiveness).

﴿Then if only we had a return, so that we might be among the believers﴾. This is from them in the manner of wishing, which indicates the perfection of regret, as if they said: "Would that we had a return," i.e., a return to the world. The answer to the wish is ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾, i.e., that we might become part of them.

The reference in His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ is to what was mentioned before of the account of Abraham. "Ayah" means lesson and sign, and the tanwin indicates magnification and grandeur. ﴿Yet most of them were not believers﴾ — i.e., most of those to whom the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, recites the account of Abraham, namely the Quraysh and whoever followed their religion. It has been said: "Most of the people of Abraham were not believers," but this is weak, because they were all non-believers.

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ — i.e., He is the Dominant over His enemies, the Merciful to His friends; or the Merciful to the enemies by delaying their punishment and not hastening it against them.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ that it means with the people of Paradise.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying ﴿And make for me a tongue of truth among the later generations﴾ that it means the agreement of the people of the religions upon Abraham.

He also related from him concerning ﴿And forgive my father﴾ that it means: bestow upon him a repentance by which he deserves Your forgiveness.

Al-Bukhari and others related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, who said: "Abraham will meet his father Azar on the Day of Resurrection, and on the face of Azar will be dust and dark gloom. Abraham will say to him: 'Did I not tell you not to disobey me?' His father will say: 'Today I will not disobey you.' Abraham will say: 'My Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected. What disgrace could be greater than my father, the most distant?' God will say: 'I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers.' Then He will say: 'O Abraham, what is under your feet?' Then he will look, and there will be a dhiykh (hyena) covered in filth; it will be seized by its legs and cast into the Fire." The dhiyk is the male of the hyenas, so it is as if Azar was transformed into the form of a dhiyk.

An-Nasa'i related it in a longer form than this.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ that it is the testimony that there is no god but God.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿So they will be thrown into it﴾ that it means they were gathered therein, ﴿they and the misguided﴾ — the polytheists of the Arabs and the gods.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him regarding ﴿Then if only we had a return﴾ that it means a return to the world, ﴿so that we might be among the believers﴾ — so that intercession might become lawful for us as it became lawful for these (people).

(p. 1059) His words, ﴿And recite to them﴾, are conjoined to the governing element in His words, ﴿And when your Lord called Moses﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 10], which has already been discussed. By "the news of Abraham" is meant his account, i.e., "Recite to them, O Muhammad, the account and story of Abraham."

The clause ﴿when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "the news of Abraham," i.e., "at the time he said." It has also been said that "when" (idh) is a substitute (badal) for "news," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), so that the governing element would be "recite." The first view is the better one.

The meaning of "What do you worship?" is "What thing do you worship?" He knew that they worshipped idols, but he intended to impose the proof upon them.

﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ That is, we continue to maintain their worship constantly, not at a specific time. It is said: "zalla yaf'alu kadhā" means he does such-and-such during the day, and "bāta yaf'alu kadhā" means he does it during the night. The apparent meaning is that they persisted in worshipping them by day, not by night. By "devotion to them" is meant persistence in their worship. He said "to them" (lahā) to indicate that this devotion was for their sake. When they made this claim, Abraham said, drawing attention to the corruption of their position:

﴿"Do they hear you when you call?"﴾ Al-Akhfash said: there is an ellipsis here; the meaning is "Do they hear from you?" or "Do they hear your supplication?"

Qatadah read it as "hal yusmi'unakum" with a dammah on the yā', meaning "Do they make you hear their voices at the time you call upon them?"

﴿"Or do they benefit you"﴾ in any way of benefit, ﴿"or do they harm you?"﴾ That is, do they harm you if you abandon their worship? This interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir). For if they neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, there is no basis for worshipping them. When they say, "Yes, they are as such," they acknowledge that their worship of them is mere play and futility, and at that point the proof is established against them. When the Friend (al-Khalil) presented them with this decisive argument, they found no answer to it except to retreat to blind imitation (taqlid), namely that they found their fathers doing so: that is, they perform this worship of these idols while these idols possess this attribute of having no hearing, benefit, or harm. This answer is the staff upon which every helpless person leans, with which every lame person walks, by which every deceived person is deluded, and to which every person who is duped submits. For if you were to ask today those who blindly follow men, who have spread over the earth in length and breadth, and say to them, "What is the proof for your imitation of a single one of the scholars, and for taking up everything he says in religion and innovates from opinion contrary to the evidence?", they would find no answer other than this one, and would utter nothing else. They would begin enumerating for you those who preceded them in imitating this from their predecessors, and following their sayings and deeds. They have filled their hearts with awe, their minds have become too narrow to conceive the truth, and they think they are the best of the people of the earth, the most knowledgeable and the most noble. So they do not listen to a sincere advisor nor to one calling to the truth. Had they reflected, they would have found themselves in great delusion and shameful ignorance, and that they are like a blind beast, and those ancestors are like the blind who lead blind beasts, as the poet said:

"Like a blind beast whose rein is led by a blind man on the crooked, bewildering road."

So you, O one who acts by the Book and the Sunnah, free from partisanship and arbitrariness, must present to them the proofs of God and establish His demonstrations upon them. For perhaps some of them who have not had the disease of imitation firmly settled in their hearts will yield to you. As for one in whose heart this disease has become firmly rooted, even if you present to him every proof and establish every demonstration, he will lend you nothing but a deaf ear and a blind eye. But you have discharged the duty of clarification that the Qur'an made incumbent upon you, and guidance is in the hand of the Creator, the All-Knowing: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. When these imitators said this statement,

the Friend (al-Khalil) said: ﴿"Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your ancient fathers?"﴾ That is: have you looked at and reflected upon these idols you have been worshipping, which neither hear, nor benefit, nor harm, so that you may know that you are in error and ignorance? Then he informed them of his disavowal of these idols that they worship.

He said: ﴿"Indeed, they are enemies to me"﴾. The meaning of their being an enemy to him, despite their being inanimate, is that if he worshipped them, they would be his enemies on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Farra' said: this is from the inverted (maqlub) construction; that is, "Indeed, I am an enemy to them, because whomever you oppose opposes you." "Enemy" (ʿaduww), like "friend" (sadiq), applies to the singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine. So said al-Farra'.

ʿAli ibn Sulayman said: whoever says "ʿaduwwat Allah" with the tā' marbutah treats it as meaning "one who opposes" (al-mu'adiyah). Whoever says "ʿaduww" for the feminine and plural treats it as meaning a relative noun (nisbah).

It has also been said that by his words ﴿"indeed, they are enemies to me"﴾ is meant their ancestors, the ancients, because of their worship of idols. This was rejected on the ground that the discourse concerns what they worshipped, not those who worship. The exception in His words ﴿"except the Lord of the worlds"﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), i.e., "but the Lord of the worlds is not like that; rather He is my protector in this world and the Hereafter."

Al-Zajjaj said: the grammarians said it is an exception not from the preceding; al-Zajjaj also permitted that it be from the preceding, on the basis that they used to worship God, Mighty and Majestic, and worship idols alongside Him; so He informed them that he disavowed what they worship except God.

Al-Jurjani said: its construction is: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your ancient fathers, except the Lord of the worlds? Indeed, they are enemies to me." He made this a case of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and made "illa" (except) mean "dun" (other than) and "siwa" (besides), like His words ﴿"They will not taste death therein except the first death"﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56], i.e., other than the first death.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the meaning is "except one who worships the Lord of the worlds."

Then he described the Lord of the worlds with His words: ﴿"Who created me, and it is He who guides me"﴾, i.e., He guides me to the interests of religion and the world.

It has been said that the relative clause is a subject (mubtada') and what follows it is its predicate, but the first view is better.

It is permissible that the relative clause be a substitute (badal) for "Lord," or an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it, or that it be in the accusative by way of praise, with the implied "I mean" (aʿni) or "I praise" (amdaḥu). The Friend has described his Lord with what deserves worship on account of Him.

Creation, guidance, and provision are indicated by His words: ﴿"And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink"﴾. Repelling the harm of illness, bringing the benefit of healing, causing death and giving life, and forgiving sins are all blessings, for which the one blessed by some of them, let alone all of them, is obliged to thank the Benefactor with all kinds of thanks, the highest and most excellent of which is worship. The inclusion of these pronouns at the beginning of these clauses (p. 1060) serves to indicate that He alone is the doer of these things to the exclusion of others. He attributed illness to himself rather than to the Lord, out of courtesy toward the Lord, although illness and other things come from God, Glorified is He.

His words ﴿"Then He will give me life"﴾ mean resurrection. The omission of the yā' in these verbs is because they are the endings of verses (ru'us al-ayy).

Ibn Abi Ishaq read all these verbs with the yā' affirmed.

When Abraham, peace be upon him, said ﴿"And the One from whom I hope He will forgive my sin on the Day of Judgment"﴾, he was humbling himself. It has also been said that "hope" (tama') here means certainty with respect to himself, and means expectation with respect to others.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "khatayaya" (my sins, plural): they said his sin was not a single one.

Al-Nahhas said: khatiʾah in the sense of khataya is in the usage of the Arabs.

Mujahid said: by "his sin" he means his words ﴿"Rather, the biggest of them did it"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63], his words ﴿"Indeed, I am sick"﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his statement that Sarah was his sister. Al-Hasan added: and his words to the star, ﴿"This is my lord"﴾ [al-An'am: 77, 78]. Al-Wahidi related from the exegetes that they interpreted the sins (khataya) in the same way Mujahid did.

Al-Zajjaj said: the prophets are human, and sin may befall them, except that major sin does not come from them, because they are protected from it (ma'sum). By the Day of Religion is meant the Day of Recompense for the servants according to their deeds. It is not hidden that interpreting the sins as Mujahid and those with him mentioned is weak, for those were allusions (ma'arid), and they too came from him only after this exchange that took place between him and his people.

Then, when the Friend had finished praising his Lord and acknowledging His blessings, he followed it with supplication, so that others might follow him in that.

He said: ﴿"My Lord, grant me wisdom"﴾. By "wisdom" (hukm) is meant knowledge and understanding. It has been said: prophethood and messengership. It has also been said: knowledge of the limits of God and His rulings, and so on. ﴿"And join me with the righteous"﴾, meaning with the prophets before me. It has been said: with the people of Paradise.

﴿"And grant me a true tongue among later generations"﴾, i.e., grant me a good reputation among the later people who will come after me until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Qutaybi said: "tongue" was placed in the position of "speech" by metaphor, because speech is by means of it. The Arabs also use it as a metonym for word, and from this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"Indeed, a tongue has come to me, with which I do not keep secrets."

God, Glorified is He, has given Abraham this by His words ﴿"And We left for them among later generations"﴾ [al-Saffat: 108], since every nation adheres to him and venerates him.

Makki said: it has been said that the meaning of his request is that among his descendants at the end of time there would be someone who upholds the truth, and so his supplication was answered in Muhammad (ﷺ) and his family. But there is no basis for this specification.

Al-Qushayri said: he meant a good supplication until the Hour, and there is no basis for this either, for "a true tongue" is more general than that.

﴿"And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss"﴾. "Among the inheritors" may be a second object, or it may be an attribute of an omitted second object: i.e., an heir from among the heirs of the Garden of Bliss. When he, peace be upon him, asked in the first supplication for the happiness of this world, he asked in this supplication for the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss, and he made it something inherited, to liken the spoils of the Hereafter to the spoils of this world. The meaning of inheritance has already been discussed in Surat Maryam.

﴿"And forgive my father, for he was among the misguided"﴾. His father had promised him that he would believe, so he asked forgiveness for him; but when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disavowed him. This has been explained fully in Surat al-Tawbah and Surat Maryam. The meaning of "among the misguided" is among the polytheists who strayed from the path of guidance. "Kana" here is redundant according to the view of Sibawayh, as has been mentioned in more than one place.

﴿"And do not disgrace me on the Day when they are resurrected"﴾, i.e., do not expose me before the assembled witnesses by rebuking me, or do not punish me on the Day of Resurrection, or do not disgrace me by punishing my father or by resurrecting him among the misguided. "Ikhza'" applies both to "khizy," which is humiliation, and to "khiza'," which is shame.

﴿"The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾: "the Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit" is a substitute for "the Day when they are resurrected," i.e., the Day on which neither wealth nor children will benefit any of the people, since the son is the closest kin and the most entitled to protection, aid, and benefit. If he does not benefit, then others among relatives and helpers are even less able to.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this and what follows it are from the words of God, but this is weak.

The exception in His words ﴿"except one who comes to God with a sound heart"﴾ has been said to be disjunctive, i.e., "but whoever comes to God with a sound heart." Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, said: it is "except" in the sense of the state (hal) of one who comes to God with a sound heart, supposing an omitted genitive construction (mudaf). Abu Hayyan said: there is no necessity for that.

It may also be a substitute for the subject of "will benefit," in which case it is in the nominative. Abu al-Baqa' said: then the implied meaning is "except the wealth of one who, or the children of one who, for he will benefit."

There has been disagreement about the meaning of the sound heart. It has been said: it is sound from polytheism, for as for sins, no one is free from them; this was said by most of the exegetes. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: the sound heart is the healthy heart, which is the heart of the believer, for the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite is diseased. It has also been said: it is the heart free from innovation and at peace with the Sunnah. It has also been said: it is the one safe from the affliction of wealth and children.

﴿And Paradise will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾, i.e., it will be brought close to them and made near for them, so that they may enter it.

Al-Zajjaj said: It means the nearness of their entering it and their looking at it.
